case40v1-exp.hypothesis:
Dishaank Technologies: Test 41

A case for discussion. Kochi, Bengaluru, Pune, Berlin, Toronto, Singapore, New Jersey and Dubai, October 2026.

1. Sunday night, 11 October 2026

The flat in Panampilly Nagar was quiet enough that Lavanthi Thottappilly could hear a ferry horn off the backwaters. The first of two open documents was a board paper her chief executive wanted by nine next morning, Monday 12 October, for the product and risk committee sitting on Thursday the 15th; it asked the committee for ₹2.60 crore to rebuild onboarding across Android, iOS, web and the partner rails over the four quarters to September 2027. The second was one sentence from a template, typed in April: Goal-first onboarding will raise activation among new investors.

Everything in the paper rested on Test 41, the experiment that sentence produced. The readout filed in August had been read as a win, as a small win and as a muddle, by three people in that order. On 2 September an engineer found something in a release log that the readout had not accounted for. On 24 September a partner in Dubai sent a dictionary that made an April slide mean something else. She had until morning to say what Test 41 had measured.

2. Dishaank, 2019–2026

Dishaank Technologies Private Limited was registered in Kochi in 2019 by Lakshman Thingalaya, who grew up in Mangaluru building payment switches, and Lohitesh Thachankary, who runs engineering from Pune. The product is a mutual-fund investing app for people who would rather not read English: goal to mandate in seven Indian languages. Dishaank holds an AMFI registration number as a distributor and no SEBI investment-adviser licence, and the gap between the two has bounded the company's design arguments ever since.

By March 2026 the app carried ₹4,180 crore of assets under distribution; 14.80 lakh people had started a systematic investment plan through it and 9.2 lakh held a live mandate. FY2025–26 revenue was ₹38.60 crore, ₹8.40 crore of it from licensing the onboarding stack, Dishaank Rails, to partners abroad.

What shapes October 2026 was settled in 2021. Offered a third-party analytics suite at ₹1.10 crore a year at then-current volumes, Thachankary built the pipeline himself. Dishaank Lens costs ₹26 lakh a year, and he set raw event rows to purge thirty days after they are written, keeping nightly cohort rollups beyond that. The argument was cost, and data minimisation ahead of the data-protection law then in draft. A rollup can be cut only on dimensions declared before it is written.

3. The market

Indian retail investing in 2026 is a volume business on rails nobody in it owns. A SIP is a UPI AutoPay e-mandate registered through NPCI; identity is CKYC, DigiLocker and Aadhaar eKYC; the economics are a share of a scheme's expense ratio, set by SEBI. The ₹250-a-month window SEBI opened has pulled in exactly the first-time, non-metro, non-English investor Dishaank was built for. Groww, Zerodha's Coin, Upstox, Angel One, Paytm Money and ET Money want the same person.

Two forces press from outside. The DPDP Act and its rules govern what Dishaank may send to whom: a marketing message needs a consent record. And a flow that takes a goal and returns an amount does something that looks, to a regulator, a little like advice.

Dishaank Rails is licensed to three Gulf and South-East Asian partners, the largest being Dilsaan Retail Group of Dubai, which embeds an India-investing feature for the non-resident Indian customers of its loyalty programme. That contract runs ₹11.20 crore over three years, ₹3.40 crore of it turning on a go-live of 1 December 2026. The team that must deliver it sits in seven cities (Figure 1).

4. What happened, and when

What follows is what was on record at each date; where a later record contradicts an earlier assumption, both appear with their dates. Exhibit 1 places them in the calendar.

2 March – 12 April 2026. Dilsaan ran a goal-first version of its embedded flow against the version it had used since launch, in two six-week windows (Exhibit 5). 28 April. At the partnership review a slide set Dilsaan's 31.4 per cent beside Dishaank's 11.2 per cent. 24 September. Dilsaan issued dictionary v2.1, in which activation is a funded account, not a live mandate.

28 April. The Test 41 specification was signed off. It planned a 48-day enrolment, 8 June to 25 July, at 6,100 non-English new installs a day — the rate recorded over 1 to 15 April, which carries the Vishu and Tamil New Year campaign — for 2,92,800 install-ids, 97,600 a cell. 5 July. The recorded mean was 4,072 a day and 1,14,016 install-ids were randomised, 38.9 per cent of plan (Exhibit 2).

8 June. Enrolment opened. Cell A kept the fund-first flow; cell B replaced it with a goal-first flow; cell C had the goal-first flow plus a three-touch reminder ladder over WhatsApp and SMS. 19 June. A release changed the deep link in the ladder's second touch to resume a user at the step they had abandoned rather than the app home screen. 2 September. An audit established that, touch 2 falling on a user's third day, it reached every cohort enrolled from 16 June on, 20 of the 28 enrolment days. It is not in the specification.

29 June. Enrolment was stopped twenty days early, on 5 July instead of the planned 25 July, so the flow could be locked before the campaign build. 12 August. The readout was filed; it treated cell C as fully exposed to the ladder. 15 September. The vendor's log recorded 23,332 of cell C's 38,000 install-ids receiving the first touch, 61.4 per cent; the other 14,668 had no marketing consent on file. A request the same day to split cell C's activation rate by whether the ladder had reached the user came back unservable: the last raw row had purged on 3 September, and consent was not a declared rollup dimension. 11 August 2025 and 6 October 2026. Growth and Finance valued an activation off one cohort and reported different figures (Exhibit 4).

5. The people

Lavanthi Thottappilly — vice-president, product, Kochi
Position: Test 41 cannot be read as a test of goal-first onboarding; she has said so twice in writing. Incentive: Monday's paper and the FY27 roadmap carry her name. Not saying: the hypothesis sentence is hers, typed in on 24 April and never revisited.
Lakshman Thingalaya — co-founder and chief executive, Kochi
Position: he will carry the ₹2.60 crore programme on Thursday if Test 41 supports it. Incentive: a Series C conversation in which Dilsaan is the reference account. Not saying: he agreed on 29 June to stop enrolment early with the sample-size table in front of him, and the board does not know that ₹3.40 crore of the contract is contingent.
Lokeshwari Theruvath — head of growth, Bengaluru
Position: cell C beat the control by 2.30 points; ship it everywhere. Incentive: an H2 target of 2.90 lakh activations, to which her variable pay is keyed. Not saying: the same ladder has run on English-language users since February 2026 and nobody outside her team has seen those numbers.
Litty Tholpady — staff data scientist, Toronto
Position: B minus A is the only contrast in Test 41 that isolates a single change, and it is 0.35 points against a detectable 0.64; she wants a re-run with the cells written down first. Incentive: she signed the 12 August readout. Not saying: she knew on 1 June that the 6,100-a-day figure came from a campaign fortnight and did not rebuild the power table.
Lohitesh Thachankary — co-founder and principal engineer, Pune
Position: Lens keeps thirty-day retention unless someone funds the rebuild, and he will not ship a flow he cannot roll back. Incentive: the platform budget and the consent-ledger upgrade. Not saying: the 19 June release was his squad's, a batch of eleven changes, and the deep link was not in the release note.
Lijin Thamarakshan — design lead, Berlin
Position: the goal screen was built to move people from install into signup, and the specification measured a step four screens lower. Incentive: a design-system investment he has wanted since January. Not saying: the Malayalam and Kannada copy on that screen was machine translation with no reviewer sign-off, so what the test population saw is not what his research tested.
Lathasri Thundiyil — head of platform sales, New Jersey
Position: schedule 2 requires “goal-based onboarding, consistent with the Dishaank consumer application”, which Dilsaan reads as a warranty; re-papering it in November costs the contingency. Incentive: ₹3.40 crore sits in her FY27 number. Not saying: Dilsaan's product head asked her on 6 October whether Dishaank's own app had moved to goal-first, and she said it was rolling out.

Liyana Thokkottu, who runs partner success from Singapore, holds the Dilsaan relationship and sent dictionary v2.1 across.

6. Exhibits

Exhibits 2 and 3 come from the Lens rollups, Exhibit 4 from Finance, Exhibit 5 from the partner.

7. Voices

Readout memo, “Test 41 v1”, filed 12 August 2026, 06:48 EDT — L. Tholpady

“Three contrasts, all on the thirty-day mandate metric. C over A, +2.30 points, z = 9.63. C over B, +1.95, z = 8.13. B over A, +0.35, z = 1.52, which this cohort cannot separate from zero.”

Slack, #t41-readout, 2 September 2026

L. Thachankary, 18:22 IST: “Audit's back. The 19 June build changed the touch-2 deep link to resume at the abandoned step. That is in cell C from the 16 June cohorts on.”

L. Tholpady, 08:54 EDT: “So C is goal-first plus a ladder plus a shortcut, on twenty of twenty-eight days, and the assignment rows purged a month ago. Lohitesh, that is the retention policy, not the release.”

Email, 25 September 2026, 09:12 IST — L. Theruvath to L. Thingalaya, cc L. Thottappilly

“The ladder reached 61.4 per cent of cell C, and the C-minus-B gap is 1.95 points across the whole cell. If the 38.6 per cent we never reached moved by nothing — and they can't have, we didn't message them — then on the people we did reach it is 1.95 ÷ 0.614 = 3.18 points.”

Email, 28 September 2026, 10:41 CEST — L. Thamarakshan to L. Thottappilly

“Look at the second row of the funnel, not the last. Signup started goes 61.09 to 67.17. The goal screen was drawn to get a person off the install screen and into the flow, and it did that, hard. Then four screens of PAN and KYC happen, which I did not touch.”

WhatsApp, Saturday 10 October 2026, 21:40 IST — L. Thingalaya to L. Thottappilly

“Lavanthi — I don't need certainty by Monday. I need a sentence I can defend on Thursday when the committee asks what Test 41 bought us. If the honest answer is ‘we don't know yet’, say so, and tell me what it costs to know and by when.”

8. The options as Thottappilly sees them on Sunday night

She has four lines on a card, in this order; Exhibit 6 costs them.

  1. Ship cell C as tested, to all seven languages, and put the 2.30-point difference in the paper. Twenty-six engineer-weeks, ₹34.30 lakh and ₹18.43 lakh a year of messaging; schedule 2 stands as written.
  2. Ship the reminder ladder and leave the flow alone. Nine engineer-weeks and ₹11.70 lakh, the same messaging cost, reaching the 61.4 per cent of users with a consent record. Schedule 2 would need re-papering before 1 December.
  3. Re-run the test over a 48-day enrolment with the cells written down in advance, and fund Lens to hold raw rows 180 days. Twenty-six engineer-weeks, ₹33.10 lakh and ₹9.40 lakh a year of storage. At the recorded 4,072 a day, 48 days enrols 65,152 a cell, which detects 0.49 pp on activation; the specification's 0.40 pp needs 72 days. There is no readout until the enrolment and a thirty-day outcome window have both closed.
  4. Put goal-first on Dishaank Rails only, so Dilsaan gets a goal-based flow, and leave the consumer app on the control. Nineteen engineer-weeks and ₹23.75 lakh, plus ₹14.80 lakh a year to carry a second flow. Schedule 2's “consistent with” wording would need re-papering before 1 December.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

Time and people. The paper is due at nine on Monday 12 October; the committee sits on Thursday the 15th; the Dilsaan go-live is 1 December. Between 12 October and 30 November there are 50 days, of which the freeze of 26 October to 9 November takes 15, both squads being on campaign support through it, leaving 35 days, or five weeks. That is 6×5 = 30 Pune and 5×5 = 25 Bengaluru engineer-weeks; the consent-ledger upgrade holds 11 and 7, leaving 19 and 18. Those two figures are what the 1 December go-live leaves; an option with nothing to deliver by then is not bound by them.

Money. ₹1.20 crore of discretionary product spend is approved for H2; the ₹2.60 crore programme needs the committee. ₹3.40 crore of the ₹11.20 crore Dilsaan contract turns on 1 December.

Regulation. The consent-ledger upgrade is committed and dated. External counsel's note of 7 October reads that a flow returning a computed monthly amount against a stated goal is defensible as distribution so long as it names no scheme, and declines to say what it becomes once a fund list appears on the next screen.

Data. Lens holds raw rows thirty days and rollups on cell, step, language and device tier. Test 41's raw rows purged on 3 September.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. What did Test 41 change, for whom, and what did its specification say would move?
  2. Exhibit 3 reports four steps for each cell. Using Exhibit 2 and the formula in its note, which of the four B-against-A differences are larger than what this cohort can detect, and which are not? What does that imply about the measurement Test 41 declared?
  3. Exhibit 5 was put to the partnership review on 28 April. What does it establish about the Dilsaan flow, and what does it not?
  4. Exhibit 4 gives two figures for one cohort. Which would you use to price the options in Exhibit 6, and what does the choice do to the order they come in?
  5. Theruvath and Tholpady both argue from cell C. Set out the population each describes, and say what measurement, taken when and on whom, would separate the three differences cell C contains.
  6. It is nine on Monday morning. What do you tell Thingalaya to put in the paper; what do you commit Dishaank to measuring before 1 December, at what cost; and what do you say to the committee if that answer loses the ₹3.40 crore?

At half past one she closed the paper and opened the April specification again. The sentence sat in its grey box, four words longer than the box wanted. It had been read in April and not opened since. Outside, the first fishing boats started up.
exp40v2-exp.hypothesis:
Writing an experiment hypothesis

“If we change X for users Y, metric Z moves because…” — and why the clause after because, the population in the middle, and the number nobody writes down are the three places where competent teams quietly lose a year.

Conventions. Every lift is stated in absolute percentage points, written “points”; relative figures are labelled relative and their base named. Power calculations are two-sided at α = 0.05 with 80 per cent power, so z0.975 + z0.80 = 1.9600 + 0.8416 = 2.8016 and 2(2.8016)² = 15.698, the constant used in every substitution below. The single one-sided test on this page runs at α = 0.025, keeping the same z = 1.960.

1. Two rooms, two sentences

On Tuesday 10 February 2026, Rishiraj Bachhawat put one sentence on a wall in Bengaluru and asked six people to break it. Bachhawat runs growth at Ibaarat Money, a six-year-old app with 4.2 million monthly actives selling mutual funds under SEBI and AMFI rules. Each week 18,500 users who have never held a systematic investment plan enter its three-screen SIP setup flow; 24.0 per cent finish it. The sentence read: a redesigned setup flow will lift SIP completion.

Rajvardhan Bhimrajka, who chairs Ibaarat's experiment council, asked two questions that took ninety minutes. Which completion — the one on the last screen, or the one that survives to a second instalment being debited? And what did Bachhawat believe the redesign would do to a user's head? He had no answer to either, and the honest form of the sentence proved a different experiment needing nearly four times the sample and eight times the calendar.

Two days later, on Thursday 12 February, Rohanika Bandukwala faced a harder version in Pune. Intezaam Claims Intelligence sells document extraction to 61 insurer and third-party-administrator accounts regulated by the IRDAI, which push 146,400 claim documents a month through the pipeline, and 68.0 per cent of those documents clear review with no extracted field edited — the clean-pass rate, counted per document. Bandukwala wanted to ship an assistive pre-fill drafting the whole form; her engineer Rishvita Barmecha had written the hypothesis. The difficulty was that Intezaam could not randomise users: reviewers sit in rooms of forty, talk to each other, and are managed by an account team negotiating one contract per insurer. The unit the business can split is the account.

2. What a hypothesis is, and the three camps

A product hypothesis is a conditional, falsifiable, pre-registered prediction with five obligatory slots: an intervention, a population defined as the system can select it, an outcome measure, a signed and sized change in it, and a mechanism explaining why the first produces the last. The fifth separates a hypothesis from a bet.

The form grafts two incompatible stocks. Fisher's The Design of Experiments (1935) gave randomisation, the null hypothesis and a p-value read as evidence against it, and refused to pair the null with any specific alternative. Neyman and Pearson, two years earlier, had built the opposite machine: two rival hypotheses, two error rates, and a rule saying which action to take. Product practice writes Fisher's null into its statistics and Neyman–Pearson's rule into its documents, hiding the seam. Popper supplies falsifiability: a hypothesis you cannot lose is not one. Ries (2011) put the because clause on the whiteboard; Kohavi, Tang and Xu (2020) added the overall evaluation criterion and the decision rule.

Three camps disagree about which slots are load-bearing. The decision-rule camp signs: if no pre-stated outcome changes what we do on Monday, the test should not run. It will not sign that the mechanism clause is necessary, holding causal stories to be garnish that licenses rescue. The mechanism camp signs: a hypothesis that does not say because yields a result that cannot be carried to the next decision, and will not sign that a metric, a population and a threshold complete the job. The belief-updating camp, largely Bayesian, signs: the output is a posterior over the effect size, and a hypothesis should state a prior. It will not sign what practitioners say most often: that a result inside the noise band means the feature does nothing.

3. Mechanics: the arithmetic nobody writes on the slide

Bhimrajka's first question is the discipline in miniature. Ibaarat can measure a proximal outcome, the share of entrants reaching the confirmation screen, 24.0 per cent; or a distal one, the share whose SIP is live on day 90, which is 24.0 per cent × 71.0 per cent persistence = 17.04 per cent. Only the second is money.

The two-proportion sizing formula, per arm, is n = 2(z0.975+z0.80)² · p̄(1−p̄) / δ², δ being the absolute difference in proportions. For the proximal metric at a 2.0-point target: n = 15.698 × 0.24 × 0.76 / (0.020)² = 2.86332 / 0.000400 = 7,158.3, so 7,159 per arm, 14,318 in total — 0.77 of a week at 18,500 entrants. Power is not the constraint; the weekly rhythm of salary credits is, and the standing rule is two whole weeks.

The distal metric requires a second-order belief. If the redesign lifts completion by 2.0 points, do those marginal users persist at the same 71.0 per cent as the inframarginal ones? By construction they are the people the old flow could not convince, and Bachhawat put their persistence at 46.0 per cent, from users who had previously completed only after a reminder. The predicted day-90 effect is therefore 0.020 × 0.460 = 0.0092, or 0.92 points — 5.40 per cent relative to the 17.04 per cent base, not the 8.33 per cent the proximal lift suggests. Half the headline evaporates before anyone runs anything.

Sizing on that effect, control 17.04 per cent against treatment 17.96 per cent, pooled p̄ = 0.1750: n = 15.698 × 0.1750 × 0.8250 / (0.0092)² = 2.26640 / 0.00008464 = 26,776.5, so 26,777 per arm. That is 2.89 weeks; three whole weeks supplies 55,500 entrants, 27,750 per arm. The distal hypothesis needs 3.74 times the sample and, since each user must be watched for 90 days, 111 days of calendar rather than fourteen. Day counts here are inclusive of the first: 21 days of enrolment plus 90 of maturation from the last enrolment day.

One step is usually left implicit, and it is a decision, not a calculation: the detectable effect should come from economics. Maintaining the redesigned flow costs about nine engineer-weeks a year; at a fully loaded ₹38 lakh per engineer-year over 48 working weeks that is 9/48 × ₹38 lakh = ₹7.125 lakh. The flow sees 18,500 × 52 = 962,000 entrants a year and a day-90-active SIP is worth ₹520 in trail revenue, so break-even is ₹7,12,500 / (962,000 × ₹520) = ₹7,12,500 / ₹50.024 crore = 0.1424 points — against a detectable 0.92, a factor of 6.5. Ibaarat is measuring not whether to ship but whether the effect is unexpectedly large.

4. The conditions, stated as claims you can check

Claim one: the outcome is observable inside a window you can afford to wait. Ibaarat passes barely — 111 days is long but survivable — and Intezaam comfortably, since clean-pass is measured within hours. A lender whose outcome is a 24-month default rate fails, and must write against a leading indicator with a stated correlation.

Claim two: the population can be split by the system in the way the mechanism requires. Ibaarat passes. Intezaam fails at the user level and passes only at account-week level — section 5's problem.

Claim three: the smallest effect worth acting on exceeds the smallest effect you can see. Ibaarat fails, as the 0.1424-against-0.92 arithmetic shows; Intezaam fails badly under account randomisation and passes under a switchback, whose 1.58-point floor sits inside the 2.0-point degradation Bandukwala would act on. A failing third claim does not forbid the experiment, only the sentence “the test will tell us whether to ship.”

Claim four: no part of the mechanism runs through other users. This fails most often and most quietly — for Intezaam if reviewers learn from each other, and for any marketplace where a treated buyer removes supply a control buyer would have bought. There the hypothesis is actively misleading rather than merely underpowered: the estimate converges to something real, but not to the quantity in the sentence, and more data makes the wrong number more precise.

5. Hard edges: clusters, seams and the AI case

Bandukwala's constraint is standard in enterprise software: with the account as randomisation unit, effective sample is not document count. Each account contributes m = 2,400 documents a month, and the intraclass correlation of clean-pass within an account — Barmecha estimated 0.08 from twelve months of history — inflates variance by the design effect DEFF = 1 + (m − 1) × ICC = 1 + 2,399 × 0.08 = 192.92. Effective sample per account is 2,400 / 192.92 = 12.44 documents, so 61 accounts split 31/30 give 385.7 and 373.2. Substituting into δ = 2.8016 × √[p(1−p)(1/n1+1/n2)] with p = 0.680 and 1/385.7 + 1/373.2 = 0.005272 gives 2.8016 × √(0.2176 × 0.005272) = 2.8016 × 0.03387 = 0.0949: a detectable effect of 9.49 points, 13.96 per cent relative. No assist of this kind was expected to move a 68.0 per cent rate by nine and a half points, and the ceiling is structural: as m grows, effective sample per cluster tends to 1/ICC = 12.5.

The escape is to change the unit, not the sample: an account-week switchback in which each of the 61 accounts spends four weeks with the assist on and four off in randomised order, 9 March to 3 May 2026. Each account's four on-weeks minus its four off-weeks give one difference; the standard deviation of those 61 differences is 4.4 points, so the standard error of their mean is 4.4 / √61 = 0.563 points and the detectable effect is 2.8016 × 0.563 = 1.58 points, 2.32 per cent relative — six times better, at the price of an explicit assumption: that reviewer skill does not carry over from an assisted week to an unassisted one.

The seams are organisational as much as statistical. A two-sided marketplace must name which side it treats and what it assumes of the other; in hardware the firmware cohort is frozen at manufacture, so the population slot is fixed before the intervention; in regulated contexts a hypothesis implying differential treatment may be unlawful whatever its statistics. For AI-native products the treatment is a distribution, not a build, so a drifting model breaks the constancy assumption and the hypothesis pins a version.

6. Nine things an expert does differently

The because clause names a measurable intermediate. “Because users find it easier” is not a mechanism; “because it removes the amount decision at step 2, so step-2 drop-off falls by more than completion rises” is. The tell: an expert predicts something that moves first and by more.

Absolute and relative are never mixed. An expert writes “2.0 points on a 24.0 per cent base”, never “a 2 per cent lift”. The error is silent and multiplicative: a 2.5 per cent relative target on 24.0 per cent is 0.6 points, and since n scales as 1/δ² that is 11.1 times the sample — about 79,500 per arm, not 7,159.

The population is written as the system can select it. “Price-sensitive users” is not a population; “users whose first three sessions contained a sort-by-price event” is. The selectable population is usually a biased subset of the intended one, and that bias belongs in the document.

The guardrails are predicted too. Bachhawat's mechanism — removing a decision rather than adding persuasion — predicts average first instalment size unchanged within ±3.0 per cent relative, where persuasion predicts a fall. An unsized guardrail is unfalsifiable; maturity shows as one whose prediction separates rival mechanisms.

Proximal and distal are chosen, not defaulted. The choice is a bet on a survival ratio and an expert writes it down. Ibaarat's is 46.0 per cent marginal persistence against 71.0 per cent inframarginal; as a number it turns an argument about metrics into one about a parameter.

The decision rule is asymmetric and written in advance. It covers three branches: positive, negative, and not distinguishable from zero. “We failed to detect an effect of 0.92 points or more” and “there is no effect” are different claims, and only the first is supported. Ibaarat's rule sends a null to a holdout, not to the bin.

The MDE is derived from the decision, then reconciled with traffic. Experts do the break-even calculation first and the power calculation second, and say which instrument they hold. A test that cannot resolve 0.1424 points can still refute a claim of 3.0 points.

Underpowered tests are biased, not merely uninformative. If the true effect is 0.50 points and the standard error 0.714 — the error implied by a 2.0-point detectable effect — the threshold sits at 1.960 × 0.714 = 1.40 points. Such a design reaches significance 10.8 per cent of the time counting both tails; its significant positive estimates average 1.74 points, 3.5 times the truth, and 3.6 per cent of all significant results carry the wrong sign.

A hypothesis is a liability, not an asset. Teams that count hypotheses written produce hypotheses that cannot lose. An expert kills a well-written one because neither outcome changes the plan, and counts the tests not run for that reason as the honest measure.

7. Where the practice actually differs

The differences across product types are real but narrower than folklore suggests. In consumer products the binding constraint is almost never sample size and almost always the distal-metric wait, so the craft lies in choosing surrogates and stating their survival ratios. In B2B it is cluster count: with 61 accounts the randomisation unit decides the experiment, and the hypothesis is written against account-weeks or not at all. Platform and marketplace products break claim four by construction, so their hypotheses carry an interference clause and concede that the estimate is a partial-equilibrium effect that will shrink at full rollout.

Hardware differs structurally rather than culturally: the population slot is frozen by manufacturing long before the intervention is written, so hypotheses run against cohorts defined by build date and channel. AI products differ on the outcome slot, where there is often no single metric and the hypothesis must name an evaluation set, its sampling frame and its staleness rate.

By stage the difference is about what is being purchased. At seed the scarce quantity is not power but the number of distinct beliefs testable before the money runs out, so hypotheses are written to be maximally surprising rather than maximally precise, and qualitative refutation is a legitimate result. Past a million monthly actives the economics invert and the discipline becomes guardrails and pre-registration. Where the difference is not real: the five slots do not change, and no stage excuses an unsized prediction.

8. Three worked examples

Exhibit A. Ibaarat Money, SIP setup redesign: enrolled Monday 2 to Sunday 22 March 2026; last cohort matured Saturday 20 June 2026.
MetricBasePredicted lift (points)Needed per armObserved lift (points)z
Completion (proximal)24.00%2.007,1592.30—
SIP active day 90 (distal)17.04%0.9226,7771.063.28

Enrolled 27,750 per arm over 21 days. Predicted distal lift = 2.00 × 0.460 marginal persistence = 0.92 points; the observed 1.06 is what 2.30 points of completion at the same 46.0 per cent implies (2.30 × 0.460 = 1.058). Sizing was planned at 26,777 per arm, where the detectable effect is 0.92 points; enrolment reached 27,750, lowering it to 0.90. The z column is computed at 27,750: standard error √(2 × 0.1757 × 0.8243 / 27,750) = 0.3231 points, so 1.06 / 0.3231 = 3.28. The proximal row is descriptive, not a test.

One. What made Ibaarat's test readable was the mechanism prediction, not the headline. Step-2 drop-off fell 3.4 points against a completion gain of 2.30, the ordering the mechanism required; had step-2 drop-off stayed flat, the team was pre-committed to calling the gain unexplained.

Two. Intezaam's switchback was written as a non-inferiority test, since Bandukwala's question was whether pre-fill degraded quality while saving time. Stated one-sided at α = 0.025 with the same z = 1.960, the hypothesis was that clean-pass under assist is no worse than 2.0 points below the 68.0 per cent control. Against a detectable 1.58 points that margin is resolvable, which is the only reason the design is legitimate: a margin smaller than the detectable effect cannot be cleared even by a product that does no harm, because the lower bound never rises above it. Such a design invites a false fail, not a false pass — or worse, a team reading “no evidence of inferiority” as a pass, the failure-to-detect slide this page warns against elsewhere.

Three, the failure. In June 2025 Ibaarat tested portfolio insight cards on a hypothesis reading: users who see insight cards will return within seven days more often. No population clause, no mechanism, and a metric whose denominator the treatment itself moved. The readout on 20 July showed seven-day returns among portfolio-tab openers falling from 38.0 to 35.0 per cent, and on Thursday 14 August the feature was switched off as harmful. It was not. On the assigned population — the only denominator randomisation protects — returns rose from 16.72 to 18.55 per cent: 1.83 points, 10.94 per cent relative, standard error 0.241 points, z = 7.59. Rupashree Bhagwagar re-read the assignment log in October; the feature went back on Monday 27 October 2025. The 28-day window assigned 100,000 across both arms, so a full rollout earns 1,830 incremental returns per window; the 74 days of suppression cost 74 × 1,830 / 28 = 4,836 returns. The template now refuses any denominator the intervention can move.

9. Failure modes and their early warning signs

The moving denominator. Early sign: the primary metric is a ratio whose denominator is itself a behaviour. Diagnostic: can the treatment change who is in the denominator? Caught late it inverts the conclusion, as Ibaarat's 74 days show.

The unfalsifiable mechanism. Early sign: the because clause survives unchanged whichever way the result goes. Diagnostic: what result would make us abandon this explanation? The cost is slow: a team that re-explores neighbouring ground at full price.

The aspirational MDE. Early sign: the detectable effect in the document is a round number nobody derived. Diagnostic: show me the substitution. Caught at readout it turns a three-week test into a meaningless null, and the team ships anyway.

Null read as absence. Early sign: the phrase “no impact” with no interval beside it. Diagnostic: what effects does this result exclude? The cost is a good feature killed and re-proposed eighteen months later.

Interference ignored. Early sign: the treated group's gain is suspiciously close to the control group's loss. Diagnostic: could a treated user have taken something a control user wanted? Caught at rollout the effect vanishes, and credibility with it.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

On pre-registration. The strict position holds that any analysis not specified in advance is a hypothesis generated by the data, and rests on the poor replication record of exploratory findings. The adaptive position holds that most product learning is discovery and that rigid pre-registration produces documents nobody reads; it rests on sequential and bandit designs with honest error control. It would be wrong if pre-registered and exploratory product findings replicated at similar rates; nobody has that dataset.

On the mechanism clause. One camp holds it is the only durable output; the other holds it is where confirmation bias enters, because a team with a story will rescue it. The second would be wrong if teams with written mechanisms abandoned them more readily than teams without — precisely the measurement nobody runs.

On thresholds. The decision-theoretic position is that α = 0.05 is an arbitrary inheritance and the rule should maximise expected value, which for a cheap reversible change implies shipping on a posterior mean above zero. The conservative position is that organisations cannot hold an honest prior under commercial pressure, so the threshold is a social commitment device. It would be wrong if Bayesian teams showed no greater rate of unreplicated ships; the evidence is anecdotal both ways.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this writes the decision rule before the hypothesis and the guardrail before the primary metric. They can say without a spreadsheet roughly how many users a given effect needs, and reach for the break-even calculation before the power calculation. They treat a disagreement about which metric to use as a disagreement about a parameter — a survival ratio, an ICC, a margin — and put a number on it rather than win the argument. And in a readout they say what the result excludes, not what it proves.

12. What each of them decided

Bachhawat ran the distal test and shipped on Tuesday 23 June 2026. His reasoning was not the z of 3.28; it was that the observed 1.06 points sat above the 0.1424-point break-even by a factor of 7.4, and that the mechanism's step-2 prediction had held. Bandukwala never ran the account-randomised test. She wrote the switchback, declared the carryover assumption inside the hypothesis, and told her board the 61-account design had a 9.49-point floor and would have produced an uninterpretable null.

  1. Ibaarat's break-even lift is 0.1424 points and its detectable effect is 0.92. When is it still rational to spend 111 days on that experiment, and what would have to be true of the organisation for the answer to be no?
  2. The switchback improves the detectable effect sixfold by adding a carryover assumption. Design the smallest test of that assumption runnable inside the same window, and say what it costs in power for the primary comparison.
  3. The 2025 test was killed on a metric that fell and rescued on one that rose, both computed correctly. Write the template rule you would add, and name a case where it would block a legitimate experiment.

13. Going deeper

What makes a good metric
The outcome slot is only as good as its metric; sensitivity and gameability are decided here.
Surfacing assumptions
The because clause is an assumption made visible; this supplies the inventory it comes from.
A/B testing fundamentals
Randomisation, assignment and sample ratio mismatch: the machinery that makes a hypothesis checkable.
Choosing experiment metrics
Primary, secondary and guardrail selection, and the multiple-comparison cost of each one.
Significance, power, sample size, peeking
Section 3's arithmetic in full, including sequential designs that legitimise peeking.
When you can't A/B test
Switchbacks, synthetic controls and difference-in-differences: what Bandukwala needed.
Experimentation culture
Whether the organisation survives a null decides whether honest hypotheses get written.
Qual + quant feedback loop
Where mechanisms come from before they are sized, and how to tell one from a rationalisation.
Feature flags and flighting
The delivery layer deciding which populations you can select, and so what you can test.
Experiment pitfalls
Interference, novelty and instrumentation effects: how section 4's conditions break.
case20v1-exp.hypothesis:
Chembarathi Pantry: The Pause Button

A teaching case on writing an experiment hypothesis

1. Opening

At 6:30 pm on Tuesday 13 October 2026, Kirthana Shettigar, Head of Product at Chembarathi Pantry, was alone on the fourth floor of the company's Indiranagar office in Bengaluru with a ticket she had not written. Its title read "Pause option in cancel flow". Its one-line rationale read: "Pause will improve retention." Engineering had finished the build on Friday 9 October. The release slot for Monday 19 October would be given away at 5 pm on Friday 16 October if no one claimed it.

Diwali fell on Sunday 8 November. The next free release slot came a fortnight after the festival. Kirthana had three days to decide whether to claim Monday's slot, and, if she did, what exactly the company would be testing. Her data scientist in Toronto had asked that afternoon: "Retention of whom, measured how, and by when?"

2. Company background

Chembarathi Pantry was founded in Kochi in 2021. Its customers choose a monthly basket of staples, namely rice, atta, cooking oil, dals and spices, and receive it from a neighbourhood dark store on a fixed day. They pay through a UPI AutoPay mandate. By 30 September 2026 it had 1,86,000 active subscribers in Bengaluru, Pune, Kochi and Hyderabad, at an average basket of ₹2,400 a month, so about ₹44.64 crore of baskets a month (1,86,000 × ₹2,400).

The company competes for the same kitchen cupboard as BigBasket, Blinkit, Zepto, Swiggy Instamart, JioMart and DMart Ready. Those firms win on speed and breadth. Chembarathi Pantry wins on predictability: the customer need not remember to reorder. A subscription that stops fitting a household, because the family is travelling or the cupboard is full, is cancelled outright rather than adjusted.

3. The situation

The ticket came from Kunjumon Sreekumar's growth team on Monday 28 September. The cancel flow had a reason prompt, added in March 2026, and Exhibit 2 shows what customers said in the eight weeks from 15 June to 9 August 2026. Exhibit 1 shows how many subscribers entered the cancel flow in the same weeks and how many still had a delivered order within 60 days of tapping Cancel. Kirthana chose those weeks because their 60-day outcomes had all closed by 8 October; later weeks were still open. Across them, 18.0 per cent of entrants still had a delivery, including subscribers who tapped Cancel and then left the flow.

The team's view depended on where they sat. Kamran Sasidharan, the data scientist in Toronto (9:00 am for him, 6:30 pm for Kirthana, while Toronto remained on summer time until 1 November), wanted the target metric fixed before launch. Karthikeyan Sankunni, who leads customer success from Singapore, had phoned 64 cancel-intent customers between 17 and 28 August whose stated reason was travel or stock at home. Eight of them said they would take a pause if offered. Kunjumon, in Kochi, owned a delivered-orders target for the October to December quarter, which ended on 31 December.

Exhibit 3 sets out three ways of using Monday's slot, and the timeline in Figure 1 shows where each would land. Planning on the baseline's 3,200 entrants a week, the three weeks from 19 October to 8 November would yield about 9,600 entrants. Diwali travel could change both the number of entrants and their reasons relative to the summer weeks.

4. The people

Kirthana Shettigar, Head of Product, Bengaluru, owns the choice of what ships and what is tested. She has been at the company since 2023 and wants a result her team can defend in January without a second argument about what it meant.

Kamran Sasidharan, Senior Data Scientist, Toronto, has been with the company since 2024. He wants every metric, population and threshold written down before the first subscriber is enrolled, and wants no early peeking at the arms.

Karthikeyan Sankunni, Customer Success Lead, Singapore, runs the team that phones customers who try to cancel. He wants a pause that does not leave customers unsure whether the next debit will happen, and he wants it live before Diwali, when callers ask for it most.

Kunjumon Sreekumar, Head of Growth, Kochi, wants the pause in front of every cancelling customer on 19 October. He expects to watch pause taps daily and does not want his quarter's delivered orders to pay for a long study.

5. Exhibits

All counts are subscribers entering the cancel flow, counted once each.

6. The options

Option A: ship to everyone on 19 October. Every subscriber who taps Cancel sees the pause from the first day, and no one is held back during the Diwali weeks. Growth reads session outcomes from 9 November against the eight weeks in Exhibit 1.

Option B: a 50/50 test, with the ticket's wording. Half of entrants, about 4,800, are held back for three weeks. The ticket stays as written. Success is read in the session: pause accepted, or the flow abandoned, with a result on 9 November. This gives Kunjumon an early number and a comparison group. It counts what happens at the tap.

Option C: a 50/50 test, with the hypothesis written in full. The population, the metric, the size of change and the reason are fixed in writing before launch, and the outcome is a delivered order within 60 days of the tap. The last enrolled subscriber's window closes on 7 January 2027 and the readout call is on 11 January 2027, twelve weeks after launch. The pause reaches half of cancelling subscribers through Diwali, and the quarter's accounts close before the answer arrives.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. Read the ticket's one-line rationale in section 1. Which of the elements of a complete hypothesis (the change, the people it applies to, the metric, the direction and size of movement, the reason) does it state, and which does it leave out?
  2. Using Exhibits 1 to 3, which metric would you name as primary for the pause, and what does each outcome listed in Exhibit 3 actually count?
  3. What size of change would you write into the hypothesis? From the baseline and arm sizes printed in the exhibits, what is the smallest change a test of that size could reliably detect?
  4. Which option would you take by 5 pm on Friday 16 October, and what would you tell Kunjumon about when he can expect an answer?

8. A note for the learner

A hypothesis is a sentence that can lose: it names a change, the people it touches, a metric, a direction and size, and a reason. One defensible path is Option C, with this wording: "If we offer a one-cycle pause to every subscriber who taps Cancel in Bengaluru, Pune, Kochi and Hyderabad, the share with a delivered order within 60 days of the tap will rise from 18.0 per cent by at least 3 points, because 41 per cent of those giving a reason say travel or stock at home, which a pause fixes and cancelling over-corrects."

The reasoning behind the numbers. In Exhibit 2, travelling (3,584) plus stock at home (5,600) is 9,184 entrants, 35.9 per cent of all 25,600 entrants. Karthikeyan's calls suggest 8 of 64, one in eight, would accept. That implies 35.9% × 1/8 ≈ 4.5 points, assuming skippers of the prompt would not take a pause. A threshold of 3 points discounts that stated intent. At 4,800 per arm and an 18.0 per cent baseline, a two-sided 5 per cent test with 80 per cent power can detect about 2.2 points, so 3 points is detectable, with about 96 per cent power. Baskets arrive every 30 days, so the skipped delivery falls 0 to 30 days after the tap and the next 30 to 60; a 60-day window therefore reaches every accepter.

The decision rule is written first: ship to everyone if the lift is at least 3 points and the 95 per cent interval excludes zero; otherwise do not ship, and treat a smaller positive lift as a new hypothesis for a new test. Kamran owns the readout. Kunjumon may watch pause take-up in the treated arm as a diagnostic, but no outcome comparison is read before 11 January.
exp20v2-exp.hypothesis:
Writing an Experiment Hypothesis

A working explainer for product managers, built around one decision at a Gujarat grocery app.

1. A slide that said "ship by Navratri"

On Tuesday 8 September 2026, Poorna Anjaria, a product manager at Harsiddhi Fresh, an Ahmedabad grocery-delivery app, opened a meeting with a slide reading, in full: "Free-delivery progress bar: ship by Navratri." The app served Ahmedabad, Surat, Vadodara and Rajkot. The bar was a strip on the checkout screen saying "Add ₹42 more for free delivery" to anyone whose basket fell under the ₹199 free-delivery line. Pradyumn Adesara, head of growth, wanted it live in all four cities before Navratri, due to begin on 11 October, the busiest ordering fortnight of the quarter. His case was brief: "Customers hate the ₹30 fee. Show them how to avoid it."

Poorna had evidence for the first half. In the exit survey for 1 to 31 August, 412 users who abandoned checkout gave a reason; 118 of them, 28.6 per cent, named the delivery fee as the main one. She had nothing yet for the second half, and she could see two ways to be wrong. The bar might change nothing. Or it might put the fee in front of users who had not noticed it, and some would leave. Prerak Anadkat, the data scientist, raised a narrower worry: if the team launched everywhere and orders rose, nobody could separate the bar from the festival. Her decision that week was therefore not whether to build the bar but what to write down before building it.

2. The idea: a prediction that can lose

An experiment hypothesis is a written prediction, fixed before the data arrive, that a specific change, applied to a specific group, will move a specific measure by a stated amount, for a stated reason. The common form is: if we change X for users Y, metric Z moves by at least M, because W.

Three older traditions stand behind it. Ronald Fisher, in Statistical Methods for Research Workers (1925) and The Design of Experiments (1935), gave science the null hypothesis, a claim of no effect that data could contradict. Jerzy Neyman and Egon Pearson (1933) added a named alternative and the idea of power, the chance of detecting an effect that really exists. Karl Popper (1934) argued that a claim informs only if it forbids something. Online experimentation, which matured in software companies from the early 2000s, met the problem all three address: with hundreds of metrics, a team that has not committed in advance can always find one that moved. No single author owns the template; it is a convergence.

The sentence Poorna could repeat in any meeting: "Before we build it, tell me what changes, for whom, which number moves and by how much, and why we believe it."

3. How it works, step by step

Poorna built the hypothesis in the five steps of Figure 1. The change comes first, stated so that an engineer could build it and a stranger recognise it: a bar on the checkout screen, with the ₹199 line and the ₹30 fee untouched. Second is the population: users in Ahmedabad and Surat who open checkout, for the first time during the test, with a basket under ₹199. Vadodara and Rajkot were held back for a later check. The unit is the user, because one person may open checkout five times, and counting sessions would treat those repeats as independent evidence.

Third, and the step practitioners leave implicit, is the metric's definition: numerator, denominator and window. Here it is the share of assigned users who place an order within 24 hours of first opening checkout, so the denominator is everyone assigned, not only those who stay. Fourth is the mechanism, which does the most work. It predicts more than the headline: the lift should be larger for baskets close to the line. Fifth is the decision rule, written before launch: ship only if the 95 per cent interval for the difference excludes zero, the point estimate is at least 1.85 pp, and contribution per order falls by no more than ₹3. The 1.85 pp floor is break-even: at 4,750 eligible users a day and ₹25 an order it returns about ₹8.0 lakh a year, finance's threshold. A significant 0.3 pp gain therefore does not ship. The floor sits below the 2.0 pp target by design, since a floor equal to the target would reject half of all true 2.0 pp effects; even so, an effect of exactly 2.0 pp would clear 1.85 pp only about 60 per cent of the time, a cost Poorna accepted knowingly. Prerak asked for a sixth item that is usually missing, the action on a null result. Poorna wrote it down: drop the bar and redirect the sprint to fee wording.

4. A worked example: can the test answer in time?

Poorna next had to learn whether the test could answer within the calendar. For two proportions, users needed per arm are n = (zα/2 + zβ)² × [p₁(1−p₁) + p₂(1−p₂)] ÷ (p₂ − p₁)². Here p₁ is the baseline rate (40.0 per cent) and p₂ the rate the change should reach. The value zα/2 = 1.960 fixes a 5 per cent two-sided significance level, the tolerated chance of declaring an effect that does not exist; zβ = 0.842 fixes 80 per cent power. Squaring their unrounded values gives 7.849, the figure used below. The difference p₂ − p₁ is the minimum detectable effect (MDE). Finance wanted a sprint to return about ₹8 lakh a year. Four-city eligible flow was 4,750 users a day (the two test cities' 1,900 being 40 per cent of it); at ₹25 contribution per extra order, 2.0 points yield 95 orders a day, ₹2,375, or about ₹8.7 lakh a year. So the MDE became 2.0 percentage points.

Table 1. Sample size at two MDEs (α = 5% two-sided, power 80%, 1,900 eligible users a day, 50/50 split).
QuantityFirst passSecond pass
Target p₂ (absolute / relative lift)42.0% (+2.0 pp / 5.0%)41.0% (+1.0 pp / 2.5%)
Variance term0.2400 + 0.2436 = 0.48360.2400 + 0.2419 = 0.4819
Users per arm7.849 × 0.4836 ÷ 0.0004 = 9,4907.849 × 0.4819 ÷ 0.0001 ≈ 37,824

Halving the MDE roughly quadrupled the sample (37,824 against 9,490, a factor of 3.99), because n varies with the inverse square of the effect. The second pass also collided with the calendar: six weeks from Monday 21 September ends Sunday 1 November and spans Navratri, when the baseline itself would move. The 14-day plan ends Sunday 4 October; the last 24-hour windows close on the 5th, so readout falls on Tuesday 6 October, five days before Navratri begins. Fourteen days also holds two full weekly cycles in each arm. Because 13,300 per arm exceeds the 9,490 required, power for exactly +2.0 pp is 91 per cent.

5. Seven nuances that separate users from understanders

Two hypotheses share one name

The product hypothesis is a claim about customers and mechanism. The statistical null hypothesis ("the bar changes nothing") is what the test computes against. Rejecting the null shows that the arms differ; it does not show that the mechanism is the reason.

Relative is not absolute

This page uses percentage points (pp) for absolute differences and "relative" for change as a share of baseline: 40.0 to 42.0 per cent is +2.0 pp and +5.0 per cent relative. A colleague's "5 per cent lift" might mean 45.0 per cent, a 5 pp gap needing only 1,531 users per arm, about a sixth of the sample. Always write both numbers and the base.

The MDE is chosen, not forecast

It is the smallest effect worth being able to see, set by economics: here, the ₹8 lakh a year that justifies a sprint. Power of 80 per cent also means a one-in-five chance of missing an effect of exactly that size. A null result rules out large effects, not small ones.

Denominator and window are part of the claim

The 40.0 per cent baseline is per user, within 24 hours. A per-session or seven-day figure would have a different baseline and a different sample requirement. Change either after launch and the pre-computed arithmetic no longer describes the test.

A mechanism can cut both ways

The same bar might raise abandonment by exposing the fee. Test two-sided, and state the predicted direction as the bet. A hypothesis whose mechanism accommodates any outcome, including the opposite one, cannot lose and so teaches nothing.

One primary metric, the rest guardrails

Each extra independent metric judged at 5 per cent adds chance of a spurious win; five give 1 − 0.95⁵ = 22.6 per cent. Guardrails such as margin per order work differently: they can stop a launch but cannot be cited as a win.

What a hypothesis cannot tell you

It cannot certify why the metric moved, extend a September result in two cities to Rajkot in November, or reveal whether novelty will fade. A thoughtful newcomer asks: who is in the denominator, what will we do with a null, and what else would be true if the mechanism holds?

6. How it differs by product and by company

In consumer products, volume makes small effects testable, as at Harsiddhi Fresh. In B2B, a vendor with 60 enterprise accounts has 60 units; no proportion test on that base can see a 2 pp shift, so hypotheses lean on larger expected effects, before-and-after account histories and structured customer interviews. In marketplaces, arms share riders and stock: a bar that lifts treatment orders can slow deliveries for control, so randomising by user leaks, and teams randomise by dark store or alternate days. Harsiddhi Fresh is partly a marketplace, which is why Prerak flagged rider load as a second guardrail beside margin. An early-stage company with few users must accept a coarse MDE: a 20 per cent relative lift (40.0 to 48.0 per cent) needs about 601 users per arm. A large company adds a registry, a template and a reviewer, so that hypotheses are comparable across hundreds of tests.

7. Common mistakes

No mechanism. Symptom: a null result is met with "interesting" and a new feature idea. Misunderstanding: that a prediction of direction is a hypothesis. Diagnostic: ask what else would be true if the idea were right; if the answer is "nothing", there is no mechanism.

Metric chosen after the fact. Symptom: a win announced on a number absent from the launch document. Misunderstanding: that more metrics mean more chances to learn. Diagnostic: compare the timestamped document with the dashboard cited.

An MDE set by hope. Symptom: a test that quietly needs 70 days, or is stopped at day nine. Misunderstanding: that the MDE is a forecast. Diagnostic: divide the required sample by daily eligible traffic before launch; if the answer is too long, change the design, never the arithmetic.

Relative and absolute blurred. Symptom: "5 per cent" quoted by two people who mean different things. Misunderstanding: that a percentage is self-explanatory. Diagnostic: write baseline, target and unit side by side.

8. What good looks like

Written out, the core of the page reads: "If we show a free-delivery progress bar at checkout to Ahmedabad and Surat users whose basket is under ₹199, the share who place an order within 24 hours rises from 40.0 per cent by at least 2.0 percentage points, because the ₹30 fee currently appears with no visible way to avoid it." Around that sentence sits the rest of the document. A good version of Poorna's week produces one page, frozen before launch: the sentence in the standard form, the metric with numerator, denominator and window, the sample-size line with every input visible, the dates, the guardrails, and the action on each possible result. Prerak can recompute the page without asking a question. Pradyumn can read it and know what his ask has been converted into. Anyone opening it after the readout can tell what the team believed, what it planned to do in each case, and whether the data agreed.

9. What Poorna decided

On Friday 11 September Poorna froze the page: 14 days from Monday 21 September, the 2.0 pp MDE, the 1.85 pp shipping floor, the ₹3 margin guardrail, readout on 6 October. Pradyumn accepted it because the schedule still reached Navratri; the six-week alternative did not. She chose the larger effect not because she expected it but because a smaller one could not repay the sprint, and the calendar could not test it. Next, A/B testing fundamentals explains randomisation and why the two arms of Table 1 can be treated as otherwise comparable, and Choosing experiment metrics deepens the third step.

Two questions to sit with. First, if the 95 per cent interval came back as −0.3 to +2.1 pp, which parts of the page would you re-read before deciding? Second, which of your own current projects could you write in the standard form today, and where does the "because" run out?
case40v1-exp.metrics.choice:
Gurutva Technologies: Forty-two Days in Kochi

A case for discussion. Gurutva Technologies Private Limited is fictional; the market, the regulators and the brands around it are not.

1. Koramangala, Sunday night

At five past eleven on Sunday 11 October 2026, Nireeksha Yeldhose had three documents open on a kitchen table in Koramangala, Bengaluru, and could not make them agree: Ginti's readout on a forty-two-day test that ended on 11 August, a finance memo of 3 September, and a two-page credit note of 24 September. Each described the same riders, and no two of them agreed.

At half past nine the next morning the product council would ask her which number decides this test and which numbers must not get worse; the chief executive had told her on Saturday that it would not take an answer in two parts. The answer carried a ship date. The bank's notice period opens on 14 October and the Diwali freeze closes the release train on 26 October, so a decision on Monday could put Set-Aside in front of 9,42,000 riders on 20 October. Exhibit 1 is the calendar she had drawn that evening.

On the back of an envelope she had written two figures, ₹91.0 lakh and ₹72.6 lakh, and had not decided which of them she believed.

2. The company, and a decision made in March 2025

Gurutva was founded in Bengaluru in June 2019 by Navaneeth Yelanthoor and two colleagues, to lend against a delivery rider's next payout. The RBI's digital lending guidelines of September 2022 moved disbursal onto a bank's books, and the default-loss-guarantee circular of June 2023 capped the cover it could offer a lender at 5 per cent of the disbursed portfolio, turning a lender into a distributor. In November 2023 it added a savings pot, held by its sponsor bank, into which a rider could route part of a payout.

On 12 March 2025 Gurutva signed the master agreement that still governs that pot. Schedule 4 fixes a guardrail: failed payout mandates measured at the gateway may not exceed 1.80 per cent of mandates attempted in a calendar month, and any change to the mandate flow needs thirty days' written notice. In the same month, to hold the bank's integration date, the company put experiment assignment inside its own mobile app rather than at the payout gateway. That decision is why a rider is randomised when the app opens rather than when money moves, why a reinstall can land a rider in the other arm, and why the gateway, where mandate failures are counted, cannot split traffic.

A Series B of ₹268 crore closed in November 2025, of which ₹216 crore has been drawn. At 30 September 2026 Gurutva had 18,60,000 registered riders and 9,42,000 monthly active; FY26 revenue was ₹78.4 crore, ₹8.1 crore of it from enterprise fleet contracts.

3. The industry

Gurutva sells to the people who move India's parcels and biryani. Its riders drive for Zomato, Swiggy, Zepto, Blinkit, Rapido, Ola and Uber, often for two at once, and the money it touches moves over UPI on NPCI's rails. The pot competes for the same ₹500 a week as Groww, Zerodha and a chit fund run by a cousin, badly on brand and well on timing, because it asks as a payout lands. Rajasthan's platform-based gig worker legislation of 2023 and the welfare-fee ordinance Karnataka has drafted would both put a levy into that same payout. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 governs what Gurutva may ask the bank about a named rider.

The company is also, for its size, spread thin. Its platform squad of six sits in Pune, its principal data scientist in Toronto, nine and a half hours behind Bengaluru until 1 November; design is contracted to Berlin, the helpdesk is in Singapore; and its largest contract is with Gharbia Mobility FZ-LLC of Dubai, worth ₹1.94 crore a year at current rider counts. Exhibit 6 sketches who holds what.

4. What happened, and what has since been said about it

Set-Aside, designed between February and June 2026, is a prompt shown once a payout clears, offering to route part of a rider's earnings into the pot. The build was frozen on 24 June and the pilot ran from 1 July to 11 August in Kochi, Kozhikode and Pune. Ginti, the platform Gurutva built for itself, randomised on app-open. Of 78,645 riders who opened the app in the window, 1,845 — 2.35 per cent — appeared in both arms after a reinstall and were dropped, leaving 76,800 analysed, 38,400 an arm. On 21 July Gharbia Mobility's Indian fleet came onto the app, and 18,200 of its riders in Kochi and Kozhikode entered the pool with twenty-two days of exposure rather than forty-two.

On 20 August Ginti published Exhibit 2, and on the strength of its headline rate the team's working position through late August was that Set-Aside lifted first deposits by 1.70 percentage points and should ship. On 3 September finance circulated a memo putting realised margin on an activated saver at ₹742 over the 180 days following activation, measured on the 1,38,500 savers of Exhibit 4's cohort. On 24 September the credit team attributed ₹171 of incremental credit margin per activated saver rather than the memo's ₹286, on a matched-pairs comparison rather than a randomised one. Both are in Exhibit 4.

On 29 September Nachammai Yeroor reconciled the helpdesk against the app's in-product help log and found the two disagree by 641 contacts, 454 of them in the treatment arm; Exhibit 5 shows both. On 2 October Gharbia Mobility's group operations office asked for a renewal decision by 20 November and for a retention number Gurutva does not publish.

5. The people

Nireeksha Yeldhose, director of product, savings and credit, Bengaluru. Position: a test has a decision rule or it is not a test, and the rule is written before the council. Incentive: her remit exists to make the pot pay for itself this year. Not saying: on 7 August she assured the bank's relationship manager that Set-Aside “does not touch the mandate path”; Ginti's event order puts the prompt one screen before the mandate confirmation.

Navaneeth Yelanthoor, co-founder and chief executive, Bengaluru. Position: first deposits are what the company can move this quarter; anything measured at ninety days is for a company with ninety days to spare. Incentive: two board cycles carried on activation counts. Not saying: ₹52 crore of the Series B is conditioned on 6,00,000 activated savers by 31 March 2027; the count was 4,12,000 on 30 September — 1,88,000 in 182 days, or 1,033 a day.

Nilabja Yelamkulam, principal data scientist, Toronto. Position: one criterion in rupees, fixed before the test, is the defensible way to trade a deposit against a support contact. Incentive: he built Ginti and is judged on whether its readouts survive finance. Not saying: he has e-mailed the bank's analytics team for mandate failures at rider level, which Schedule 6 does not let him request without the bank's data officer signing off.

Nagalakshmi Yedthare, director of engineering, Pune. Position: the gateway rebuild that would let Gurutva randomise where money moves is eleven engineer-weeks, deferred four times since March 2025; of the twelve engineer-weeks her six have between 12 and 26 October, seven are committed to the bank's API migration. Incentive: her squad is measured on reliability through the peak. Not saying: two of her six platform engineers have accepted offers elsewhere and leave on 31 October.

Nelson Yekkebail, lead product designer, Berlin, on contract since March 2025. Position: the pilot measured whether a rider taps a prompt, not whether a rider saves. Incentive: his contract renews on shipped work. Not saying: the variant the council reviewed in June defaults to 2 per cent of each payout; the build frozen on 24 June carries a flat ₹50 a day, and his revised file is dated 2 July.

Nachammai Yeroor, customer success lead, Singapore. Position: contacts per thousand riders is a guardrail with a number on it, and the number moved by half again. Incentive: her FY27 headcount plan assumes a contact rate falling for three quarters. Not saying: 384 of the window's helpdesk contacts were raised in bulk by Gharbia's fleet supervisors on riders' behalf, under a permission granted on 29 July.

Nimrat Yethadka, head of enterprise sales, New Jersey. Position: the fleet segment renews on a retention number and activation is not one. Incentive: the renewal is 24 per cent of her book. Not saying: she has already told Gharbia's group operations office that Gurutva will report a contractual ninety-day balance from November.

6. Exhibits

Exhibit 2 is what the council has read. Every rate in it is over 38,400 riders in one arm, and the minimum detectable effects are recomputed from that arm size, not quoted from the design document.

Exhibit 3 is Yelamkulam's answer, written on the Friday: one number in rupees per randomised rider. Exhibit 4 is where its money comes from and Exhibit 5 its cost.

7. Voices

“If we are putting a rupee value on it, put the real one. Sixty-eight per cent are still holding at day ninety, so the ₹742 is worth about ₹505 a saver once you take the churn off. Price the fleet renewal on that and it still clears.”

N. Yethadka, e-mail to Yeldhose, Tuesday 6 October, 10:41 EDT

“Nimrat, the ₹742 already has the churn in it — it is realised margin over 180 days, not a promise at day one. Multiplying it by 0.68 charges the same leakage twice. And ₹742 is the wrong number anyway: the credit team's ₹171 at least came from a comparison. Use ₹627 and the criterion is +₹7.71, not +₹9.66.”

N. Yelamkulam, reply, Friday 9 October, 16:12 EDT (Saturday 10 October, 01:42 IST)

“A prompt tap is a prompt tap. We tested whether the sentence works. Nobody has tested whether this prompt leaves a rider with ₹400 put away in August still holding it in November, and that is the sentence I wrote the design for.”

8. The options as Yeldhose sees them

Four are on the envelope, all priced off one volume base — the 9,42,000 monthly-active riders of 30 September 2026, of whom 62,400 are Gharbia's — and one unit cost, ₹1.42 lakh per engineer-week, from the platform squad's loaded ₹68.2 lakh per engineer a year over 48 chargeable weeks. Deferred value is quoted at the criterion's +₹9.66; at +₹7.71 each figure scales, to rounding, to 79.8 per cent of it.

A. Decide on activation. The 7-day first-deposit rate is primary, the 42-day balance secondary, and mandate failures at the Schedule 4 cap and helpdesk contacts per thousand are the guardrails. Ships to the full base on 20 October inside the notice already served: three engineer-weeks, ₹4.26 lakh, no deferral.

B. Decide on the day-90 balance. Hold until the 9 November readout; the freeze then puts the ship on 16 November, twenty-seven days later than A. One engineer-week at ₹1.42 lakh and ₹13.6 lakh of value not earned. Nothing is rebuilt, and the gateway still cannot split traffic.

C. Rebuild and re-run. Move assignment to the payout gateway, where mandate failures are counted, and re-run forty-two days from 23 November on a criterion fixed in advance. Eleven engineer-weeks, ₹15.62 lakh: five before the freeze and six in the week after it lifts, on the squad of six. Full exposure moves to 4 January — thirty-four days at none and forty-two at half, or fifty-five full-exposure-equivalent days, ₹27.8 lakh.

D. Ship to the fleet contract. Give Set-Aside to Gharbia's 62,400 India riders on 18 November, before the renewal, and read ninety-day balances off the client's payroll file. Six engineer-weeks, ₹8.52 lakh, and twenty-nine days of deferral on that segment, ₹0.97 lakh; one 180-day window on those riders is ₹6.03 lakh. The other 8,79,600 are not exposed, and the segment reads back the fleet's twenty-two-day cohort.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The product council sits at 09:30 IST on Monday 12 October. The thirty-day notice served on 14 September names the Set-Aside prompt and nothing else, so it opens the mandate flow on 14 October for that change alone; notice for any other flow served on Monday would land on 11 November, inside the freeze. Schedule 4 caps failed mandates at 1.80 per cent of mandates attempted in a calendar month, measured at the gateway, with a cure period and a right to suspend new mandates. The release train is frozen from 26 October to 15 November around Diwali on 8 November. Gharbia Mobility's letter of 2 October asks for a decision by 20 November on a contract worth ₹1.94 crore a year, and asks for a retention figure. The quarter's discretionary product budget has ₹24 lakh left in it. The day-90 balances of the pilot's last-exposed riders close on 9 November, and the rider-level data that would tie a mandate failure to an arm sits with the bank.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Exhibit 2's first-deposit rate is over 38,400 riders an arm. State that denominator exactly, and say which of Gurutva's 18,60,000 registered riders could not enter it.
  2. Exhibit 2 puts a 0.22-point move in riders with a failed mandate against an MDE of 0.24, and Schedule 4 caps failed mandates at 1.80 per cent of mandates attempted. At what power, and against which threshold, should the council read that row?
  3. Recompute Exhibit 3's criterion on Exhibit 5's in-product counts. How far does it move, and what does that say about its support term?
  4. Exhibit 3's money leg rests on the ₹742 of the 3 September memo; Exhibit 4 also carries the ₹627 of the 24 September note. How would you choose between them by 09:30 Monday, and what if you could not?
  5. Yedthare's eleven engineer-weeks, the freeze of 26 October to 15 November, her five uncommitted weeks before it and the resignations of 31 October are all on this page. Put them together: what do the four options' dates become?
  6. Exhibit 2's day-90 row cannot be read before 9 November and Gharbia decides on 20 November. It is 09:30 on Monday: what do you decide, what do you commit to measure, and what do you say to the board?

The council is ten and a half hours away

Yeldhose turned the envelope over. Under the two figures was a third she had struck out, from an arithmetic she had done twice and did not trust. On the other side was a line copied from Yekkebail about a rider with ₹400 put away in August, and beside it the date 9 November, circled. In Toronto it was half past one in the afternoon and Yelamkulam was online; in Singapore, half past one in the morning. She had until half past nine to decide which of these numbers was the test.
exp40v2-exp.metrics.choice:
Choosing experiment metrics

Primary, secondary and guardrail: which metric decides the test, and which ones must not get worse.

1. Two rooms, a month apart

On Tuesday 17 February 2026, above Lower Parel, Tushita Dharod had four candidate metrics on a whiteboard and eight working days before randomisation. Dharod ran product at Khushaal Money, a savings and mutual-fund app with a redesigned auto-invest flow waiting behind a flag. Enrolment opened Monday 2 March and closed Sunday 15 March: 4,80,000 eligible users, 2,40,000 an arm.

None was controversial on its own. Setup completion rate, which growth had used for two years. First mandate debit, which payments preferred because an unfunded mandate is worth nothing. Day-90 retained investor, which strategy called the only honest number. And 90-day net revenue per exposed user, the only candidate in rupees. The argument was which would be allowed to decide. Tarjani Dungarwal, the staff data scientist, arrived with the funnel and an observation that reframed the meeting: three of the four could not detect the effect the team expected.

A month later, on Thursday 19 March, Tanush Davda faced a narrower version in Pune. Kaarobar Systems sold GST filing software to 3,140 mid-market manufacturers, ₹58.09 crore of recurring revenue at ₹1.85 lakh an account. His test would randomise 1,120 accounts on Monday 6 April, 560 each way. The window had to run 21 days, to Sunday 26 April: the 20 April GSTR-3B deadline was the busiest filing day it could contain, and a 14-day window would have missed it. Tapasvini Derasari's memo said what Davda suspected: at 560 accounts an arm, almost nothing he cared about was measurable.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

A primary metric decides the test: named before randomisation, given a direction, with the launch rule written against it. A secondary explains the primary and may never overturn it. A guardrail must not get worse, and is tested as a constraint rather than a goal. An overall evaluation criterion, or OEC, is a single pre-registered scalar standing in for long-term value, so that one test yields one verdict.

The apparatus came from three traditions. Neyman and Pearson gave it the idea that a test is a decision rule with two error rates, not a search for truth. Ross Prentice, in 1989 on clinical trials, gave it the criterion that a surrogate is admissible only if the treatment's whole effect on the outcome passes through it — which almost nothing satisfies. The web experimentation literature of the late 2000s, Kohavi especially, gave it the OEC and the discipline of naming it first. Amazon's controllable inputs and lagging outputs gave it the organisational form most teams inherit.

They do not agree. The OEC school signs "a test must have exactly one pre-registered decision quantity" and refuses "that quantity should be the business outcome itself." The input-metric school signs "the primary must be what this team can move inside one cycle" and refuses "one composite can carry a launch decision." The surrogacy school signs "a proxy is admissible only against a criterion tested on past experiments" and refuses "a high user-level correlation is evidence." The decision-theoretic school signs "choose the set that minimises expected regret." The vanity-metric critique signs one proposition only: the primary must be able to go down.

3. Mechanics: the arithmetic nobody writes on the whiteboard

Dungarwal's funnel is Figure 1: a rate chain, whose discipline is that every level reconciles with the one above it.

Four levels were candidate primaries, per exposed user: setup completion 6.000%, first debit 3.900%, day-90 investor 2.730%, revenue ₹37.00. Dungarwal's question was not which mattered most but which the test could see. For an equal-split two-sided test at the 5% level with 80% power, the smallest detectable relative effect turns on the coefficient of variation.

relative MDE = CV × √(15.6978 ⁄ n), where 15.6978 = 2 × (1.95996 + 0.84162)² and n is the sample per arm. For a binary metric at base rate p, CV = √((1 − p) ⁄ p).

That line does most of the work. A rarer event is a noisier one: halve the base rate and the CV rises by roughly √2. And continuity is not inherently helpful: Khushaal's heavy-tailed revenue metric has a CV of 6.50 — ₹240.50 of standard deviation on ₹37.00 of mean — worse than any binary in the tree.

Marginal completers reach a first debit at 42.25% against the average 65.0%, then retain at 70.0%: 576 × 0.4225 = 243 funded mandates, × 0.70 = 170 day-90 investors, 2.59% of 6,552. Two second-order moves deserve naming, since competent teams skip both. Winsorising revenue at the 99th percentile cuts the CV from 6.50 to 4.10 and the relative MDE from 5.257% to 3.316% — the sensitivity of 2.5 times the traffic, for a capped and slightly biased total. CUPED, regressing out pre-period revenue, multiplies the standard deviation by √(1 − ρ²); at ρ = 0.55 that is 0.8352, giving 4.391%.

The third move went wrong. The finance partner proposed a proper OEC: give each completer an imputed 90-day value of ₹600 × 0.650 = ₹390.00 — ₹600 already averages over every funded mandate, lapsed or not, so the 0.700 retention must not be applied twice — and subtract ₹1,150 for each uninstall within 30 days. The control mean is 390 × 0.06 − 1,150 × 0.038 = −₹20.30, whose first term is the tree's auto-invest line exactly. Take corr(complete, uninstall) = −0.09, so the covariance is −0.09 × √(0.0564 × 0.036556) = −0.00409 and the variance is 390² × 0.0564 + 1,150² × 0.036556 + 2 × 390 × 1,150 × 0.00409 = 60,589 on the unrounded covariance: a standard deviation of ₹246.15 and an absolute MDE of ₹1.99 an exposed user. Two things follow. The fixed ₹390 values all 576 marginal completers at the average, so the OEC models ₹0.94 where the revenue chain gives ₹0.61 — 54% high. And even on that inflated effect it has 26% power, because the uninstall term, which the treatment almost certainly does not move, carries 80% of the variance. Composites are not free.

4. When the idea applies, and when it misleads

Three conditions, as testable claims. First: the primary needs an effect-to-MDE ratio above about 1.0 for the effect the team genuinely expects. Khushaal passes on setup completion at 1.25 and fails below it; Kaarobar fails on every candidate in Table 2 at the 10.0% lift Davda expected, worst at account level. Second: the primary must sit downstream of the change and upstream of the money, with no intervening step the treatment also moves. Khushaal's primary and Kaarobar's filing rate pass; Khushaal's second guardrail fails, conditioned on completing setup, so the arms do not compare the same population. Third: the metric must fit a window the data spans. Khushaal's event log retains 120 days, and the 14-day CUPED pre-period pushes the span back to 16 February, so 16 February to the last day-90 outcome on Saturday 13 June is 117 days, 3 to spare. A 28-day pre-period would have needed 131 and was dropped. The 90-day uninstall guardrail first proposed went the same way: the device attribution feed retains 45 days, so 30 is the longest the signal supports.
