5. Hard edge cases

In multi-product companies the seam is ownership: payments' primary is lending's guardrail, and the two hold different priors about the ₹1,150. Mature organisations make that number a company-level constant nobody may redefine inside a test plan. In two-sided marketplaces the randomisation unit is the problem: a supply-side change tested on drivers contaminates riders, so the honest primary is market-level, measured in switchback cells, and the honest guardrail sits on the side you did not randomise. In regulated products the guardrail is a legal floor, not a statistical one — a disclosure must appear — and a floor cannot be traded against a point estimate.

Hardware-plus-software carries a lag the software side rarely internalises: a returns rate takes a shipping cycle to appear, so the in-test primary is a proxy and the question is who reconciles the two a quarter later. AI-native products are the sharpest version. Offline evaluation sets and model win rates are proxies with excellent power and unknown surrogacy, and finding out they were the wrong proxy is paid for in training cycles rather than one shipped feature. What mature companies do, rather than what their blog posts say, is maintain a slow, well-powered holdout — a population excluded from everything for a quarter — the only instrument that measures what the proxies stand in for.

6. Nine distinctions that separate the expert

A value-weighted OEC built on one binary has exactly the power of that binary. Multiplying setup completion by ₹390.00 changes units: the CV stays 3.958, the relative MDE 3.201%, the p-values agree to three decimals. The tell is a rupee OEC and a completion rate with different significance stars. The weighting buys tradeability, not power.

A proxy's correlation with the outcome is not its ability to detect a change in the outcome. Every Khushaal day-90 investor completed setup first, so the proxy is a gate and the phi coefficient between the two indicators is fixed by the base rates at √(0.0273 × 0.94 ⁄ (0.06 × 0.9727)) = 0.663. The tell is a user-level correlation quoted in a metric-selection meeting.

What governs surrogacy is the correlation of lifts, not of levels. Across twelve Khushaal experiments from January 2025 to January 2026, the lifts on setup completion and day-90 investor correlated 0.41; signs agreed in eight of the twelve, and of the five that moved setup significantly, two moved day-90 the other way. On twelve points the 95% interval runs −0.21 to 0.80, so the surrogacy evidence is nearly uninformative. The tell is the 0.41 cited without the interval.

A guardrail conditioned on a treatment-affected step is not a guardrail. Khushaal's care-contact rate is computed over completers, and the treatment moves who completes. The arms have different denominators by construction — a collider — with no signable direction of bias. The tell is a guardrail whose denominator differs between arms; the fix is everybody exposed.

The MDE is not the significance threshold. The MDE is 2.8016 standard errors, the effect caught four times in five; significance needs 1.95996. At Kaarobar's pooled 1,140 accounts an arm the difference has a standard error of 2.09 pp, so the MDE is 5.85 pp but anything above 4.09 pp clears: an observed 5.53 pp is below the MDE and significant at p = 0.008.

Variance reduction is cheaper than sample, and nobody budgets for it. Winsorising cost Khushaal an afternoon and bought the sensitivity of 2.5 times the traffic. The diagnostic is the primary's pre-period correlation, which on most teams nobody has computed. The tell is a plan asking for more days before it asks for ρ.

The unit of analysis is not the unit of randomisation, and the gap is a design effect, not a free lunch. Kaarobar's 6,440 users an arm look like a relative MDE of 8.79%; the design effect of 2.89 forced by an intra-class correlation of 0.18 puts it back to 14.94%, against 18.13% at account level — real, and small. The tell is an interval that narrows when a team changes row granularity with no intra-class correlation in sight.

Lengthening the window inside a cluster asymptotes, computably: effective sample tends to clusters divided by the intra-class correlation. Kshipra Health Systems, at 210 clinicians an arm and ρ = 0.42, caps at 500 effective units however many days are added. The tell is a team extending four weeks to twelve to rescue power.

Choosing the metric after seeing the data is what pre-registration was invented to stop. Four metrics each at the 5% level give a family-wise false-positive rate of 1 − 0.95⁴, or 18.5%. The tell is a deck whose headline metric is not the one in the plan. What works is a dated rule naming the primary, its direction, its threshold and each guardrail's MDE.

7. How it changes across product types and stages

The formula does not change; which term dominates does. Consumer products have enormous n and tiny base rates, so base rate binds and the winning move is to take the primary up the funnel. B2B and enterprise have small n and clustered observations, so cluster count binds and the winning move is more accounts, not a longer window. Platforms and marketplaces are constrained by interference, which the formula does not model. Hardware is constrained by lag. AI products are constrained by surrogacy: the proxies are abundant and well powered and nobody knows what they stand in for.

Stage matters less than people claim. A seed-stage company with 400 weekly actives cannot run this arithmetic and should use qualitative evidence and pre-post with eyes open. From roughly series B the arithmetic becomes the constraint and stays it. The genuine stage effect is organisational: early companies can change the north star in a meeting and late ones cannot, which makes a bad north star far more expensive late than changing one early.

8. Three worked examples

Khushaal shipped. Setup completion moved from 6.000% to 6.247%, a relative 4.12% against an MDE of 3.201%, p < 0.001. The powered guardrail moved from 3.800% to 3.772%, inside its 0.155 pp MDE. Day-90 investor rose to 2.808% and revenue to ₹37.74, neither significant nor expected to be — the readout printed 32% and 14% beside them so no null read as a zero.

Kaarobar did not ship on the first window: 258 of 560 control accounts filed against 289 of 560 treatment, 5.54 pp at p = 0.064. Davda had pre-committed, unseen, to a second window of 1,160 fresh accounts from Monday 1 June to Sunday 21 June, holding the 20 June deadline so the two were like-for-like. It gave 268 of 580 against 300 of 580, 5.52 pp. Pooled, 526 and 589 of 1,140: 5.53 pp, z = 2.64, p = 0.008. He shipped, noting in line two that the ticket guardrail's 33.49% MDE had proved nothing.

Kshipra Health Systems is the failure. Its clinical-documentation assistant was tested on 420 clinicians at NABH-accredited hospitals, 210 an arm, from Monday 11 May to Sunday 7 June 2026, with suggestion acceptance as the primary. Acceptance rose from 31.0% to 38.2%. Allowing for clustering within clinician, the effective sample is the 500 units of section 6, and 7.2 pp on a standard error of 3.01 pp is z = 2.39, p ≈ 0.017 — significant, not overwhelming. Tejashwar Dudhwala's team declared victory anyway.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Proxy drift. The proxy keeps winning and the north star flattens. Warning sign: three consecutive wins with no movement in the quarterly review. Diagnostic: what is the lift-to-lift correlation over the last twelve tests? Caught late, the cost is a year of features and a team that distrusts its instruments.

Guardrail theatre. A guardrail that has never once fired. Warning sign: a readout saying "no significant harm" with no number beside it. Diagnostic: what is its MDE, and what harm would it miss? Caught late, harm ships with a green tick on it.

Metric substitution after the readout. Warning sign: the deck's headline metric is not in the plan. Diagnostic: show me the dated pre-registration. Caught late, the whole experiment history becomes uninterpretable, because nobody can tell which results were chosen afterwards.

Denominator drift. Warning sign: the arms have different exposure counts, usually because a trigger sits downstream of the treatment. Diagnostic: were both arms counted at the same point in the flow? Caught late, every effect is biased by an unknown amount and direction.

The composite nobody can decompose. Warning sign: a one-number OEC whose components have not been printed in six months. Diagnostic: which term carries the variance? Caught late, the organisation optimises an average it no longer understands, and its dominant weight is usually the worst-evidenced.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

One number or a small panel. The OEC position is that organisations act well on one result and badly on three, that a composite forces the trade-offs to be argued before the data arrives, and that every dashboard becomes a negotiation in the end. The panel position is that a composite hides what a launch decision needs, that the arithmetic above shows how badly one can be built, and that a written rule over three metrics pre-commits without the opacity. The first fails if teams rebuild the components anyway; the second, if they renegotiate the rule afterwards.

Whether a proxy may ever decide a launch. The Prentice-style position is that a surrogate is admissible only when the treatment effect on the outcome is fully mediated by it, and almost no product proxy has been tested that way. The pragmatist answers that the alternative is not better measurement but none, since outcome metrics are unpowered at any feasible sample. The pragmatist is wrong if proxy-selected changes never accumulate into north-star movement; the purist, if waiting costs more than the wrong calls.

How a guardrail should be tested. One camp argues the guardrail's null should be inverted: the null is that harm exceeds tolerance, so passing needs evidence of safety rather than absence of evidence of harm. The other accepts this is formally correct and calls it unsustainable — though not for the reason usually given, since a one-sided non-inferiority test at the same margin needs about 79% of the superiority sample, not twice it. The real cost is that every guardrail then needs a tolerance agreed beforehand, which teams do not maintain. Most large programmes have landed on a hybrid neither camp would defend in print.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this recites primary, secondary and guardrail, and produces a tidy list. Someone who has internalised it does four things differently. They compute the MDE before arguing about which metric is meaningful, because meaningfulness that cannot be measured is not a candidate. They state the power of every null result, so a flat line is reported as a flat line of a stated width. They name the guardrails they could not power rather than omitting them. And they treat surrogacy as an empirical claim with a maintained evidence base: a file of past lift pairs, updated quarterly, that anyone may see.

12. What each of them decided

Dharod pre-registered setup completion as the primary, published the ₹390.00 imputed-value OEC beside it as reporting, not a decision rule, powered the uninstall guardrail over the full 2,40,000, and kept the care-contact rate in the readout with two words on it: descriptive only. Her reasoning: the only candidate with an effect-to-MDE ratio above one was the only one capable of producing a decision. Davda chose the account-level binary over the richer per-account count purely on the coefficient of variation, 1.083 against 1.400, and moved the churn guardrail to a review 90 days after launch, outside the experiment, where it could be measured.

  1. Day-90 investor is closer to what Khushaal cares about than setup completion, and cannot decide the test. On what grounds, if any, should a company run a test it knows is underpowered on the metric it cares about?
  2. The imputed-value OEC has the power of setup completion with one term and 26% with two. What rule should govern admitting a second term into a composite?
  3. Davda pooled two windows and reported p = 0.008 on an effect below his design MDE. Replication or second bite, and what written beforehand would change your answer?

13. Going deeper

Writing an experiment hypothesis — where a vague hypothesis is forced to become falsifiable. Guardrail metrics — the constraint side, where the power arithmetic is most often skipped. Proxies for long-term value — surrogacy done properly, with the holdout designs that test it. A/B testing fundamentals — the assignment machinery these metrics sit on. Significance, power, sample size, peeking — section 3's formula derived, and what sequential looks do to it. When you can't A/B test — what replaces the primary when randomisation is impossible. Experimentation culture — why pre-registration survives in some organisations. Qual + quant feedback loop — finding out why a guardrail moved. Feature flags and flighting — what sets your exposure denominator.
exp20v2-exp.metrics.choice:
Choosing Experiment Metrics

Which metric decides the test, and which ones must not get worse?

1. Four days to define success

On Thursday 12 March 2026, Saurin Chudasama, head of product at Jholi Fresh, an Ahmedabad grocery-delivery company serving three Gujarat cities, had four days to write down what a successful experiment would mean. The test was built. A "reorder shelf" on the home screen would show each returning customer her five most frequently bought items, each one tap from the basket. Launch was fixed for Monday 16 March.

The design was not the difficulty. The dashboard offered forty-one candidate numbers, and each executive favoured a different one. Shrenik Chotai, who ran city operations, wanted revenue to decide, because his quarterly target was set in gross merchandise value (GMV, the rupee value of goods ordered). Satvik Chheda, the data scientist, doubted that revenue could decide anything within thirteen days. Shaily Chavda, the finance partner, asked what would stop the company buying faster ordering with later deliveries.

Two earlier tests that year had been declared wins on tap-through rate and then vanished from the order data. A metric too noisy to move would leave the shelf "flat", shipped or shelved on opinion. A metric too easy to move would ship something that only looked good.

Figure 1 fixes the dates that govern everything below. Metrics are locked on the 12th, before anyone has seen a result. Customers enter over one week and are each watched for seven days, long enough to include every weekday once, which matters in a business where Sunday behaviour differs from Tuesday's.

2. The idea

A primary metric is the single measurement on which the ship-or-stop decision rests. A secondary (or diagnostic) metric explains why the primary moved. A guardrail is a measurement that must not worsen beyond a stated tolerance, whatever the primary does. An overall evaluation criterion (OEC) is the full decision rule that combines them. Ron Kohavi and colleagues, working on web experimentation at Amazon and later Microsoft, set the term out in their 2009 survey of controlled experiments.

The device exists because of arithmetic. Forty-one metrics each tested at a 5 per cent significance level would, with no real effect anywhere, produce about two "significant" movements (41 x 0.05 = 2.05). Teams that read all of them will always find a win. Choosing one primary before launch keeps the error rate honest; the guardrails keep the win from being bought at the customer's expense. The economist Charles Goodhart observed in 1975 that a measure used as a target stops measuring what it did, which is why a guardrail set must stand beside any single target.

Saurin's sentence for the meeting: "The primary metric decides whether we ship, the guardrails decide whether we are allowed to, and everything else only helps us understand."

Figure 2 separates the roles by what each may do. The primary and the guardrails both reach the decision rule, but they answer opposite questions: one asks for evidence of gain, the other for evidence of no serious harm. Secondary metrics sit apart, and that separation is the discipline: they may explain a result but cannot rescue or sink one.

3. How it works

The mechanics have six steps, and the third and fifth are usually left implicit. First, state the mechanism in the hypothesis: the shelf removes search effort, so more returning customers should order in a week. Second, draw the driver tree, the decomposition of the business outcome into the quantities that multiply to it. Third, fix the unit and the window: customers, seven days from first exposure, because the randomisation unit and the analysis unit should match. Fourth, pick the primary from the tree by its closeness to the mechanism. Fifth, give each guardrail a numerical tolerance. Sixth, write the decision rule.

Figure 3 shows why the tree matters: it makes the choice a choice among named levels rather than forty-one loose numbers. The reorder shelf plausibly acts on the order rate (more customers order at all), possibly on orders per orderer, and could perhaps lower order value. Saurin chose the order rate, the share of enrolled customers who place at least one order in their seven days, because it sits closest to the mechanism. The guardrails sit outside the tree because they track costs the tree does not show. The sixth step then turns the choices into a sentence a stranger could apply: ship if the primary's lift is significant at 5 per cent and each guardrail's upper bound stays under its tolerance.

4. A worked example

Satvik's argument was about variance. For a metric with standard deviation σ across customers, the smallest true change a test can reliably detect (its minimum detectable effect, MDE) at a 5 per cent two-sided significance level and 80 per cent power, with n customers per arm, is δ = √(15.698 σ² / n). The constant is 2 x (1.95996 + 0.84162)² = 15.698, used unrounded throughout, as are the standard deviations shown to three places. The enrolment week brought 2,40,000 customers, so n = 1,20,000 per arm.

MetricBaselineSDRelative MDE, 1,20,000 per armRelative MDE, 60,000 per armPer arm for a 2% lift
Order rate0.4000.4901.40%1.98%58,867
Orders per customer0.901.501.91%2.70%1,09,012
GMV per customerRs 310.50Rs 7202.65%3.75%2,11,018

Take the order rate. Its variance is 0.4 x 0.6 = 0.24, so δ = √(15.698 x 0.24 / 1,20,000) = 0.0056, or 0.56 percentage points: 1.40 per cent of 0.40. Orders per customer, with variance 2.25, gives 0.0172 orders, 1.91 per cent of 0.90. GMV, with variance 720² = 5,18,400, gives Rs 8.23, 2.65 per cent. Relative MDE scales with the ratio of the standard deviation to the baseline (1.22, 1.67 and 2.32), and 1.91 / 1.40 = 1.36 is the same ratio as 1.667 / 1.225. Revenue is not less important than orders; it is noisier, because a few large baskets dominate its spread.

The product team expected a lift near 2 per cent. At full traffic that is detectable on the order rate and, narrowly, on orders per customer, but not on GMV. The second pass changes one input. Suppose the shelf had reached only one city, giving 60,000 per arm. Every MDE grows by √2: the order rate becomes 1.98 per cent, still inside 2; orders per customer, at 2.70, falls out; GMV, at 3.75, is hopeless. The same hypothesis would then have one workable primary instead of two.

Figure 4 makes the second pass visible: halving traffic pushes each bar out by the same factor, and the metric that survives is the one that started shortest.

5. Nuances a learner must absorb

A primary is a rule, not a favourite

One primary does not mean one number reported. It means one number whose result, under a pre-written threshold, ships or stops the change. Secondary metrics may disagree; they then prompt questions, not verdicts. If order value falls while the order rate rises, the team asks why, but the rule written on 12 March still governs the decision. Without that discipline, every awkward result reopens the argument about what the test was for.

Sensitivity is variance relative to baseline

"Sensitive" has a calculation behind it: the standard deviation over the baseline, and the traffic available. A metric is not sensitive because it is close to the product, nor insensitive because it is financial. Ask three questions before relying on a sensitivity claim: what is its standard deviation, what is its baseline, and how many customers will the test actually enrol?

Correlation with the outcome is not the ability to detect change

Tap-through on the shelf may correlate strongly with ordering across customers and still say nothing about whether the shelf causes more orders; customers who like reordering tap more. A proxy must also move when the cause moves, by an amount that tracks the outcome's own change. The first property is correlation; the second is what the test needs, and the first does not imply it.

A guardrail needs its own power

A late-delivery tolerance of 0.5 points at a baseline of 8.0 per cent needs 15.698 x 0.08 x 0.92 / 0.005² = 46,214 orders per arm, using the baseline variance. The control arm had 1,08,000, so the guardrail was testable. A tolerance the test cannot resolve is decoration.

Ratio metrics and clustering

Late deliveries per order treats orders as independent, but a customer's orders are related, so the real standard error is somewhat larger than the simple one. Analyse at the customer level, or use methods built for ratios.

Windows must fit the story

A seven-day order rate cannot see whether the shelf builds a habit or merely pulls orders forward. Novelty also fades. The metric's window bounds what it can claim, and no metric, however well chosen, tells you why customers behaved as they did; that takes interviews.

Targets get gamed

If orders per customer decided, a team could split baskets into two orders. This is Goodhart's observation at small scale; the order-value and late-delivery guardrails exist to expose it.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace; early and large

Consumer products have the traffic to use rates and frequencies, as above. B2B products randomise accounts, not people, and have few: with 400 accounts per arm and a standard deviation equal to the mean, the same formula gives √(15.698 / 400) = 20 per cent relative MDE, so B2B teams use bigger changes, longer windows or paired designs. Marketplaces must guard the other side: a buyer-side lift that makes riders or sellers wait longer has borrowed from supply. For Jholi Fresh that is the late-delivery guardrail, since riders are the scarce side.

An early-stage company often cannot power any revenue metric and should say so, choosing larger effects and shorter causal chains. A large one carries a library of metrics with known variances, which makes the sensitivity table a lookup and the main risk is committee growth: guardrails multiply until nothing can ship.

7. Common mistakes

Choosing after the fact. Symptom: the headline metric differs between the launch memo and the read-out deck. Misunderstanding: a metric is a lens chosen after looking. Diagnostic: a dated metric specification, locked before launch, as in Figure 1.

An unpowered primary. Symptom: tests keep finishing "flat". Misunderstanding: that a flat result means no effect, when it may mean no resolution. Diagnostic: compute the MDE from last quarter's variance before launch, as in the table above.

Vanity metrics. Symptom: tap-through rises and orders do not. Misunderstanding: that activity is value. Diagnostic: ask what decision changes if the number moves; if none, it is a diagnostic at best.

8. What good looks like

By Thursday 12 March Saurin's one-page specification, signed off by Shrenik, Satvik and Shaily, named the order rate as primary, listed order value as secondary, set both guardrail tolerances, and stated the rule: ship if the order-rate lift is significant and the upper bound of each guardrail's rise stays under its tolerance. The read-out on Monday 30 March found the order rate at 40.9 per cent against 40.0, a lift of 0.9 points, 2.25 per cent relative, with a standard error of 0.20 points.

Orders per orderer stayed at 2.25, so the 49,080 ordering customers placed 1,10,430 orders. Late deliveries were 9,055 of them, 8.20 per cent, a rise of 0.20 points whose upper bound was about 0.43 before allowing for clustering. Contacts held at 6.10 per 100 orders (6,736), a rise of 0.10 with an upper bound near 0.30. Order value fell to Rs 338, so GMV per customer was Rs 311.04, Rs 0.54 above control against a standard error of Rs 2.94: noise.

9. Closing

On Tuesday 31 March Saurin recommended shipping to all three cities. Both guardrails stayed inside their pre-set tolerances and the primary moved by more than four standard errors. He reported the Rs 7 drop in order value and the flat GMV as the cost to watch, and told Shrenik that revenue had never been able to decide this test, since its MDE of Rs 8.23 exceeded the whole observed difference. The next topic is proxies for long-term value, because a seven-day order rate is itself a stand-in for retention.

Questions to sit with. First: Shrenik's target is in GMV. What would have to be true of the traffic and the variance for GMV to be an acceptable primary? Second: the late-delivery tolerance of 0.5 points was chosen by judgement. Who should own that number, and what evidence would you ask them for?
case20v1-exp.metrics.choice:
Edavam Fresh: What Decides the Test?

A teaching case on choosing experiment metrics

1. Opening

On Monday 12 October 2026, a little after seven in the evening, Manjula Vattakunnel closed the door of a small meeting room at Edavam Fresh's office in Infopark, Kochi, and wrote one question on the whiteboard: "What decides this test?" Four days remained. By 6:00 pm IST on Friday 16 October the plan for the next experiment had to be locked: the number that would decide it, the numbers that must not get worse, and the rule for reading them. Engineering would freeze the build on Saturday 17 October, and the test would start on Monday 19 October.

The test concerned a cart "top-up shelf", a strip of six suggested items shown beneath the free-delivery line. The chief executive wanted the feature, if it worked, live for Diwali on Sunday 8 November. A fourteen-day test would end on Sunday 1 November, results would be read on Wednesday 4 November, and the decision taken on Thursday 5 November. Manjula, the Director of Product, had three colleagues with three different views of what mattered most, and the call was hers.

2. Company background

Edavam Fresh was founded in Kochi in 2020 to deliver groceries and household essentials from small dark stores. By October 2026 it ran 38 of them: 12 in Kochi, 6 in Thiruvananthapuram, 14 in Bengaluru and 6 in Pune. It had 2,40,000 active customers, meaning those who had ordered in the previous 28 days. They placed an average of 1.65 orders a week at an average order value (AOV) of ₹420, a weekly merchandise value of ₹16.63 crore (2,40,000 × 1.65 × ₹420).

The field was crowded. Blinkit, Zepto and Swiggy Instamart contested the same Bengaluru and Pune customers; BigBasket and JioMart served scheduled baskets; and in Kerala the neighbourhood kirana, ordering by phone and WhatsApp, set the standard for trust. Most Edavam customers paid by UPI. Engineers sat in Bengaluru and Pune, the data science lead in Toronto, a product designer in Berlin and the dark-store operations team in Pune. Customer data in tests was used under the consent notice written for the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023.

3. The situation

The shelf was designed in Berlin and built in Pune. From Monday 28 September to Sunday 4 October Edavam ran a one-week pilot with 20,000 customers in each of two arms; the results, read out on Tuesday 6 October, are in Exhibit 1. Customers who saw the shelf spent more per order, ordered slightly less often and received a late delivery more often. The thread that followed the readout ran for days, and the three colleagues in section 4 each came away with a different view of what the pilot had shown. In the days since, Manjula had asked each of them to state what result would change their mind.

A higher free-delivery threshold, tested in February 2026 (Exhibit 2), lifted AOV; it was shipped to all other customers on 2 March, the test arms stayed assigned for eight weeks, and it was reversed on 20 April. A daily push-notification cadence tested in June lifted orders and was not shipped. The board's objective for the quarter ending 31 December was an AOV of ₹450.

Time zones shaped the debate. Marykutty Vazhappilly in Toronto, 9.5 hours behind IST until clocks change on 1 November, joined the Friday call at 8:30 am her time. The Berlin designer, 3.5 hours behind until 25 October, had already posted her view in the team channel: whichever number won, she wanted the six-item layout tested as built. Figure 1 shows the calendar.

Figure 1. Calendar, 28 September to 16 December 2026. Scale: 8 pixels per day from the start of 28 September; bars run from the start of their first day to the start of the day after their last, so each date marker sits at the start of its day.

4. The people

Manjula Vattakunnel, Director of Product, Kochi, joined in 2023. She owns the test plan and answers for the result on 5 November.

Mohandas Veliyath, Head of Growth, Bengaluru, was among the first ten employees. He wants AOV to decide. The shelf was designed to lift basket size, the board's ₹450 objective is an AOV figure, and the treatment arm in the pilot already stood at ₹456. He would like the test to read in fourteen days and ship before Diwali.

Marykutty Vazhappilly, Senior Data Scientist, Toronto, joined in 2022. She wants orders per customer over eight weeks to decide, citing the February test, and doubts that a one-week pilot of 20,000 customers per arm can settle a difference of three hundredths of an order.

Mukundan Valappil, Head of Dark-Store Operations, Pune, runs pickers and riders across all 38 stores. His concern is Diwali week, when staffing is thinnest. He wants late deliveries protected and has said that he will not accept a shelf that adds more than a point to the late share.

5. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 is the pilot, Exhibit 2 the two earlier tests, and Exhibit 3 the three ways Manjula could set the test.

6. The options

Option A: AOV decides. The shelf ships if AOV rises beyond chance; cancellations and late deliveries are watched as guardrails. It matches the board's ₹450 objective and reads on 4 November. Orders per customer and contribution are reported as secondary figures with no power over the decision, and the comparison needs no cost allocation from finance. It leaves eight-week buying behaviour unmeasured.

Option B: contribution per customer decides. The primary figure combines orders, basket size, delivery cost and refunds across every assigned customer. AOV and orders per customer are secondary; late-delivery share and support contacts per 100 orders are guardrails, with limits agreed with Mukundan before launch. It reads on 4 November. Finance must freeze its cost allocations first, and a fourteen-day window leaves later repeat behaviour unmeasured.

Option C: orders per customer over eight weeks decides. Both arms stay assigned from 19 October to 13 December, with contribution and late share as guardrails. It measures buying habit over an eight-week window like the February read. The readout falls on 16 December, so the decision on a full rollout comes after Diwali.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. Exhibit 1 reports seven measures for each arm, besides the customer count. For each, say what question it answers and what it cannot tell you.
  2. Exhibit 2 records two earlier decisions. What would each test have decided had a different measure in the table carried the decision, and what, if anything, does that suggest about how Edavam sets its rules?
  3. Choose which measure decides the test, which are secondary and which are guardrails. State your rule for a result in which the primary measure rises and a guardrail worsens.
  4. What would you tell the chief executive on Friday 16 October about what the test can and cannot say by 5 November, and what would lead you to change the plan after the data arrive?

8. A note for the learner

An experiment needs one primary metric that decides, secondary metrics that explain the movement, and guardrails that must not get worse. When several outcomes matter, an overall evaluation criterion folds them into one number whose composition is agreed before any data arrive.

One defensible path is Option B with a stronger tail. Set contribution per customer as the primary figure and require its 95 per cent interval to sit above zero. Fix guardrails on Friday: a late-delivery rise of no more than 1.0 point, and no fall in orders per customer beyond a margin the data science team names. On the pilot's numbers the shelf would not clear the late-delivery limit, which is the reason to write it first. If the test passes, roll out from 5 November to the 80,000 customers outside it and keep the 80,000 control customers unexposed until 13 December, so that eight-week orders per customer can still be read. Pre-agree that a fall there reverses the rollout. Record the rule, the margins and their owners in the plan document before launch, so the result is read against a rule written earlier.
case40v1-exp.flags:
Bodhika Technologies: Five Working Days to the Freeze

Bengaluru, Sunday 18 October 2026

1. The night before

At twenty minutes to midnight on Sunday 18 October 2026, Jenson Rayirath had three windows open in his flat in Indiranagar: Switchboard, the flag console his company had built itself in 2023, showing a targeting rule he had drafted and not saved; Exhibit 5, which he had finished at two that afternoon; and the pre-read his chief executive had sent the board on Friday, containing the sentence Checkout 3 adds ₹16.80 crore of merchant GMV through the festive fortnight — fourteen days at full exposure, 2.4 points, on our current base.

Rayirath was vice-president of product at Bodhika Technologies, a Bengaluru payments orchestrator whose hosted checkout sat in front of 2,340 Indian online merchants (Exhibit 1). Checkout 3, the rebuild his team had worked on since July, was live behind a flag on 418 long-tail merchants. Everything else ran Checkout 2.

Bodhika's change freeze began at 00:00 on Monday 26 October and lifted on Tuesday 10 November, two days after Diwali. Five working days lay between Monday morning and the freeze, and whatever share of traffic Checkout 3 held at midnight on the 25th was the share it would hold through the heaviest fortnight of Bodhika's year. Rayirath had four plans and four estimates of what they were meant to deliver, and the estimates did not agree.

2. Bodhika, and a decision made in March 2023

Bodhika was founded in Bengaluru in 2019 by Jeevanand Rajappan and two engineers from a card-network integrator. Its hosted checkout routed shoppers to UPI, cards, net banking, wallets or pay-later across whichever acquirer was healthy, and charged ₹2.40 a successful order rather than a share of the merchant discount rate. In the year ended 31 March 2026 it earned ₹41 crore, of which ₹19 crore was platform fees; by October 2026 platform fees ran at ₹2.34 crore a month. Of its 318 staff, most sat in Bengaluru and Pune.

In March 2023 the company made the decision that shaped the week ahead. It built its own flag service rather than licensing one, for two reasons: the Reserve Bank's 2018 directive on the storage of payment system data made the team uneasy about a foreign SDK evaluating rules on shopper attributes, and the server-rendered checkout page was cached at the edge, so the cache key had to stay small. Switchboard shipped keyed on merchant_id; a device-platform attribute followed in June 2024. Those are the two attributes a Switchboard rule can read. A shopper is anonymous until the one-time-password step, which falls after the flow being changed, so Switchboard cannot put one shopper in a variant and the next in another.

3. The industry

UPI carried most of Bodhika's volume, and NPCI's rails made that volume free to the merchant and unpriced to the acquirer, so an Indian orchestrator could not earn on the payment itself. Razorpay, Cashfree, Juspay and PayU sold against Bodhika mostly on success rate, and on per-order pricing. A percentage point of checkout success was the number merchants negotiated on, which is why RBI's card-on-file tokenisation rules, RuPay credit lines on UPI and changes to UPI intent behaviour in Android and iOS releases counted inside Bodhika as revenue events.

The calendar concentrated the stakes: Flipkart's Big Billion Days and Amazon's Great Indian Festival, their quick-commerce echo at Zepto, Blinkit and Swiggy Instamart, and Diwali events of Nykaa's and Lenskart's own. Bodhika's 2025 festive fortnight carried 1.72 times the pre-festive October base. Outside India its revenue exposure sat almost entirely in Bashaer Retail Group, a Dubai grocery and pharmacy chain signed on 11 February 2026, alone 15.5 per cent of platform sessions and ₹4.53 crore a year of fees.

4. What was believed, and what the dates now say

Exhibit 6 sets out the sequence. Checkout 3's build began on 14 July 2026, its case resting on a faster UPI intent handover. On Wednesday 2 September the team ran a shadow replay: fourteen days of tier-D session logs, 19 August to 1 September, scored against the new flow's step graph. It returned 78.5 per cent against the 76.1 per cent those sessions had actually recorded, a difference of 2.4 points. No live shopper saw Checkout 3 that day, and the figure appears in the board pre-read of 16 October.

On Monday 21 September the flag was turned on for two tier-D merchants, which over 21–29 September converted at 82.0 per cent against 79.8 per cent over the nine days before, a difference of 2.2 points. On Tuesday 29 September Jhumur Remesh, in Toronto, established from the merchant records that both sold a single subscription SKU and that the comparison was a before-and-after with no concurrent control.

On Monday 5 October a Switchboard configuration change reached the Mumbai edge point of presence 11 minutes 04 seconds after it was made; on Friday 9 October the team rehearsed a rollback. Exhibit 4 records both. Checkout 3 writes its session state to checkout_session_v3, which Checkout 2 cannot read, and the migration carries no dual-write.

On Monday 12 October Jacintha Rasquinha, in Berlin, shipped a rebuilt UPI intent sheet. Rows 1 to 3 of Exhibit 2 span both sheets; row 4, covering 13 to 15 October, came after it.

5. The people

Jenson Rayirath, vice-president, product, Bengaluru. Joined January 2024 from a payments bank; his FY2027 objective is a 1.5-point rise in platform checkout success, and he wants a number the board cannot argue with. He has not said that on a call on 9 October he told Bashaer's digital commerce head that Checkout 3 would be live on their storefront before Diwali.

exp20v2-exp.flags:
Feature flags and flighting

1. A Friday decision

At 5.40 p.m. on Friday 4 September 2026, Meghavi Vaghasiya, director of payments product at Elanvi, an Ahmedabad bill-payment and UPI app with about 400,000 paying users a day, had one decision left before the weekend. Repeat Pay, a feature that lets a customer re-run a previous bill payment in one tap, was ready. How should it reach customers?

Tuesday 14 July shaped the question. A different change had been switched on for every eligible customer at 11.20 a.m. A defect charged some customers twice. Support noticed at 1.40 p.m.; the old behaviour could be restored only by redeploying the backend, which finished at 3.00 p.m. In those 3 hours 40 minutes, 1,520 customers were double-debited. At ₹1,100 a case, counting the refund float, the contact handling and the payments those customers then stopped making, the afternoon cost ₹16.72 lakh.

Month-end was the constraint. Volumes on a month's last day ran about half as high again as on an ordinary day, and the change freeze began on Wednesday 23 September. Full release by Monday 14 September would leave nine clean days. Mansukh Vithlani, who led platform engineering, proposed a staged release behind a feature flag. Mahek Vadgama, the data scientist, had tabulated what each stage could detect. Meetul Vekariya, who ran customer risk and support, asked how fast they could undo it. Meghavi had until 10.00 a.m. on Monday 7 September, when the first stage would open.

2. The idea

A feature flag is a conditional in the code whose outcome is decided while the app runs, by configuration that can change without shipping new code. The code says: if the flag is on for this user, show the new button; otherwise show the old screen. Flighting is the discipline built on top: exposing a change to a deliberately ordered series of audiences, called flights or rings, and checking evidence before each widening.

The problem was a coupling. Deploying means putting code on servers or phones; releasing means letting customers experience it. Fused, every deploy is a gamble. Flickr's engineers wrote around 2009 about shipping unfinished work behind switches, Facebook used dark launches and a tool called Gatekeeper at about the same time, Microsoft staged Windows builds through insider rings from roughly 2014, and Pete Hodgson's 2017 essay on Martin Fowler's site supplied today's vocabulary. Meghavi's sentence for the meeting: “Deploying ships the code; releasing is a decision, and the flag lets us take it in small steps and reverse it in minutes.”

3. How it works

Mansukh's team created a flag with the key repeat_pay, an owner, a default of off and an expiry date. Whenever the app reaches the Repeat Pay surface, the SDK (the software library embedded in the app) evaluates the flag in the order shown below.

The percentage step carries the arithmetic. The SDK hashes the user's identifier together with the flag's salt (a fixed string that makes this flag's grouping independent of every other flag's) and takes the remainder after dividing by 10,000. That number is the user's bucket. At a 20% share the new flow is served to buckets below 2,000. A customer whose bucket is 3,417 sees the old flow at 1%, 5% and 20%, and the new flow at 50%, because 3,417 is below 5,000. Because the bucket never changes, widening the share only adds people: nobody flips back and forth, and each rung contains the one before it.

Three steps are usually left implicit. Propagation: the flag service caches configuration for 60 seconds and each phone polls every 300, so a change reaches every phone within 360 seconds, 6 minutes in the worst case and about 3 on average. The failure default: when the flag service is unreachable, the SDK serves the old flow. Exposure logging: the SDK records which variant each user was served, because analysis by who was merely eligible measures the wrong group.

4. A worked example

Mansukh's ladder had four rungs, each opening at 10.00 a.m. With 400,000 payers a day, a rung's exposure in user-days (one eligible user for one day) is its share times 400,000 times its days.

MDE (minimum detectable effect) = 2.8016 × √(0.92 × 0.08 × (1/on + 1/off)): baseline payment completion 92.0%, 5% two-sided significance, 80% power (2.8016 = 1.960 + 0.842). A planning form using baseline variance in both arms rather than the pooled-null form; it differs from an exact solve by up to about 7% at rung 1, less at larger rungs.

The total, 784,000 user-days, is 1.96 full-exposure days. Describing the plan as “50% for a week” would price it at 0.5 × 7 = 3.5 days, or 1,400,000 user-days. The ramp reached 50% only on Friday 11 September, four days in, so that figure overstates exposure by 79 per cent. The same trap catches incident arithmetic.

Suppose Repeat Pay double-debited 0.05% of exposed user-days. Duplicates appear only in the bank reconciliation file, which covers one calendar day and arrives at 3.00 p.m. the next; the stop rule is 12 duplicates in one file. Rung 1 yields about 1.2 expected cases in its first file and rung 2 about 5.8, so neither trips it. The second pass changes one input, the defect rate. Falling from 0.05% to 0.02% did not shrink the damage proportionally: the milder defect stayed under the stop rule through a whole rung and lived 1.9 times as long in exposure terms. Case D is the error to avoid: it treats all 3.25 days as 20%, roughly doubling case A.

5. Nuances

Four kinds of flag

Hodgson's taxonomy separates release flags (days to weeks), experiment flags (a test's duration), ops flags such as kill switches (permanent) and permission flags such as paid tiers (permanent). Repeat Pay's flag is a release flag and must die; the kill switch is an ops flag and should not.

Flighting is not an A/B test

An A/B test measures an effect; flighting limits harm while exposure grows. A canary is the infrastructure cousin: a new server build takes a slice of traffic, whereas a flag works per user. Calling a ladder an experiment invites reading differences nobody powered for.

A gate that reads yesterday

The step to 20% at 10.00 a.m. Wednesday could see only Monday's file. Tuesday's file, covering rung 2, arrived at 3.00 p.m., five hours after the step. A guardrail’s lag is part of the ladder’s design.

Power differs by rung

Mahek treated 0.5 percentage points as the largest drop in completion Elanvi would tolerate. Rungs 1 and 2 cannot resolve it at 80% power: their MDEs are 1.21 and 0.55, and rung 2 has a 72% chance of seeing a true 0.5-point drop. Early rungs therefore catch loud, zero-baseline failures such as duplicates; rungs 3 and 4 (0.24 and 0.17) judge the rate. Four independent looks at the 5% level would give an 18.5% chance of at least one false alarm; the looks share data, so the true figure is lower but still above 5%.

Assignment is not exposure

Compare everyone assigned to the new flow with everyone assigned to the old, whether or not they opened Repeat Pay. Restrict to those who opened it and behaviour selects the comparison. Log both; decide in advance which carries the verdict.

Rings are not random samples

A ring of staff, or of beta enthusiasts, is convenient and unrepresentative. Hash buckets are random with respect to behaviour; rings are not. Use rings to find breakage, buckets to measure.

What a kill switch cannot undo

Turning the flag off stops new harm; it does not refund a debit already posted or restore a migrated record. Nor does a rung reveal effects slower than itself, such as novelty wearing off.

Flag debt and the questions to ask first

Every live flag doubles the paths through the code; ten interacting flags permit 1,024 combinations. Before relying on one, ask who owns it, when it expires, what happens when the service is down and which metric stops the ladder.

6. Consumer, B2B, marketplace; small and large

In a consumer app like Elanvi the unit is the user, samples are large and hashing works. In B2B the unit is usually the customer account, because two users in one company cannot see different versions of a shared workflow. With 180 accounts a 5% rung is 9 accounts, too few for any rate statistic, so rungs become contractual: named customers who agreed to preview, with an agreed rollback. In a marketplace a flagged buyer who wins a scarce seller depletes the unflagged, so teams randomise by city or time slot, which cuts the independent units sharply.

An early-stage company may need only a configuration file, since ten users cannot power any rung. A large company needs a platform: ownership, expiry dates, audit trails and automated stop rules. Either end errs by buying the other’s tooling.

7. Common mistakes

Pricing the end state. Symptom: an incident bill far from forecast. Misunderstanding: a ramp percentage is an exposure. Diagnostic: sum logged exposures by rung, as in Table 1.

Reading green at a low rung as safe. Symptom: dashboards flat at 1%, then trouble at 20%. Misunderstanding: no signal means no problem. Diagnostic: print each rung’s MDE beside its result.

An untested kill switch. Symptom: “rollback” means a redeploy and a meeting. Misunderstanding: an existing switch works. Diagnostic: flip it in a drill and time it against the 6-minute worst case.

Flags that never die. Symptom: engineers afraid to delete branches. Misunderstanding: removal is optional cleanup. Diagnostic: count flags past expiry.

8. What good looks like

Done well, the rollout log reads like a ledger. Each rung has a stated share, a window, an exposure figure summed from the exposure log rather than the plan, and a stop rule naming its data source and lag. A 2% holdback stays unexposed after full release, and the flag carries an expiry date. Nobody argues afterwards about what the numbers meant.

9. The decision, and what to learn next

Meghavi approved the ladder at 9.50 a.m. on Monday 7 September with three changes. Mansukh would add a faster signal, repeat payments to the same biller for the same amount within ten minutes, logged in the app and visible in minutes rather than a day. Meetul’s team would drill the kill switch before launch. A 2% holdback would stay off until Monday 28 September, 14 days after full release (a configuration state, which the change freeze permits), and the flag would be deleted by Wednesday 28 October. Her reasoning: the ladder cost seven days and bought a smaller blast radius and a six-minute undo.

Next, read about experimentation platforms, which turn flags into assignment, exposure logging and analysis at scale: flags are how variants reach users, a platform how their effects are measured.

Questions to sit with. First: if Elanvi's baseline completion rate were 97% rather than 92%, which rungs could detect a 0.5-point drop, and what would that change in the ladder? Second: for a feature you own, what is the slowest signal your guardrail depends on, and which rung would be open when it arrives?
exp40v2-exp.flags:
Feature flags and flighting

Shipping to a slice of users and rolling back safely: what a ramp buys, what it does not, and its price.

1Two decisions, one day apart

On Thursday 15 October 2026, Nishigandha Yamunadas, vice-president of product at Gathri Money Technologies, a Bengaluru savings-and-payments app with 1.5 million daily active users and 2.4 million sessions a day, was asked a question she could not answer. Gathri's new autosave rule engine, autosave_v2, had reached users behind a flag over ten days, from Monday 7 to Wednesday 16 September, in four rungs: one per cent, then five, twenty, fifty. A fifty-fifty holdback ran for the fortnight of 14 to 27 September and the read landed on 1 October: weekly save completion of 24.31 per cent in treatment against 24.00 in control. The board's operating partner looked at that chart and asked why the ramp consumed ten days when the effect was legible in two. Nishigandha believed the ten days bought something real. Nobody at Gathri had yet priced a rung, so she could not say what, in rupees.

On Friday 16 October, in Pune, Nitiraj Yajodia had the opposite difficulty. He heads product at Gunavatta Health Systems, whose hospital information system runs in 168 Indian hospitals: 127 on Gunavatta's hosted tenancy, 41 on servers in the hospital's own data centre, upgraded only by the quarterly release train. Nitiraj had promised his board a five per cent cut in medication order-entry time from a redesigned order set, measured rather than asserted, in a market where ABDM compliance and NABH accreditation make clinical-workflow changes expensive to justify twice. His analytics lead, Nazneen Yamkhedia, had just shown him that a tenant-randomised test across every hospital he can flag cannot see five per cent: the smallest effect that design detects is 5.8 per cent. His target was not ambitious but arithmetically unavailable.

The same machinery produced both problems, pointing opposite ways in the two firms.

2The idea, and the three schools that disagree about it

A feature flag is a runtime predicate, evaluated per request, selecting between two or more code paths. Its one structural achievement is to separate deployment — code arriving on production servers — from release — behaviour arriving at a user. Once those come apart, "has it shipped?" acquires a distribution over the population rather than an answer.

Flighting is built on that separation: allocating the treatment branch to a randomly chosen slice of users, widening it in rungs, each rung carrying a measurement and a rule for advancing or reversing. Three ancestries remain visible. Flickr's 2009 account of branch-free development behind flags supplied the deployment case; Humble and Farley's Continuous Delivery in 2010 supplied branch-by-abstraction and release decoupling; and the controlled-experiment platforms at Microsoft and Google, written up later by Ronny Kohavi and colleagues, supplied the idea that a flag is above all a randomisation device.

Those ancestries have hardened into schools. The delivery school holds that a ramp is a harm-bounding device and measurement a welcome side effect; it signs "a rung exists to limit how many people a defect reaches" and will not sign "a rung without a holdback tells you whether the feature worked". The experimentation school holds that the flag is the randomisation mechanism, so any ramp without a concurrent control wastes an allocation already paid for; it signs "untested is unshipped" and never "we ramped to a hundred per cent and the metrics looked fine". The operability school, from site-reliability practice, holds that a flag is control-plane configuration whose real artefact is the kill switch and the error budget it spends; it signs "every flag is an outage you have chosen to be able to cause" and never "flags are free".

3Mechanics: a ramp is an integral, a kill switch is a sum

Two quantities are routinely asserted rather than computed. The first is exposure. Gathri's September ramp is drawn below; the usual description — "fifty per cent for ten days" — is wrong by over a factor of two.

Add the rungs as the chart plots them — 1, 1, 5, 5, 20, 20, 20, 50, 50, 50 — and the shaded area is 222 percentage-days, 2.22 days of full-population exposure, against the 500 and 5.00 from multiplying the end state by the window. But the chart credits each step day wholly to its new rung, while the steps land at 10:00, so every step day carries ten hours at the rung below. Honouring that gives 201.2 percentage-days, 2.01 full-exposure days, 3,017,500 user-days rather than 7,500,000: the convenient figure overstates by 2.49 times, and the chart itself by about ten per cent. The convention is part of the number. Anything priced off a schedule — blast radius, sample accrual, incident cost, error budget — must be integrated rung by rung, at the step times the rollout used.

The second is kill-switch latency. Gathri's commitment reads "under ten minutes", and its own alert design cannot meet it. The alert evaluates a five-minute tumbling window and needs two consecutive breaches, and since a defect can begin anywhere inside a window, the first partial one may not breach, so it fires ten to fifteen minutes after onset — the ten-minute mark falls inside detection, before anyone has been told. Acknowledge-verify-flip adds four, so the decision alone is fourteen to nineteen minutes. Then the value travels: the configuration document is CDN-cached with a sixty-second time-to-live and foregrounded clients poll every five minutes. Worst case, 15 + 4 + 1 + 5 = 25 minutes separate the first affected request from the last client still on the old path.

Those minutes cost differently at each rung. Gathri's 2.4 million daily sessions average 1,667 a minute and run three times that at the 20:30 peak, so a worst-case kill window at peak spans 125,000 sessions: 1,250 exposed at one per cent, 6,250 at five, 25,000 at twenty, 62,500 at fifty. Against a 99.9 per cent monthly objective — 43.2 minutes on a 43,200-minute month — that incident charges 25 × 0.50 = 12.5 minute-equivalents at fifty per cent, 28.9 per cent of budget, against 0.25 and 0.58 per cent at one.

4When flighting applies, and when it quietly misleads

Four conditions make the practice work, each testable rather than cultural. First, the randomisation unit must be at once the unit of harm and the unit of measurement. Gathri passes: a save either completes or not, and users do not interact. Gunavatta fails at the user level, because clinicians in one hospital share order sets and see each other's screens, so the unit must be the tenant — and only 127 tenants can be flagged. Second, exposure must accrue faster than the detection lag. Gathri's one-per-cent rung delivers 15,000 users a day against alerting that needs two five-minute windows, so it passes for high-frequency defects and fails for anything surfacing through support. Third, reversal must be cheaper than roll-forward: true for a rendering change, false once a flag writes state, which is why migrations, disbursements and notifications are flagged on the read path, never the write. Fourth, the flag must be removable, and Gunavatta's on-premise 41 fail outright: configuration shipped into a hospital data centre cannot be retracted between quarterly trains.

The practice is actively misleading in one case, and it is the case most teams occupy. A ramp bounds the count of users a defect reaches; it does not improve the rate at which that defect appears in any cohort. If your detector is a rate — error percentage, conversion ratio, ticket share — ramping buys no sensitivity and costs calendar time in which harm accrues.

5Hard edges: seams, interference and the things nobody flags

Four situations break the clean model. In two-sided marketplaces, treating one side changes the other's experience: flagging a new fare display for twenty per cent of riders alters the request mix every driver sees, violating the independence user-level randomisation assumes; mature marketplaces therefore ramp by city or time-slice and accept the collapse in sample size. In regulated settings, a flag that changes a clinical pathway is a configuration change subject to change control; Gunavatta's hosted tenants need a dated, signed record of which allocation each hospital held on each day, which makes the flag service a regulated system of record.

In hardware and firmware the ramp is an over-the-air campaign, the rungs are device cohorts, and rollback is often unavailable once a bootloader has been flashed; cohort size is the only real control. In AI-native products the flag usually selects a model or prompt version whose output distribution is itself stochastic, so a clean-looking rung may hide a tail the sample never reached; allocation also interacts with caching, since a cached treatment response leaks into control.

At the organisational seam, mature firms say flags are owned by their authors and removed within the SLA. What they do is keep a permanent one-per-cent holdback on major surfaces so a control always exists, run a weekly flag-debt review that mostly rubber-stamps extensions, and carry a tail of flags whose owner has left. Gunavatta's seam is sharper: a change that is a flag for 127 customers is a release note for 41.

6Eight distinctions that separate the expert from the competent

A rung bounds the count, not the rate. The competent practitioner says a one-per-cent rung is safer because fewer people are at risk — true — then expects it to find the defect, which does not follow. The tell is a guard metric defined over the whole population: its sensitivity is a rate, identical at every rung. The expert scopes guard metrics to the flagged cohort before the first rung opens.

Exposure is an integral, and the integral carries a convention. The obvious reading multiplies final allocation by elapsed days. The tell is any sentence of the form "it was at fifty per cent for a week": Gathri's ten days at a nominal fifty gave 2.22 full-exposure days on whole calendar days, 2.01 once the 10:00 steps are honoured, and 5.00 on neither reading. An expert asks which day the rung opened, and at what hour.

The kill switch is a sum, not a click. Teams quote dashboard latency and forget the cache time-to-live and client poll interval, 60 and 300 seconds at Gathri. The tell is a rollback objective given as one number with no breakdown. Clients offline, backgrounded or on an old build are a further tail nobody owns.

A gate cannot read data that has not landed, and the day it can read may be the wrong day. Gathri's ramp gate consults a daily batch arriving at 07:30 covering the previous calendar day, while rungs step at 10:00, so the finest gate interval the architecture permits is one day; steps closer together than the evidence refreshes are a timer with a dashboard. Worse, the twenty-to-fifty step on Monday 14 September read Sunday 13 September, and because Friday stepped at 10:00 the only complete days at twenty per cent were that Sunday and the Saturday before it. Weekend traffic is not weekday traffic, and the tell is a schedule whose decisive readings fall on one.

Bucketing must be sticky, and stickiness must survive identity changes. If allocation is hashed on a session or device identifier, a user who reinstalls or signs in on a second handset crosses arms, contaminating the comparison and flickering the product in front of one person. The tell is a split drifting off 50/50 over a fortnight.

Flags compose multiplicatively. Gathri's checkout path has nine flags simultaneously live: 512 reachable combinations, of which the integration suite exercises 14 of the 512, or 2.7 per cent. The obvious reading is that each flag has been tested independently. The tell is a defect reproducible only with a particular pair of flags set, and never on the bench.

An off flag still executes. The dead branch is still compiled, the predicate still evaluated, the configuration fetch still able to fail. What governs behaviour then is the default baked into the client, not the console value. The tell is an incident in which the flag service degraded and the product behaved as nobody had chosen.

Permanent flags are architecture; expired temporary flags are an unnamed fork. Entitlement gates and kill switches should never be removed and do not belong in the debt queue. A release flag past its removal date differs in kind: a second product version no roadmap mentions and no suite tests. The tell is a removal ticket deferred three times, "still ramping".

7How the practice changes by product type and stage

In consumer products the binding constraint is almost never sample size but interference, novelty effects and the sheer number of concurrent flags. Gathri can detect half a per cent and still cannot say which of nine live flags caused a regression. In B2B and enterprise the constraint inverts: Gunavatta has 127 flaggable tenants, so between-tenant variance dominates, user-level randomisation is unavailable, and the useful designs are within-tenant — switchbacks and stepped wedges — rather than parallel arms. Contracts also make allocation negotiable as it never is in consumer: a hospital can demand exclusion, which is non-random attrition.

In platforms and marketplaces interference is primary and the honest answer is cluster randomisation with a far larger detectable effect. In hardware, rungs are cohorts and reversal may not exist. In AI products the mechanics are genuinely the same as consumer software — a difference often overstated — except that guard metrics must cover an output distribution rather than an error code.

Stage matters less than is claimed, with one exception. A company before product-market fit has no statistical power and should use flags purely as kill switches. The transition is not about headcount; it arrives the week the population can detect an effect the business cares about.

8Three worked cases

Gathri, autosave_v2. The 14 to 27 September holdback enrolled 4.2 million unique users, 2.1 million per arm. At a 24.00 per cent control rate the difference's standard error is the square root of 2 × 0.24 × 0.76 ÷ 2,100,000 = 0.0417 percentage points; with 1.960 + 0.842 = 2.802 for two-sided five per cent significance at eighty per cent power, the minimum detectable effect is 0.117 points, 0.49 per cent relative. The observed 0.31-point difference is 7.4 standard errors, interval 0.23 to 0.39. The holdback produced that, not the ramp.

Gunavatta, order_set_v2. Nazneen priced three designs on one base: the 127 hosted tenants less a canary, over twelve weeks.

Exhibit: three designs for one question, on one population and window.

All rows: significance 0.05 two-sided, power 0.80, multiplier 2.802; baseline 94.0 s; 126 tenants, 12 weeks, 1,512 tenant-weeks. Row 1 is 2.802 × √(2 × 11.0² ÷ 63) = 5.49 s. Rows 2 and 3 use the within-tenant weekly SD and assume independent weeks; serial correlation inflates both, period adjustment row 3 further. A 4.7 s (five per cent) effect under row 1 needs 2 × 11.0² × 2.802² ÷ 4.7² = 86 tenants per arm, 172 in all — more than Gunavatta has.

The wedge ran from Monday 6 July to Sunday 27 September against a 94.0-second baseline measured over the eight weeks to Sunday 5 July. Order-entry time fell 2.4 seconds, 94.0 to 91.6: 2.55 per cent, interval 1.79 to 3.01 seconds. About half what Nitiraj promised. The 41 on-premise hospitals got it unflagged in the 12 October train.

Gathri, kyc_refresh_v3 — the failure. From Monday 8 June 2026 the same ramp shape carried a re-verification flow that trapped users whose address proof was over 24 months old. Daily, 1.9 per cent of actives fall due and 6.0 per cent of those hold such a proof, so the defect struck 0.114 per cent of exposed users — 17 on a full day at one per cent, 855 at fifty. Nothing fired: the alert watched the overall completion rate, and 0.114 per cent of the exposed cohort is 0.114 per cent at every rung. Support caught it. One affected user in nine raises a ticket; the rule was a day's count over the anomaly bar, 4.5 per cent above a 2,100-ticket baseline or 94.5 tickets, with the flag pulled at 23:10 that evening. The one-per-cent rung gives 1.9 tickets. Monday 15 June, the fifty-per-cent rung's first day, opened at 10:00 and produced 641 affected users and 71 tickets — under the bar. Tuesday 16 June, a full day, produced 855 and 95, and the flag went off at 23:10.

Integrating the rungs at their actual step times gives 149.4 percentage-days, 1.494 full-exposure days, and 2,555 affected users remediated by hand at ₹118 a case: ₹3.01 lakh. Now apply the same rule to the counterfactual. The bar needs 94.5 tickets, which needs 851 affected users in a day, which needs about half the population; a straight release to a hundred per cent at 10:00 on Monday 8 June clears it inside its first day — 0.5486 of a day exposed before 23:10, 938 users, 104 tickets. The ramp did not save anyone. It cost 1,617 extra users, and 1,730 of the 2,555, or 68 per cent, were harmed before the first day on which the detector could fire at all. A rate-sensitive detector leaves a slower ramp nothing to buy but calendar time in which harm accrues. The recovery was a monitoring rebuild, not a better ramp: three engineers for three weeks scoping every guard metric to the flagged cohort, nine engineer-weeks at one engineer's fully loaded ₹43.2 lakh a year — 9/52 of it, ₹7.48 lakh — taking the incident to ₹10.49 lakh.

9Failure modes and their early warnings

The first is population-scoped alerting, above. Its warning sign is a guard metric whose denominator is everyone; the diagnostic is "what would this alert read if the defect hit every flagged user?"; late, it costs the whole ramp window of harm. The second is the ramp as theatre, rungs advancing on a timer because the gate's data refreshes more slowly than the schedule steps. Ask what evidence advanced the last rung and when it arrived. The third is flag debt; Gathri's inventory stood as follows.

Exhibit: Gathri flag inventory, 16 October 2026.
