Of the 184 release flags, 61 are past the 30-day removal SLA, which is 33 per cent. The oldest reached full allocation on 30 August 2025 and has been live 412 days; Gathri adopted its flag platform in March 2023.

The early warning for debt is not the count but the deferral comment on removal tickets; the diagnostic is to pick the oldest flag and ask what the product does when it is deleted. If nobody knows, the fork is already permanent. Fourth is irreversible state behind a reversible flag — one that has written rows, sent notifications or moved money, where switching it off restores the code path but not the world. Ask what the off state does to records the on state created; late, this becomes a data-repair project.

10Where experts genuinely disagree

The sharpest live disagreement is whether a ramp measures anything. The delivery position, at its strongest, is that ramping and experimentation are different activities sharing infrastructure: a ramp's job is to bound harm and its gates should be availability and error rates, nothing else, because mixing a product read into a safety mechanism corrupts both and tempts teams to hold rungs open for statistical rather than operational reasons. Its evidence is the Gathri failure, where the remedy was a monitoring rebuild and no holdback would have helped. It would be wrong if a concurrent holdback cost near zero, which in high-traffic consumer products it nearly does.

The experimentation position, equally strong, is that every rung is a randomised allocation already paid for, so declining to attach a control discards free evidence; firms that separate the two ship unmeasured features defended with before-and-after charts. Its evidence is the published record of controlled experiments overturning confident intuitions. It would be wrong wherever interference or contract makes the control arm unrepresentative — Gunavatta exactly.

A second disagreement, between Nitiraj and Nazneen, is unresolved. Nitiraj holds that a parallel tenant-level A/B is the only design his customers' audit committees will accept, since every alternative asks one hospital to receive two behaviours over time. Nazneen holds that a design which cannot detect the effect under discussion is not evidence, and that a switchback at 0.92 per cent is better science even if harder to explain. A third, quieter dispute is whether flag debt is debt: the operability school treats permanent flags as architecture, the delivery school treats any flag outliving its feature as a defect.

11What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this writes a ramp schedule. Someone who has internalised it writes the guard metric first, scoped to the flagged cohort, and derives the schedule from how fast that metric accumulates signal. They know their own system's cache time-to-live and client poll interval without looking. They ask, before any rung opens, what the flag's off state does to rows the on state wrote. They can say in one sentence what the current ramp buys that a straight release would not, and will say "nothing, this is a timer" when that is the answer. They treat the removal ticket as part of the feature. And when someone describes an exposure as "fifty per cent for a week", they ask for the rung dates and times.

12What each of them decided

Nishigandha kept the ten-day shape and changed what it reports. Rungs below twenty per cent, she concluded, catch catastrophic errors rather than subtle ones — against a rate defect they catch nothing — so she compressed the first two into a 36-hour canary and moved the saved time into the holdback. She also ruled that no ramp may advance on a gate whose data arrives more slowly than its steps.

Nitiraj took the 2.55 per cent to his board with the interval attached and withdrew the five-per-cent target: the wedge's 1.79 to 3.01 seconds excludes the 4.7 the promise needed, so the target was not unmeasurable but measurably missed. He has asked Nazneen to design a switchback for the next release.

  1. Gathri's ramp cost 1,617 more affected users than a straight release would have, because its detector's sensitivity was a rate. Under what detector design would the same ramp have saved users instead, and what would building that detector first have cost?
  2. Nitiraj's audit argument and Nazneen's power argument cannot both govern the next release. Which is a constraint, which a preference, and what would settle it?
  3. Gathri's twenty-to-fifty step was gated on a Sunday. Propose a ten-day schedule in which no decisive reading falls on a weekend, and price it.

13Going deeper

  • A/B testing fundamentals — the holdback, not the ramp, produced Gathri's read.
  • Feature flags and progressive delivery — bucketing, targeting and configuration distribution underneath.
  • Experimentation platforms — what makes a holdback cheap enough to attach by default.
  • Writing an experiment hypothesis — turns a rung gate into a decision rule.
  • Significance, power, sample size, peeking — the arithmetic that priced Gunavatta's three designs.
  • When you can't A/B test — switchbacks, stepped wedges, interrupted time series: Gunavatta's toolkit.
  • Experimentation culture — why mature firms keep a permanent holdback at all.
  • Qual + quant feedback loop — tickets caught the KYC defect; wire that channel deliberately.
  • Choosing experiment metrics — cohort-scoped guard metrics are what prevent another June.
case20v1-exp.flags:
Ashtamudi Pay: Switching On Instant Payout

A teaching case on feature flags and flighting

1. Opening

At 9.30 on Thursday 15 October 2026, Isaiah Panikkar, chief product officer of Ashtamudi Pay, sat down in the company's Kochi office and opened a message that Ineesha Parayil had posted from Toronto at 9.30 the previous evening, which was 7.00 in the morning in Kochi. It summarised a nine-day pilot of Instant Payout, a feature that credits a merchant's sales to the bank account within minutes instead of the next working day. The pilot had reached 5 per cent of merchants. Its blended failure rate was 1.5 per cent, against a launch limit of 2.0 per cent.

A marketing agency had booked a ₹90 lakh campaign for Saturday 24 October. Unless Isaiah told it otherwise by 6 pm on Tuesday 20 October, the campaign would run as booked. Diwali fell on 8 November. He had five days to decide how widely, and how fast, to switch the feature on.

2. Company background

Ashtamudi Pay was founded in Kochi in 2019 to give neighbourhood merchants a billing and QR app: kirana stores, pharmacies, bakeries and tea stalls across Kerala, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu. By October 2026 it had 2,40,000 active merchants, who together processed about ₹72 crore on an ordinary day. Payments ran over UPI, the rails operated by NPCI, and the company settled to merchants' bank accounts the next working day through a sponsor bank, under the RBI's payment aggregator rules.

Larger names competed for the same shopkeepers, among them PhonePe and Paytm, and Razorpay for the more digital ones. Ashtamudi's edge was local-language support, in Malayalam, Kannada and Tamil, and a field team that visited markets every month. Engineering sat in Bengaluru and Pune, and a small customer-success team in Singapore served the trading firms that supplied some of its larger merchants. Merchants kept asking for faster money. A grocer buying festival stock from wholesalers at Chalai in Thiruvananthapuram or Chickpet in Bengaluru often paid in cash the same morning, and waited a day for her own sales to arrive.

In 2024 the engineering team had built an in-house flag service. Each merchant ID was hashed into one of 100 buckets, and a feature reached a merchant only if the bucket fell under a threshold set in a console. The threshold could be raised, lowered or set to zero in under a minute, with no new app release.

3. The situation

Instant Payout was built in August and September. On 28 September the sponsor bank agreed to carry it, but with an aggregate limit of ₹30 crore of instant payouts a day; the limit resets at midnight, and payouts beyond it are declined and fall back to next-day settlement. The launch brief of 22 September set a guardrail: a failed-payout rate no higher than 2.0 per cent.

The pilot ran from Monday 5 to Tuesday 13 October. The flag put 12,000 merchants, 5 per cent of the base, in the flighted group. The other 2,28,000 stayed on next-day settlement. Merchants had to opt in, and 4,560 of the flighted 12,000, or 38.0 per cent, did. Ineesha's headline was the blended failure rate. Her appendix, reproduced as Exhibit 1, split payouts by time of day.

She had also projected demand against the bank's limit (Exhibit 2). The pilot had run on ordinary days. In the ten days to Diwali in 2025, 11 to 20 October, daily volume had been 1.5 times normal, and the same uplift was expected from 30 October to 8 November this year, giving ₹108 crore a day. Figure 1 places these dates on one line.

Beyond Kochi, the decision touched people in other time zones. The on-call rota for flag changes ran from Bengaluru by day and Toronto for the Indian night, and a threshold change took effect immediately wherever it was made.

4. The people

Ikhlaas Pulikkal, head of growth, Mumbai. He owned the ₹90 lakh campaign and the merchant-acquisition target for the quarter. He wanted every merchant able to see Instant Payout when the creative went live on 24 October, because a campaign that promised a feature most viewers could not find would waste its spend.

Ilyas Padiyar, head of engineering, Bengaluru. He had carried the pager for the payout service since 2022. He wanted any widening of the feature to be reversible within minutes, and to know in advance what number would trigger a reversal.

Ineesha Parayil, data scientist, Toronto. She had designed the pilot's hash split and wrote the read-out. She wanted the decision tied to a stated rule and not to the mood of a meeting, and she was uneasy about extrapolating a quiet nine days to the festival window.

5. Exhibits

The three exhibits below are discussed in sections 3 and 6.

6. The options

Option A: launch to everyone on 24 October. The threshold goes to 100 on the morning the campaign starts. Ikhlaas's creative runs as booked, there is no change charge, and merchants have 16 days of access before Diwali (Exhibit 3). The flag remains as a switch that can set the threshold to zero if something breaks. The cost is that the first measurement of the whole base is taken in the campaign week itself.

Option B: ramp by flag. The threshold rises to 25 on 24 October, 50 on 27 October and 100 on 30 October, three days at each of the first two levels. Each step needs agreed gates to hold, and a failed gate sets the threshold back to the previous level. The campaign moves to 31 October at a ₹9 lakh charge, and merchants have 10 days at full exposure.

Option C: wait until after Diwali. The threshold stays at 5 through the festival, the campaign is cancelled at a ₹27 lakh charge, and the whole base is switched on from Monday 16 November. The feature stays off for merchants who would have bought stock before 8 November, and the field team has nothing new to carry into markets.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. What does the pilot in Exhibit 1 establish, and what decisions can it support?
  2. Using Exhibit 2, which exposure levels can the company run on a festival day, and what would have to change to run a higher one?
  3. If you were to ramp by flag, what gates and thresholds would you set at each step, and who would be authorised to reverse a step?
  4. Which course of action should Isaiah take by Tuesday 20 October, and what would he say to Ikhlaas and Ilyas?

8. A note for the learner

A flag separates deploying code from exposing it. Once the feature is in the app, the threshold decides who sees it, so the launch becomes a series of small, reversible exposures with a measurement after each. Flighting is the discipline of choosing those slices, deciding in advance what the measurement must show before the next slice opens, and keeping the way back open. The pilot's hash split is also what makes its flighted group comparable with the rest of the base.

One defensible path is Option B, with its date-driven ramp replaced by a limit-driven one. Take 25 per cent on 24 October and 50 per cent on 27 October. Hold at 50 per cent through the festival window: Exhibit 2 puts that at ₹20.52 crore a day, which leaves room for opt-in to rise from 38 per cent to about 55 per cent before it meets the ₹30 crore limit (108 x 0.50 x 0.55 = 29.7). Advance past 50 per cent when the bank raises its limit. Gate each step on failure rate measured by time window, not blended, and hold payouts attempted between 22:00 and 06:00 until the morning, since that is where Exhibit 1 shows the failures. Name Ilyas's on-call engineer as the person who may set the threshold back without asking anyone. Move the campaign to 31 October, so that its promise is made only after the 50 per cent level has run for four days.

This path gives up some reach and pays ₹9 lakh, and in return the number that limits the launch, the bank's ceiling, is respected. Other reasoned answers exist; what they share is a stated rule for moving up and a stated trigger for moving back.
case20v1-exp.culture:
Case 20 · Experimentation culture

Tilgul and the Diwali Test Queue

1. Opening

Tuesday, 20 October 2026, 7:40 a.m., Ahmedabad. Esmail Lakhtaria, vice president of product at Tilgul, had a one-page note from the chief executive open on his laptop. It asked for one answer by Friday 23 October: who at Tilgul may run an experiment, and how soon? The board would meet on Thursday 29 October, a vendor's platform quote lapsed the next day, and the release freeze for the Diwali sale ran from Monday 2 to Friday 13 November.

Ekaant Lunkad's note ended with a sentence Esmail had read four times. “We say data over opinion. Show me the Tilgul where that is true by next Diwali, and tell me what it costs.” Esmail had three possible answers. None was free.

2. Company background

Tilgul was founded in Ahmedabad in 2019 by Ekaant Lunkad and two school friends. It is a marketplace for regional sweets, snacks and festive gifts, from Surat ghari to Bikaner bhujia, supplied by 1,800 independent sellers in 140 towns. In FY2025-26 (April to March) it moved goods worth ₹640 crore, kept a 15 per cent take, and so booked ₹96 crore of net revenue. About 14 lakh buyers use the app each month, and UPI carries most payments. The October to December quarter brings roughly a third of the year's sales.

The competition is wide: the festive gifting stores of Amazon and Flipkart, quick-commerce shelves on Blinkit, Zepto and Swiggy Instamart, and the sellers' own websites. The roughly eighty people in product and engineering are spread out: engineers in Bengaluru and Pune, a contract designer in Berlin, a senior data scientist in Toronto, a customer-success lead in Singapore and a sales head in New Jersey. One corporate-gifting client, a hospitality group in Dubai, buys in volume every festive season.

3. The situation

In 2023 the engineers built simple feature toggles, and six squads now run controlled tests. The rule is that every test design is reviewed by one of four analysts before launch, and every result is read out by one afterwards. The analysts are Elvy Lodaya in Toronto and three colleagues in Bengaluru.

Exhibit 1 covers tests concluded from July to September 2026. The squads concluded 34 and nine won on the metric agreed beforehand, a win rate of 26.5 per cent. By 20 October thirteen changes had shipped, four of them without a win. The median wait for an analyst's sign-off ranged from 9 to 18 days across squads. Each test takes about three analyst-days of review and readout, and the four analysts spend about 40 per cent of some 62 working days a quarter on tests.

Exhibit 2 shows three of the shipped changes. The Checkout squad's urgency timer won on conversion. The customer-success lead in Singapore, however, reported contacts per 1,000 orders at 21 in the four weeks before it shipped and 27 in the four weeks after, a comparison of the two four-week periods, with no control group. The Pricing squad's lower free-delivery threshold read p = 0.12 against a 5 per cent bar; the chief executive shipped it on 2 October, saying the festival would do the rest.

The distant colleagues see it differently. The Berlin designer, who is three and a half hours behind Ahmedabad until 25 October and four and a half after, says her design changes wait longest. The New Jersey sales head fears an unstable site in front of the Dubai client. Figure 1 sets out the calendar.

4. The people

Ekaant Lunkad, chief executive, Ahmedabad. He wants every squad testing by January and wants the Diwali quarter protected from anything that could disturb checkout. He trusts his instinct on gifting prices and says so.

Elvy Lodaya, senior data scientist, Toronto. She leads the analysts and wants to keep review. Her weekly session is at 8:00 a.m. Toronto time, 5:30 p.m. in Ahmedabad until clocks change on 1 November and 6:30 p.m. after. She fears that self-serve testing brings peeking at results and metrics chosen after the fact.

Ernest Luniya, head of growth, Mumbai. He wants speed. A fortnight-long queue, he says, kills a festival idea before it can be tried.

Ekbal Limbasia, engineering manager, Pune. Every test leaves code branches behind. He will support more tests only if cleanup and automatic stop rules come with them.

  1. Using Exhibit 1, what can and cannot be said about why squads conclude different numbers of tests in a quarter?
  2. For each test in Exhibit 2, what would you need to know to say whether the decision to ship was supported by the test?
  3. What would each option ask Ekaant, Elvy and the squad leads to do differently from today, if anything?
  4. Which option would you put to the board on 29 October, and what would you tell it you will measure by 31 March 2027?

8. A note for the learner

Experimentation culture asks what it takes for a whole company to test nearly everything. The best-known answer, from Booking.com, is a system in which anyone may launch a test, the decision rule is written before launch, and the result outranks the seniority of the person who proposed the change. Tooling is the smaller part. The larger part is whether a leader will be overruled by a result, and whether the ordinary win rate is accepted as normal.

A well-reasoned answer therefore reads the exhibits for the system and not for the individual test. It asks where the constraint sits, whether decisions follow evidence, and what would show that a change in operating model worked.

One defensible path is Option C, with three conditions. First, the pilot squads are Search & Discovery, which runs the most tests, and Pricing & Promotions, which waits longest. Second, the launch form carries a customer-contact guardrail for every test. Third, Ekaant writes down that any decision to ship against a result is logged with its reason, starting with the delivery-threshold change. The reasoning is that a pilot spends ₹39 lakh to learn whether review, not ideas, is the constraint, and tests the leader's behaviour before the platform is extended to all six squads. The February review would compare the pilot squads with the other four on tests concluded, queue time and shipped-without-a-win counts.

Case 40 · Experimentation culture

Ninety-Six Tests and One Undertaking

Vittam Technologies Private Limited, Bengaluru · October 2026

1. Sunday night

At 9.40 p.m. on Sunday, 25 October 2026, Gauravika Morakhia sat at her dining table in Indiranagar, Bengaluru, with two documents open. The first was a memo she had circulated on Friday, 23 October, setting out five ways Vittam Technologies could change how it experiments. The second was the undertaking her company signed on Monday, 5 October: the risk disclosure on Vittam's order-confirmation screen would be remediated and in production by 31 December 2026.

Morakhia had been chief product officer for four years and nine months. In that time the experiments Vittam ran each quarter had risen from eleven to 112 and then settled at ninety-six, and the chief executive quoted the figure to investors. On Friday, 16 October, central analytics set six of them against a holdback group and measured a gain of 3.2 per cent against the 21.2 per cent the squads' readouts compounded to.

The product review was at 10 a.m. on Monday — half past midnight in Toronto, half past five in Berlin, half past twelve in Singapore. The audit committee would take its plan up on Monday, 14 December. Morakhia had five options on paper, and the memo did not say which she favoured.

2. How Vittam got here

Vittam was founded in Bengaluru in 2017 by Girindra Mankad and two colleagues, as a zero-commission app for direct mutual-fund plans; broking followed in 2020 through Vittam Securities Private Limited. By September 2026 it had 1.42 crore registered users, 23.6 lakh transacting in a month, and ₹38,400 crore of assets on the platform; FY26 revenue was ₹742 crore against an FY27 plan of ₹960 crore. Of 1,180 employees, 410 sat in product and engineering, in 22 squads, 14 of which own a customer-facing surface.

Two decisions from 2023 shape what Morakhia can do. On Monday, 20 March 2023, Mankad signed a one-page charter headed Data over opinion. It let every squad launch an experiment without central approval, and tied thirty per cent of a squad lead's bonus to the share of that squad's shipped changes backed by an experiment. The clause went into the FY24 appraisal template and has carried forward unchanged; the FY27 cycle closes on 31 March 2027.

In June 2023 the platform team built VXP on the feature-flag library the app already used. That library identified a device, not a person, because the web product then had no signed-out identity. Assignment has been by device since; the web product relaunched in November 2024 and now carries a quarter of order volume.

3. The industry

Vittam competes for the same retail investor as Zerodha, Groww, Angel One and Paytm Money, in a market where AMFI's monthly reporting has shown industry assets past ₹65 lakh crore and SIP inflows above ₹25,000 crore a month. Direct plans pay no commission, so the economics sit in broking, margin funding and a subscription tier.

The plumbing is shared and regulated: SIP mandates run on UPI AutoPay through NPCI, depository accounts sit with CDSL, onboarding runs through CKYC. SEBI governs how schemes, returns and risks are presented to an investor; the Digital Personal Data Protection Act of 2023, where the event data behind an experiment may be processed. The board committed in March 2026 to a data-residency migration due on Friday, 11 December 2026.

The exposure is not only Indian. A white-label app is run in the Gulf by Vahdat Wealth Partners DMCC, a Dubai distributor with 41,000 non-resident Indian clients, on a three-year contract signed 1 February 2025. Giriraj Murarka sells the same proposition from New Jersey; customer success runs from Singapore, analytics from Bengaluru, Pune and Toronto, design from Berlin.

4. What happened, and what was believed at the time

Figure 1 sets out the sequence. On Friday, 12 June 2026, a squad in the Invest & Orders pod ran a two-arm test on the order-confirmation screen. One arm showed the scheme risk disclosure expanded, as always; the other collapsed it behind a tap. The collapsed arm completed 2.4 per cent more orders and shipped to all users on Friday, 26 June.

On Wednesday, 1 July 2026, after seeing it demonstrated, Gulrukh Mistry obtained an interim rule: any experiment touching order placement, disclosure, fees or returns display needed compliance sign-off. On Friday, 14 August, Gitanshu Madhvani reported that 31 of the 112 experiments run in the April–June quarter had arm counts too unequal for a fair coin. On Tuesday, 29 September, an inspection observation reached Vittam Securities, asking it to show that scheme risk disclosures had been presented consistently to all users from 1 April to 30 June 2026. On Monday, 5 October, Vittam undertook to remediate by 31 December; on Friday, 9 October, the audit committee asked for a plan by the 26 October review.

Four beliefs sit on the record, each beside a later dated fact. March 2023: the charter was premised on a central gate being what slowed learning. 30 September 2026: Exhibit 5 shows 11 of 54 gated submissions withdrawn by their squads and 9 still open. June 2023: the design review recorded device-level assignment as equivalent to user-level for signed-in flows. 6 October 2026: 18.4 per cent of transacting users were active on more than one device in a month. July 2026: Mankad told an all-hands that the June quarter's 112 tests proved a learning culture. 16 October 2026: the holdback readout, Exhibit 3. 1 July 2026: Mistry's note called the interim rule a closing of the exposure. 29 September 2026: the observation covers 1 April to 30 June.

Figure 1. Sequence of events, March 2023 to March 2027 (stations in date order; not drawn to a time scale)

5. The people

Gauravika Morakhia, chief product officer, Bengaluru, joined January 2022. She owns the memo, the undertaking and the FY27 revenue plan. She has not said that she approved the 12 June test design inside a batch of nineteen, in eleven minutes, without opening it.

Girindra Mankad, co-founder and chief executive, Bengaluru. The 2023 charter is his, and he defends it as the reason Vittam ships faster than firms three times its size. He has not told the product organisation that a Series E term sheet under negotiation names experiment velocity among its covenants.

Gulrukh Mistry, head of compliance, Mumbai, joined August 2024. She wants every regulated surface gated and the April–June exposure reconstructed user by user. Her team of two cleared 34 of 54 submissions last quarter. She has not told the audit committee that she now believes that reconstruction cannot be done from VXP's logs.

Gitanshu Madhvani, senior data scientist, Toronto, joined March 2023. He found the arm imbalance, built the holdback, and wants a quarter's pause to rebuild assignment first. He does not mention that he raised device-level assignment in the June 2023 design review and dropped the objection when the launch date held.

Gunakar Mamtora, engineering director and owner of VXP, Pune, joined 2019. He puts a user-level rebuild at 74 to 96 engineer-weeks and argues a bought platform will not understand Indian order flows. He has not circulated his own August estimate of 48 weeks, written before three of his nine engineers moved to the residency migration.

Gayanti Modhwadia, principal designer, Berlin, on contract since November 2024. She designed and ran the 12 June test and argues the collapsed disclosure was read more carefully, not less. She has not said that the pattern came from a previous employer's app and was never put to Vittam's legal team.

Gulmeher Maloo, customer-success lead, Singapore, joined 2021. She carries the Vahdat relationship and wants the white-label tenant excluded from every experiment, permanently. She has not answered the two informal questions Vahdat's operations head has put about what Vittam tests on those clients.

Giriraj Murarka, head of sales, New Jersey, joined 2023. He wants more tests on non-resident onboarding, where approval rates lag resident rates. He has not flagged that he has promised a Gulf roadshow in January built on an onboarding flow that does not yet exist.

“Our platform costs about two and a half lakh rupees for every test we launch. The answer to that is more tests, not a committee that makes each cost more.”

“Six squads claim twenty-one per cent compounded; the holdback says seven-tenths of a point. 8. The options as Morakhia sees them

The memo set out five, each costed by Mamtora's team against the same quarter's volumes.

A. Register and read. Keep self-serve launch rights. Require every experiment to register a primary metric, a minimum detectable effect and a stop date in VXP before assignment begins, with readouts generated centrally rather than by the squad. Six engineer-weeks, ₹5.3 lakh. Assignment stays at device level, and nothing is reconstructed for April to June.

B. An experiment council. Five reviewers — two from compliance, two from analytics, one from product — see every design before launch, regulated or not. At Q2 volumes that is about 116 designs a quarter: the 96 launched plus the 20 submitted and never launched. Two of the five are new posts — one compliance officer, one Bengaluru analyst — ₹81 lakh a year, against a headcount frozen at 410 until February 2027.

C. Split the estate. Define a free zone and a gated zone in code, with the boundary enforced by the platform. On Q2's volumes, 62 of 96 launches would fall in the free zone and 34 in the gated. Gated designs would require user-level assignment, which those surfaces allow because all of them sit behind sign-in. Eighteen engineer-weeks, ₹15.8 lakh.

D. Licence a platform. A vendor quotes ₹2.60 crore a year, billed annually in advance, for a system that assigns by user identity. Four of the nine VXP engineers would stay for integration, at ₹1.84 crore a year. The vendor processes events in Singapore and Virginia.

E. Stop the line. Launch no new experiments for a quarter and rebuild assignment in-house, user-level, across the whole estate including signed-out web, with a backfill of the register. Mamtora's estimate is 74 to 96 engineer-weeks. The six Q2 changes stay live. The FY27 bonus clause and the 31 March 2027 appraisal cycle are unchanged.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The product review is at 10 a.m. IST on Monday, 26 October. The audit committee takes the plan on Monday, 14 December, and the undertaking of 5 October puts the remediated disclosure in production by 31 December 2026. A freeze covers the order and payment path from Monday, 18 January 2027 to Wednesday, 31 March 2027.

Capacity is bounded. From Monday, 26 October to Friday, 15 January is twelve working weeks; the Diwali block-leave week of 9 to 13 November leaves eleven. The platform team is nine engineers, three of them committed to the residency migration until Friday, 11 December, which covers six of those eleven weeks. That gives 9 × 11 less 3 × 6, or 81 engineer-weeks, of which 22 go to running VXP, leaving 59. Hiring is frozen at 410 in product and engineering until the FY28 plan is approved in February 2027, and ₹1.20 crore of the FY27 technology budget is uncommitted.

Two commitments bite. The Vahdat agreement requires 30 days' written notice before any change to the tenant's order flow, so a change live on 31 December must be notified by Tuesday, 1 December. The residency migration must land on 11 December whatever else happens.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Exhibit 1 records 96 experiments launched across fourteen squads in Q2; Exhibit 5 records 54 submissions to the compliance queue that quarter. From those two alone, what can be established about Vittam's rate of learning, and what cannot?
  2. Exhibit 3 sets six claimed lifts against a holdback. What does the holdback support on its own numbers, and what would you want to know about how it was built before relying on it?
  3. The March 2023 charter ties thirty per cent of a squad lead's bonus to the share of shipped changes backed by an experiment. Predict what that clause does to each column of Exhibit 1, then test it.
  4. Exhibit 6 states a baseline rate, a per-arm cohort, a significance level, a power and a planned minimum detectable effect. Check those five against one another, and work out what follows for the 31 December undertaking.
  5. Option C would split the estate into a free zone and a gated zone. Apply that split to the experiments Vittam ran from 1 April to 30 June 2026: where would the boundary have fallen, and who had the standing to draw it?
  6. It is Monday morning. What does Morakhia put in front of the product review, what does she say to the audit committee on 14 December, and what would she have to be wrong about for it to fail?

At 11.50 p.m. a message arrived from Berlin, where it was twenty past seven. Modhwadia had sent a screenshot of the June arm, the collapsed disclosure neat under its chevron, and one line: Tell me which rule. Morakhia did not reply.

She went back to the memo's first page, to the sentence she had meant to open with. Vittam ran ninety-six experiments last quarter. It was true, and she had checked it twice. The review was ten hours away.

Experimentation Culture: What It Takes for a Whole Company to Test Everything

1. A queue and a memo

On Monday 14 September 2026, Kinnari Sancheti, head of product at Caravel Stays, sat opposite her chief executive with a one-page memo and a number she disliked. Caravel, founded in 2016, lists 41,000 properties in 380 towns, from Manali homestays to Pune business hotels. In the three months to 31 August its central growth team of six people had run 10 A/B tests. (An A/B test shows two versions of a page to randomly split halves of users and compares what each half does.) Two had won. Each test had waited a median of 19 days between request and launch, in a queue that Kinnari's own team managed. The queue was not laziness. Every request needed a data scientist to check the design, an engineer to wire the variant and Kinnari herself to approve the metric, and those three people were also running the business.

Kapil Sarawgi wanted the queue gone. "Booking.com tests everything," he said. "Why can't our twelve squads?" The Diwali booking peak was nearly eight weeks away, and the squads were already drawing up changes they wanted to try on it. Kinnari had to decide how much freedom to give them, and what would stand in for her signature.

The stakes were in Kinnari's memo. Caravel's search-results page gets 60,000 sessions a day, converting to a booking at 5.00 per cent. A change lifting that rate by 5 per cent relative (to 5.25 per cent) adds 150 bookings a day. At an average booking of ₹3,200 and a 14 per cent commission, each booking earns ₹448, so such a winner is worth ₹67,200 a day. Nineteen days in the queue cost ₹12.77 lakh per winner. But if twelve squads launched tests that nobody checked, Caravel would ship noise as fact before its busiest season.

2. The idea

An experimentation culture is a company where the default way to judge a product change is a controlled experiment that any team may launch without asking permission, under rules the platform enforces rather than people. It exists to solve two problems: decisions won by the highest-paid person's opinion (often shortened to HiPPO), and a central analytics team that becomes the bottleneck for everyone else.

Online controlled experiments were pioneered at Amazon, Google and Microsoft in the early 2000s. Booking.com's contribution, described in a 2017 paper by its own data scientists and later in Harvard Business Review, was making them democratic: any team could test, and by its own published account roughly nine in ten tests did not win. The sentence Kinnari could repeat in a meeting: "We do not argue about whether a change is good; we make it cheap to find out, and safe to be wrong." The first half is about cost: when launching takes minutes, a team can afford to test a modest idea. The second half is about fear: people stop proposing risky ideas when a failed test counts against them.

3. How it works

The system has four layers, and the third is the one practitioners leave implicit. Permission: a squad launches without approval. Platform: software assigns users at random, logs every outcome, and runs automatic checks, notably for a sample ratio mismatch (an observed split between arms that chance cannot explain, usually a bug) and for guardrail metrics (measures that must not worsen, such as cancellations or page load time). Decision rule: before launch the squad writes down its primary metric, the smallest effect worth detecting, the run length and what it will do with each result. Memory: every test, including losers, is logged where anyone can search it.

At Caravel, Kaivalya Surana's platform team owned steps 3 and 4, and Kirtida Sompura's data scientists owned the metric definitions. Nobody sat between a squad and its launch button. The check in step 4 replaced the person in the queue. The hard part was step 2, because writing a rule in advance forces a squad to say, before any data exists, what result would make it abandon its own idea. Most squads had never been asked that, and early drafts read like hopes rather than rules. Kirtida's template asked for four lines only: the metric, the smallest lift worth chasing, the run length, and the action for a win, a loss and a flat result.

4. A worked example

Kirtida first sized one test. The squad wants to detect a 5 per cent relative lift on the 5.00 per cent baseline, at 5 per cent two-sided significance and 80 per cent power (the chance of detecting the lift if it is real). The sessions needed per arm are n = (zα/2 + zβ)² × [p₁(1−p₁) + p₂(1−p₂)] ÷ (p₂−p₁)², where the unrounded z-values are 1.959964 and 0.841621. Because weekday and weekend behaviour differ, she rounds run length up to whole weeks.

The second pass changes one input, the baseline. A squad judging itself on the 2.00 per cent add-on rate needs 2.6 times the sessions and holds the page for twice as long. That is the first cultural fact: a metric choice is a claim on shared traffic. Squads that choose deeper metrics are not wrong to do so, but they should know the price in weeks before they ask for the page.

Kirtida then asked what 50 tests a quarter would report. She assumed 20 per cent of ideas truly lift the metric, and that real lifts are MDE-sized. A null idea turns up significant in the positive direction 2.5 per cent of the time.

The second pass here halves the prior. Winners fall from 9 to about 5, yet false wins hold near one, so a fifth of what Caravel celebrates would be luck. This is the second cultural fact: the more tests a company runs, the more it needs the log, because a single surprising win is weak evidence and a repeated one is strong.

5. Nuances a learner must absorb

Democratic is not unregulated.

Freedom to launch is only safe because the platform, not a reviewer, blocks tests lacking a written rule, tripping a guardrail or showing a sample ratio mismatch.

A culture is not a tool.

Buying an experimentation platform gives a company software. Culture is whether a director will accept a loss from a test against her own conviction. Test that, not the licence. Ask what happened the last time a result contradicted the chief executive.

Win rate is a diagnostic, not a target.

Table 2 shows why a rate near 10 per cent can be healthy: even a 20 per cent prior yields only 18.0 per cent. A rate above 35 per cent should alarm, because it implies a prior far higher than any in the table, or weak decision rules and cherry-picked tests.

Traffic is a commons.

One surface carrying one-week tests can hold 13 a quarter (91 days ÷ 7). More tests need separate surfaces, or independent random assignment across them, and tests touching the same page need coordination. The platform team should publish the traffic calendar so a squad sees the congestion before it queues.

A squad's win is not the company's win.

A change that lifts one squad's click rate may raise cancellations elsewhere. Guardrails exist for this, and Caravel's two-sided marketplace adds a further risk: guests and hosts share inventory, so one arm's gain can come out of the other arm's. A discount that fills a Goa villa for the treated guests may simply empty the villa for the control guests.

The decision rule comes before the data.

Peeking daily and stopping at the first significant reading inflates false positives well above the nominal rate (5 per cent in either direction). The planned run length is the commitment.

Experiments cannot tell everything.

They are weak for a bold bet with no traffic yet, for effects that take months, and for novelty that fades. Data-over-opinion does not retire opinion: opinion is where the ideas come from. The experiment only judges them.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace; small and large

SettingWhat changes
ConsumerHuge traffic, fast tests, and the main risk is volume of low-quality tests.
B2BFew accounts, so sample sizes are unreachable; teams lean on interviews, staged rollouts and comparisons within an account.
Marketplace (Caravel)Two sides interact, so a user-level split can mislead; hosts and guests need separate guardrails.

Table 3. The same culture, three shapes.

In every row the same four layers of Figure 2 apply. What differs is which layer is scarce: traffic in B2B, trustworthy assignment in a marketplace, and attention to quality in consumer products.

Size matters as much as model. A start-up with 2,000 sessions a day, 1,000 per arm, would need about 122 days for the Table 1 test, so it should test only large changes. A large company's problem is the reverse: abundant traffic, many tests, and a need for governance. At Caravel's size the second problem was the live one: with twelve squads and a festive deadline, the cost of a bad test was higher than the cost of a slow one.

7. Common mistakes

Symptom seen from outsideUnderlying misunderstandingCheapest diagnostic
Leadership celebrates tests launched; the win rate climbs above 35%.Activity is learning.Count tests with a written rule before launch.
Wins arrive after two or three days.Early significance is final.Compare each stop day with the planned run length.
"Open to all", yet launches wait for sign-off.A review is a safeguard, not a gate.Measure the median days from request to launch.

Table 4. Three failures and their detectors.

Each detector uses data the platform already holds. None needs an audit team, which matters because the whole point is to remove people from the path rather than add them.

8. What good looks like

Handled well, Caravel's squads launch on their own, each with a rule written in a template. The platform stops any test that skews its split or breaches a guardrail. Every result, losers included, lands in a log, and Kirtida's team spends its time on metric quality rather than on approvals. Kaivalya Surana's team publishes a weekly note listing tests started, stopped and breached, so that the system's behaviour is visible without anyone chasing it. Leaders can say "we lost that test" in a meeting without defending themselves. The measure of health is how fast the company learns, not how often it wins.

9. The decision

Kinnari told Kapil Sarawgi that Caravel would drop the queue from Monday 5 October 2026, a little under five weeks before the Diwali peak, on three conditions: no launch without a written rule, automatic checks as the only gate, and a shared log. The target was 50 tests across twelve squads in the 13 weeks from 5 October, with a review on Monday 4 January 2027, the first day after them. She chose it because the queue cost ₹12.77 lakh per winner, while Table 2 showed how much of a winners list can be luck, which only written rules and a shared log could keep honest. "Tests everything" was a slogan; the system she built would test what could be tested, and would say plainly where it could not. A loss under the new rules would cost a squad nothing, which was the property she cared about most.

Next, read experiment velocity (how many tests per quarter, and how much each one teaches) and learning rate, then why dark patterns emerge without malice, then experiment governance and ethics, because a system that rewards winning tests will, without malice, drift towards winning by any means.

Questions to sit with. (1) If Caravel's true prior were 10 per cent and the squads' win rate reached 30 per cent, which explanation would you investigate first? (2) Which test in your own organisation would you least want to lose, and what does that say about its culture?
exp40v2-exp.culture:
Experimentation culture

What it takes for a whole company to test everything, and what the arithmetic says about those that cannot.

1. Two decisions, three days apart

On Thursday 15 October 2026 Loveleen Turakhia had to defend a number she had produced. Devadaru Stays, the Bengaluru accommodation marketplace she joined in January 2021, carries 2.8 million sessions a week on its search page, converting 3.2 per cent into bookings: 89,600 bookings a week at an average value of ₹6,400 and a 14 per cent take rate, which is ₹896 of net revenue a booking, ₹8.028 crore a week, ₹417.5 crore a year. In the quarter ended 30 June 2026 her fourteen teams launched 126 experiments, read out 112, declared 23 winners and shipped 19. Those nineteen estimates summed to a +11.4 per cent lift in booking conversion. On Tuesday 14 July 2026 the five per cent global holdout Lavnish Tolia's platform team has re-drawn each quarter since 2023 read out at +6.1 per cent. Lalitkumar Tapuriah, the chief financial officer, wanted one number for the FY28 plan, and wanted to know whether a holdout that cuts the return on a quarter's programme spend from 29.8 times to 15.9 should survive.

Three days earlier, on Monday 12 October, Leeladhar Thacker faced the opposite problem. Dishantar Freight Cloud, founded in Pune in 2019, sells a transport-management system to 412 enterprise accounts — ₹96 crore of recurring revenue, 9,888 weekly active planners, 24 an account. Thacker, chief product officer since March 2024, had just won board approval for an experimentation practice. The same minute approved a hiring freeze effective 1 November 2026 and running to the close of FY27, 31 March 2027. Larisa Timbadia, his head of data science, had modelled it on five analysts. She has three.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

An experimentation culture is the standing arrangements — platform, decision rights, metric definitions, norms — under which a randomised comparison is how a change earns the right to ship, and its result outranks the seniority of whoever proposed it. The first clause is a measurement claim. The second is a governance claim, and it is the one that fails.

The history is older than software. Fisher's randomised field trials at Rothamsted in the 1920s established that randomisation licenses a causal reading; the Medical Research Council's 1948 streptomycin trial carried it into medicine. What the web added was not the method but the marginal cost. When assignment is a cookie hash and the outcome already sits in a log, a comparison costs hours, and a strategic question — which things do we test? — turns operational. Booking.com's programme is the canonical operational answer: any employee may launch against live traffic without permission, because the platform, not a committee, enforces safety. By 2015 the tooling was commoditised, by 2020 attention had moved to trustworthiness, by 2025 to evaluation systems for probabilistic products.

Four schools now disagree substantively. The democratisation school signs that the learning rate is set by the number of independent tests, so gates should give way to automatic guardrails; it will not sign that a council should vet hypotheses. The trustworthiness school signs that an untrustworthy result is worse than none, and spends on A/A tests and invariant checks; it will not sign that volume is the objective. The decision-theoretic school signs that a shipping threshold must depend on the prior that ideas of this kind work; it will not sign that p < 0.05 is one. The theory-first school signs that experiments can only rank what someone already thought of, so idea quality binds; it will not sign that more tests is more learning. Devadaru is run by the first two in uneasy coalition; Dishantar cannot afford the first at all.

3. Mechanics: what the arithmetic permits

Every argument about experimentation culture reduces to a sample-size identity. For a two-arm comparison of proportions at power 1−β and two-sided α, the sample per arm is n = (zα/2 + zβ)2 × 2p(1−p) / Δ2. At 80 per cent power and α = 0.05 the leading constant is (1.96 + 0.84)2 = 7.84, so 2 × 7.84 = 15.68. Three of the four — cohort size, baseline rate, power, minimum detectable effect — fix the fourth.

Devadaru's search page in a two-week, 50/50 test gives 2.8 million sessions an arm. With p = 0.032, Δ2 = 15.68 × 0.032 × 0.968 / 2,800,000, so Δ = 0.000416 — 1.30 per cent of baseline. Dishantar randomising its 9,888 planners 50/50 over four weeks gives 4,944 an arm; with p = 0.26 the identity returns Δ = 0.0247, 9.50 per cent relative. Its planners cluster inside accounts: at an intra-cluster correlation of 0.08 with 24 planners an account the design effect is 1 + (24−1) × 0.08 = 2.84, cutting the effective sample to 1,741 an arm and widening the detectable effect to 16.01 per cent. Regressing the outcome on each planner's pre-period value at correlation 0.62 removes 1 − √(1−0.622) = 21.5 per cent of the interval, taking the planner-level figure to 7.45 per cent.

The second-order consequence is the one practitioners miss. Devadaru's 126 experiments a quarter is 9.7 a week, and at a two-week median duration about 19 run concurrently. Nineteen concurrent tests contain 171 pairs; if a material interaction arises in one pair in two hundred, 0.86 are live at any moment, which is why its platform keeps mutually exclusive layers for one surface. Dishantar cannot overlap at all: 9,888 planners are one population with one primary metric, so a second concurrent test halves the cohort and widens the detectable effect by √2.

4. When it applies, and when it misleads

Four conditions can be stated as testable claims. First: the effect you care about exceeds the effect your traffic can detect. Devadaru passes: a 1.30 per cent relative lift is worth ₹5.43 crore a year on a ₹417.5 crore base, and ₹6.4 crore of programme cost over 504 experiments a year is ₹1.27 lakh each. Dishantar fails on most surfaces: its detectable effect is 7.3 times Devadaru's, and at one analyst's fully loaded ₹42 lakh a year and 2.6 analyst-weeks a test, analyst labour alone is ₹2.10 lakh a test, against Devadaru's ₹1.27 lakh of whole-programme cost, platform and tooling included. Those are different bases, so the real gap is wider than the two figures show.

Second: the unit of randomisation is the unit of the decision. Devadaru decides and randomises per session. Dishantar decides per account — one planner cannot see a different product from the colleague beside her — so it either randomises accounts and accepts 16.01 per cent, or randomises planners and measures something smaller than the decision.

Third: the outcome is observable inside the decision window. Where it is not, the culture misleads, because the surrogate gets optimised and the outcome does not. Devadaru's booking conversion is visible in hours; its cancellation and repeat-stay consequences take ninety days. A programme that ships on the first and never audits the second does not fail loudly: it ships defensible wins against a metric that has stopped standing for anything.

Fourth, and the one Timbadia got wrong: the capacity exists inside the window the constraint actually leaves. Her first model multiplied five analysts by the 171 days from board approval on 12 October 2026 to the close of FY27 — 855 analyst-days, 122.1 analyst-weeks, 47 experiments at 2.6 each. But the freeze bites on 1 November, so both requisitions must clear by 31 October, and Dishantar's median data-science hire takes 11 weeks: 77 days after 31 October is 16 January 2027. Five analysts exist for 75 of those days, not 171, and only if requisitions open on the last permitted day.

Dishantar's analyst capacity, 12 October 2026 to 31 March 2027; day counts include both endpoints. 663 analyst-days is 94.7 analyst-weeks — 36 experiments at 2.6 each, against the unconstrained model's 47. The 192 analyst-days between them overstate true capacity by 29 per cent.

5. Hard edge cases, and what mature companies really do

Two-sided marketplaces break independence: a test improving a traveller's conversion consumes inventory the control group would otherwise have booked, so the travel-side effect overstates the network effect. Devadaru's answer is the one most marketplaces reach for and few publish: supply-side changes run as time-sliced switchbacks over whole cities, accepting wider intervals for an uncontaminated contrast. Regulated surfaces are harder: a pricing or disclosure variant routine on a search page needs sign-off, so Devadaru keeps a register of surfaces where randomisation is prohibited.

Hardware-plus-software sits worst. The software half iterates weekly and the firmware half quarterly, so an experiment depending on a firmware capability cannot be randomised within a release: the arm is defined by which device the customer bought, which is selection, not assignment. AI-native products break another assumption: the treatment is non-deterministic, two users in one arm receive different artefacts, and within-arm variance is driven as much by sampling as by the change. Mature companies fix the decoding seed and retrieval index for the test and report within-arm variance beside the contrast. What they say they do is run a clean A/B. What they do is freeze four things that are not the treatment and hope nobody shipped a prompt change on Tuesday.

6. Eight things an expert sees that a competent practitioner does not

A rising win rate is usually bad news. The tell is a win rate climbing while the average effect among winners falls. The obvious reading — the teams pick better now — is almost never right, because better picking should raise both. What has normally happened is a shift to safe increments: small, reliable effects, and no information bought about anything risky. Devadaru's 20.5 per cent is defensible; 35 per cent would not be.

Velocity is not always the binding constraint. The tell is a team asking for analysts while its traffic budget is fully subscribed. Dishantar's analyst capacity supports 36 experiments; its traffic supports six, since each four-week test needs the whole population and the window is 171 days. Two more analysts would not move the second number by one. Capacity added to a traffic-bound programme buys only under-powered tests.

The most democratic programme is also the most governed. The tell is a company that removed launch approval without adding one invariant. Freedom to launch is safe only when sample-ratio mismatch, metric drift and guardrail breaches are caught by machinery nobody can overrule. Booking.com's openness is bought with a heavy platform, not a relaxed attitude. Removing the committee without the machinery moves risk to whoever reads the dashboard last.

Peeking is an incentive problem in statistical clothes. The tell is not the interim look but who asks for it: when it comes from the person whose quarter depends on the answer, the sequential correction is beside the point. Four interim looks at a nominal two-sided 0.05 carry an actual type-I rate near 12.6 per cent, and the fix, a locked readout date, is cheap. What is not cheap is the norm that an early read is available on request: then nulls get abandoned rather than recorded.

Shipping on a flat result is a decision, and most programmes make it by default. The tell is a register with no outcome between "won" and "abandoned". A flat result on a change that cuts maintenance cost is a ship; on one that adds a surface it is not. The obvious reading, that flat means no information, is wrong: a tight interval around zero is often the most informative outcome. Devadaru's 112 readouts yielded 23 winners; the other 89 are the part of the culture nobody audits.

A test that confirms what everybody believed is the cheapest to run and the costliest to read. The tell is a run of launches whose hypotheses were never contested in review. The posterior barely moves, so the test buys almost nothing; worse, a run of them persuades the organisation it is working while untested beliefs go unexamined for years. The expert reads a confirmed hypothesis as a question about review.

A guardrail that has never blocked anything is not a guardrail. The tell is a latency or page-weight invariant that has fired zero times in eighteen months. Either the threshold sits beyond anything the product could do, or it is waived at ship time. Both read identically, and both mean the programme is uninsured. The expert asks which ships a guardrail stopped and treats an empty list as a finding.

The winner's curse is budgetable in advance. The tell is a plan that adds up shipped point estimates. A declared winner is drawn, by selection, from the upper tail of its sampling distribution, overstating the truth by more as the true effect approaches the detectable one. Devadaru's +11.4 per cent claimed against +6.1 per cent measured is the expected shape, not a scandal, and a programme that has never measured the gap just reports the bias with more confidence.

7. How this differs by product type and stage

The real differences are differences in section 3's identity. Consumer products with millions of sessions can be genuinely democratic, because the detectable effect sits below the interesting one; B2B products with thousands of users cannot, and their honest answer is fewer, larger, pre-registered bets plus qualitative work. Enterprise software adds an obstacle unrelated to sample size: change-control terms giving a customer the right not to be experimented on. Marketplaces break the independence assumption rather than the sample-size one; their fix is a different design, not a bigger cohort. Hardware breaks assignment itself.

Where the difference is asserted and is not real: AI products are not exempt from randomisation, merely higher in within-arm variance, and offline evaluation sets complement live tests rather than replace them. By stage, a pre-product-market-fit company should not build a culture at all: its traffic cannot detect anything and its changes are large enough to see without it. The inflection arrives when changes become small relative to the base. Devadaru crossed it around 2021; Dishantar, at 9,888 weekly planners after seven years, has not, on most surfaces, and may never.

8. Three worked examples

Devadaru's holdout. Over the thirteen weeks from 1 April to 30 June 2026, five per cent of sessions — 140,000 a week, 1,820,000 — were held back from that quarter's shipments, against 34,580,000 exposed; the holdout is re-drawn each quarter, so it prices that quarter's work alone. That design detects a 1.17 per cent relative effect at 80 per cent power — the unbalanced form puts p(1−p)(1/n1 + 1/n2) under the same constant — so +6.1 per cent was resolvable. The nineteen shipments landed through the quarter, not on day one, so mean exposure was under thirteen weeks and +6.1 per cent is a floor on the fully exposed effect. On the ₹417.5 crore base, +11.4 per cent is ₹47.6 crore a year and +6.1 per cent ₹25.5 crore; the ₹22.1 crore difference is 5.3 points of the 11.4 claimed, 46.5 per cent. Those run-rates were bought by one quarter's work, so they belong against that quarter's cost — 126 × ₹1.27 lakh = ₹1.60 crore — making the measured figure 15.9 times a quarter's spend against 29.8 claimed.

Dishantar's auto-assign test. Run as a pilot in the quarter to 30 September 2026, it was the evidence behind the October board vote. Timbadia randomised planners, paired on pre-period volume, adjusted on the covariate: a detectable effect of 7.45 per cent against a product belief of +15 per cent. Over four weeks, use of the auto-assign suggestion moved from 26.0 to 28.9 per cent, +11.2 per cent relative. The 95 per cent interval's half-width is (1.96/2.80) × 7.45 = 5.2 relative points, so the result is +6.0 to +16.4 per cent — a lower bound that still justified the build.

Drishtikon Labs, and the failure. The Hyderabad AI-native legal-research firm, founded 2021, 38,000 weekly users, declared in the quarter to 30 June 2026 that a new retrieval model had lifted answer acceptance from 41.0 to 44.8 per cent. The same release also raised the answer-length cap. A 2×2 factorial re-run split the 38,000 users into four cells: 19,000 a side per main effect, a detectable effect of 1.41 points. The cap accounted for +2.7 points; the model's main effect was +1.1, below the design's own floor — so the conclusion was not that the model did nothing but that Drishtikon could not tell. The recovery was a one-change-per-arm rule and a release lock. Experiments fell from 31 to 19 in the quarter to 30 September 2026 and winners from 12 to 7 — yet 5 of the 12 earlier winners survived confirmation re-runs, 41.7 per cent, against 6 of the 7 later ones, 85.7 per cent.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Five recur. Sample-ratio mismatch waved through: the sign is an arm split of 50.4/49.6 on millions of sessions; the question is whether the assignment and outcome logs were joined on the same key; caught late, every result on that surface is unusable and nobody knows since when. Metric sprawl: the sign is a readout template with a dozen metrics and no overall criterion; the question is which one would have reversed this decision; caught late, teams select whichever metric moved. Peeking normalised: the sign is a dashboard with live p-values; the question is what the pre-registered readout date was; caught late, the false-winner share climbs from 22.0 to 41.5 per cent at a 10 per cent prior. The programme becomes a queue: the sign is readout-to-decision time passing a fortnight; the question is how many ships a review has blocked; caught late, teams route around the programme. The holdout is retired when it embarrasses someone: the sign is retirement proposed in a budget meeting rather than a design review; the question is what replaces the unbiased estimate; caught late, the only check on reported returns is gone.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Permanent global holdouts. For: it is the only unbiased estimate of a programme's cumulative value; without it a company reports the sum of biased estimates for ever. Against: it denies five per cent of users the product, its estimate is confounded by everything else that changed in the window, and the held-back population diverges over long horizons. The first fails if divergence is large; the second if, as at Devadaru, the gap is 46.5 per cent of the claim.

Open launch versus gated. For openness: gates select for politically safe hypotheses, and the throughput cost compounds. For gates: at Dishantar's detectable effects an ungated programme spends a scarce population on tests that cannot resolve. Openness fails where traffic is scarce, gating where rejections are never audited against what they would have shown.

Velocity versus idea quality. The velocity position rests on the observation that programmes running more tests find more wins; the quality position notes you would see the same if idea quality were constant and the extra wins false. Each fails on the other's prediction about effect sizes: rising velocity with constant mean effect favours the first, with falling mean effect the second. Most companies never measure it.

Winners and noise per 200 read-out tests at 80 per cent power. The false-positive rate is the positive-direction half of the two-sided type-I rate, since teams ship on significant-and-positive: 2.5 per cent at a nominal 0.05, 6.3 per cent when four interim looks inflate it to about 12.6 per cent. Holding power constant flatters the third row.
