Devadaru's own record reads back through the identity. Its declared-winner rate is 23 of 112, or 20.5 per cent. Solving 0.80π + 0.025(1−π) = 0.205 gives π = 23.2 per cent, under which the false share is 0.025 × 0.768 / 0.205 = 9.4 per cent. That is reassuring, and not the number Tapuriah was looking at. False positives explain perhaps a tenth of the declared winners; the holdout says 46.5 per cent of the claimed value never arrived. The residue is winner's curse, interaction between concurrent changes, and novelty decay — which leave every result correct and the sum wrong.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has studied experimentation argues about p-values. Someone who has internalised it argues about denominators, decision rules and who may stop a test. They write the decision rule — what ships at what result, including flat — before the test starts, and keep the register of what happened to the nulls. They state their detectable effect from memory, because it determines which arguments are worth having. They treat a request for an interim read as an organisational signal, not a statistical one. They know their win rate and what prior it implies. And they are unsentimental where the company cannot measure a thing and must decide another way.

12. What they decided

Turakhia kept the holdout and changed what it was for. She stopped reporting the sum of shipped estimates, moved the headline to the holdout, and asked Tapuriah to plan FY28 on ₹25.5 crore rather than ₹47.6 crore. Her argument: a 15.9-times return that survives audit is a more durable budget than a 29.8-times return that does not.

Thacker did not build a Devadaru. He took Timbadia's corrected capacity, cut the programme to a few pre-registered four-week planner-level tests with covariate adjustment, and put the rest of the analyst time into instrumentation and qualitative work on unpowerable surfaces. He told the board its purpose was to settle three or four contested questions a year.

Question 1. Devadaru's holdout reduces the programme's reported return. What measurement would have to exist before a company could responsibly retire one?

Question 2. Dishantar's analyst capacity and its traffic imply different maximum experiment counts. How should a product leader decide which constraint to plan against, and what does each choice commit the organisation to?

Question 3. Drishtikon's declared-winner count fell after it tightened its rules. Under what conditions, if any, is a falling count evidence that a programme is improving?

13. Going deeper

A/B testing fundamentals — section 3's identity is the whole of it; without fluency there, no cultural argument can be settled. Experiment velocity and learning rate — makes section 6's first two nuances measurable and shows which constraint binds. Why dark patterns emerge without malice — how a programme optimising a surrogate reaches outcomes nobody chose. Experiment governance and ethics — the register of prohibited surfaces, and the consent question enterprise contracts raise. Writing an experiment hypothesis — what keeps confirmed beliefs from consuming capacity. Significance, power, sample size, peeking — the formal treatment behind the 12.6 per cent figure. When you can't A/B test — switchbacks, interrupted time series and synthetic controls: Dishantar's toolkit. Qual + quant feedback loop — what fills the gap when the detectable effect exceeds the interesting one. Feature flags and flighting — what makes open launch safe, and where sample-ratio mismatch starts. Choosing experiment metrics — the criterion whose absence produces sprawl.
exp20v2-exp.governance:
Experiment Governance and Ethics

What are we not allowed to test on our users?

1. A test that had already won

On Tuesday 3 March 2026, Ishana Pramanick, director of product at Ananta Mobility, a Kolkata ride-hailing company with 18 lakh riders a month, opened a one-page proposal from the growth team. Between 12 and 25 February the team had run an experiment on 6,00,000 riders, split into three arms of 2,00,000. In one arm, the booking screen carried a ₹9 "trip protection" add-on that was already ticked. In the control arm the box was unticked.

The growth team's reasoning was ordinary. Booking-screen defaults were a known lever, and cover that protects a rider against a cancelled trip is a real service. The result was striking. Add-on revenue in the control arm was ₹36,000 over the fourteen days; in the pre-ticked arm it was ₹1,98,000. Inesh Pakhira, head of data science, had confirmed that the gap was far outside random noise. The proposal asked Ishana to ship the pre-ticked box to every rider.

Nobody had done anything improper by the company's own rules, because the company had no rules on what could be tested, only on what could be shipped. The test needed no approval, and its design document described a "checkout conversion" metric and nothing else. Yet the Central Consumer Protection Authority's 2023 guidelines on dark patterns, which list thirteen deceptive design practices, name "basket sneaking", adding an item at checkout without the customer's consent. If Ishana approved, Ananta might be selling to riders who had not chosen to buy. If she refused on instinct, she would have no evidence and a furious growth team.

2. The idea

Experiment governance is the set of rules that decides which tests may be run on users, who must review the risky ones, and what users are told. It exists because an experiment, unlike a feature, is a decision to treat some people differently on purpose and to measure the result. The measurement is the point, and it is also the temptation: a test is judged by the metric it was built to move.

The discipline borrows from medicine. After abuses in twentieth-century human research, the United States National Commission published the Belmont Report in 1979, naming three principles: respect for persons, beneficence (do no harm, maximise benefit) and justice (do not load the burden on one group). Technology companies later adapted these into review boards and risk tiers for online experiments, in the 2010s.

The problem governance solves is therefore a quiet one. Each team optimises its own number, each test is defensible alone, and the sum is a product that treats users as a source of conversions. Nobody has to decide to deceive; the selection of winning variants does it for them.

Ananta never set out to design a dark pattern, a screen built to trick people. It had only a culture of testing and a metric. That is how such designs usually emerge: no one intends harm, and unchecked variants that extract money simply win.

A test may only ask a question whose losing answer we would be willing to explain to the people it was run on.

3. How it works

Governance has six steps. First, classify the test by what it could damage: money, safety, personal data, or the interests of vulnerable people. Second, pre-register it: write down the hypothesis, the decision rule, and the harm measure before seeing any results. Third, review in proportion to the class. Fourth, limit exposure: cap how many users see the variant and wire a kill switch. Fifth, disclose. Sixth, record the outcome in a registry, so that the next team inherits the lesson.

The tiers matter because review is expensive. A reviewer's time is scarce, so the aim is to spend it where harm is plausible and let the harmless majority move quickly. The registry matters for the opposite reason: it makes the whole portfolio of tests visible, so a pattern such as three separate teams all pre-ticking boxes can be seen before it becomes a habit.

Three steps are usually implicit. The harm measure must be written before the revenue is known, otherwise it gets chosen to fit the answer. Someone must hold a veto who is not paid on the metric. And "disclosure" has two meanings: the standing notice users get that testing happens, and the specific correction owed when a test has wronged them.

Applied to Ananta, the pre-ticked box was a Tier 2 test at minimum, since it changed a default that spends rider money, and arguably Tier 3. The tier is judged by what the variant could do to a rider, never by how small the engineering change is: a one-line default can be the riskiest change of the quarter.

4. A worked example

Inesh Pakhira repeated the analysis with one added measure. Between 4 and 6 March he surveyed 400 buyers from each arm and asked whether they had meant to buy the protection. The decision rule, set before looking, was this: block a variant if the revenue it takes, beyond control's, from buyers who did not intend to buy exceeds 20 per cent of its incremental revenue over control. Take-up in the arms was 2.0 per cent (4,000 of 2,00,000) for control, 11.0 per cent for B and 6.0 per cent for C. Table 1 shows the arithmetic.

ArmBuyersRevenue (₹)Incremental (₹)Unintended share (survey)Unintended buyersExcess over controlExcess revenue (₹)Share of incremental
Control, unticked4,00036,000none6.0% (24/400)240nonenonenone
B, pre-ticked22,0001,98,0001,62,00038.0% (152/400)8,3608,12073,08045.1%
C, off with explanation12,0001,08,00072,0007.0% (28/400)8406005,4007.5%

Table 1. Revenue is buyers times ₹9. Unintended buyers are the survey share applied to all buyers in that arm; excess subtracts control's 240.

Take arm B line by line. Buyers 22,000 at ₹9 is ₹1,98,000, and subtracting control's ₹36,000 leaves ₹1,62,000 of incremental revenue. Survey share 38 per cent of 22,000 gives 8,360 riders who did not mean to buy; subtracting control's 240 leaves 8,120, or ₹73,080. Divided by ₹1,62,000, that is 45.1 per cent, far above the 20 per cent line. B is blocked, despite winning on revenue.

Now change one input: the default. Arm C leaves the box unticked but explains the cover in a sentence. Buyers fall to 12,000 and incremental revenue to ₹72,000, but excess unintended revenue is only ₹5,400, which is 7.5 per cent of ₹72,000. C passes.

5. Nuances a learner must absorb

Disclosure is not consent

A line in the terms of service saying "we run experiments" tells riders testing happens. It does not ask permission for this test. Real consent is rarely workable in an A/B test, because asking changes the behaviour measured, so governance relies on review, limits and remedy instead.

Significance is not permission

Pakhira's gap was statistically unmistakable, and that is irrelevant to whether it was acceptable. A larger sample makes the estimate sharper and also makes the harm larger, because every extra user in the variant bears it.

Complaints undercount harm

In arm B, 1,980 riders requested refunds, 9.0 per cent of buyers. Yet the survey implied 8,360 unintended buyers, so, if refunders are among them, requests caught only 23.7 per cent. A complaint-rate guardrail measures the people who noticed and bothered.

The survey has its own error

The 38.0 per cent figure comes from 400 respondents, with a standard error of 2.4 points and a 95 per cent interval of roughly 33.2 to 42.8 per cent. At the lower end, excess revenue is still 39.2 per cent of incremental, so the verdict holds. A survey cannot be trusted blindly, only bounded.

Law is a floor

Compliance with the Authority's guidelines tells you what is prohibited, not what is wise. A variant can be lawful and still spend your riders' trust faster than it earns revenue, which no single test will show.

Averages hide who is hurt

Unintended purchases may concentrate among new riders, late-night bookings or people on small screens. A review should ask which subgroup is most exposed, and check that group separately before approving.

Reversibility sets the cap

A harm that can be undone, such as a refunded ₹9, tolerates wider exposure than one that cannot, such as a leaked address. Start small, ramp in stages, watch the harm measure at each stage, and give someone authority to switch the variant off the same day. A kill switch nobody is allowed to pull is decoration.

Who reviews matters

A panel made of the people whose bonuses depend on the metric is not a review. Reviewers need no stake in the uplift, and at least one should speak for the user, whether from support, legal or research.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace

In consumer products, the risks are money, attention and data, and the rider is both the subject and the customer. In B2B, the test subject is often an employee of a client, while consent sits with the client's administrator; tests touching billing or admin settings need contract-level approval, not only internal review. In a marketplace such as Ananta, a test on riders can cut driver earnings, so reviewers must name both sides and ask who loses.

Size changes the machinery. An early-stage company with twenty people needs one named approver, a one-page template and a shared log; a panel would be theatre. A large company needs tiers, a registry, an independent panel, and an audit of how often tests skip review, because with hundreds of tests a year nobody remembers the details.

7. Common mistakes

Treating the winning metric as approval

Symptom: launch decks cite uplift and nothing else. Misunderstanding: that the metric measures everything that matters. Cheapest diagnostic: ask "who paid for this uplift, and did they mean to?"

A gate that nobody can pass

Symptom: review takes weeks and teams relabel tests as "analytics changes". Misunderstanding: that every test deserves equal scrutiny. Diagnostic: count tests per tier and the median review days; a thin Tier 1 is a warning.

Ethics by complaint count

Symptom: "we had few complaints" closes the discussion. Misunderstanding: silence is consent. Diagnostic: field a 400-per-arm intent survey, as Pakhira did, before trusting the complaint line.

8. What good looks like

Had the growth team filed a card before 12 February, it would have been classified Tier 2 within two days, and the reviewers would have asked the missing question. The test, Tier 2 but with a voluntary cap as for Tier 3, would have run with a cap of 50,000 riders per arm and a stated rule that any rider charged by a variant could claim the money back in one tap.

The result would have been the same, B rejected and C approved, but at a quarter of the exposure and with no rider out of pocket. Good governance is not slower; it moves the argument to before the damage. Growth keeps its pace on Tier 1 work, and the team learns that a hard question asked early costs a couple of days, not a refund programme.

9. What Pramanick decides

On Friday 13 March, Ishana rejected the pre-ticked box and approved C. She also offered all 22,000 arm-B buyers a one-tap refund, capped at ₹1,98,000 if every one accepted, and required that the next quarter's tests carry registry cards. Her reasoning: 45.1 per cent of B's uplift was money from riders who had not chosen to pay, and the cost of making them whole was smaller than the trust it would otherwise spend. The growth team lost its headline number but kept the working feature, and Pakhira was asked to publish the survey method so other teams could reuse it.

To go further, study guardrail metrics and decision rules, since governance depends on writing the rule before the result, and then the dark-patterns literature, which catalogues how unchecked tests produce harm.

Two questions to sit with. Which test at your company would you be uncomfortable explaining to the users it ran on? And who today holds a veto on the metric you are paid to move?
exp40v2-exp.governance:
Experiment governance and ethics

What a firm may test on the people it serves, who decides, and what it owes them afterwards: two decisions, a tier ledger, a misread ramp, and a guardrail measured over three days.

1. Two desks, one week in February

On Monday 9 February 2026 Jayanti Ruidas, vice-president of product at Balaka Health, had a submission on her desk returned stamped CHANGES, twelve days after filing. Balaka is a sleep-and-mood application with 11.4 million monthly active users, a third of whom have completed a depression screener inside it. The submission proposed a push notification to users inactive for seven to thirty days, framing a streak as a loss: your 47-day streak expires tonight. Of users in that window, 12.4 per cent return within seven days unprompted; the team expected 1.5 percentage points more. Junali Rajbanshi, who runs data science and chairs Balaka's experiment council, had not refused the test. She had changed it, and the changes added six days.

Three days later, on Thursday 12 February, Jyotishman Rajchoudhury met the same question without Ruidas's instruments. Brihat Labs sells an assistant that drafts support replies for enterprise help desks: 240 accounts, 9,400 licensed seats, 34 drafts per seat per day. A new model, v4, scored on 30 January against 2,400 held-out tickets, was judged acceptable on 78.0 per cent of drafts by two raters against 71.5 for v3.2, while drafts carrying a confidently wrong policy citation rose from 30 of the 2,400 to 48. A wrong citation reaches not Brihat's users or their employees but the customers' complainants, who agreed to nothing. The master agreement promises notice before a material change, and general counsel Jayashri Rudrapal would not say whether a model swap is one.

2. The idea, and the four camps that will not merge

Experiment governance is the standing set of rules deciding, before any test is proposed, what a firm may run on the people it serves, who approves each class, what is measured to stop one early, and what is told to whom. Its ethics are the rules' content; its governance is what binds them.

The vocabulary is borrowed from clinical research: the Nuremberg Code of 1947 and the Declaration of Helsinki of 1964 established voluntary informed consent; the Belmont Report of 1979 reduced the field to respect for persons, beneficence and justice, which the United States Common Rule turned into review boards and a minimal-risk threshold. Benjamin Freedman's 1987 clinical equipoise added that a trial is licit only while experts are genuinely uncertain which arm is better. Product experimentation met this abruptly: a 2014 paper reported an emotional-contagion experiment on 689,003 users of a large social network. The industry's answer was institutional: tiered review and automatic stopping, codified by Ron Kohavi, Diane Tang and Ya Xu in 2020. Regulation arrived from the side, in Europe's GDPR and Digital Services Act and India's DPDP Act of 2023.

Four camps divide on three questions. Is the object of judgement the design or the treatment? Is the baseline no experiment, or an untested launch? Must consent be asked?

The review-board camp signs a product experiment is research on human subjects and needs independent prospective review, and will not sign that accepting terms of service is consent. The counterfactual camp signs shipping untested exposes every user to an unvetted treatment, so testing is the conservative act, and will not sign that every test needs prospective consent. The consumer-protection camp signs if you would not ship the winning arm to everyone, you may not run it on anyone, and will not sign that harm scales with exposure. The institutional camp signs an unreviewed risky test is a governance failure however it turned out, and will not sign that well-meaning practitioners are a sufficient control.

3. Mechanics: tiers, ramps, and powering the thing you fear

Mature practice has three components: a tiering rule that routes a submission before anyone argues, a ramp with pre-committed stage decisions, and powering the test on its guardrail rather than its win metric.

Balaka's rule asks three questions in order. Does the change alter what a user is told about their own state, charged, or shown as clinical content? Could it worsen a condition through a mechanism slower than the guardrail window? Would the honest response to a winning arm be to decline shipping it? Yes to either of the first two escalates; yes to the third is a refusal. A declared latency class, added on 25 September 2025, makes the second answerable.

Of the 250 submissions, 66 reached a reviewer at all, or 26.4 per cent; of those 66, thirty-one were changed or stopped, or 47.0 per cent. At council level it is 13 of 17 (76.5 per cent).

Ruidas's submission was Tier 2 on the second question. Its declared mechanism was a rise in the distress-flag rate: the share of contacted users who within 72 hours silence all reminders or file a negative report. On the ordinary message that is 1.90 per cent, with a written tolerance of 0.50 points more.

Rajbanshi's first change was the ramp. Of 63,600 users crossing the seven-day lapse line daily, 2,600 had ever opened the crisis-routing screen and were excluded, leaving 61,000 eligible.

This is where governance arithmetic usually goes wrong. Costing the test at its end state, 8 per cent for fourteen days, gives 1.12 day-equivalents and 68,320 exposed users; the ramp delivers 0.75 and 45,750, or 67.0 per cent of that. Whoever wants the test called safe quotes the second figure and then borrows the first's power. The ramp lowers total exposure, and with it each eligible user's chance of being exposed; what it cannot lower is the risk run by anyone it does expose.

Her second change is the formal core: the question is not whether the test detects its win, but whether it detects the harm it is permitted to risk. At 80 per cent power and a two-sided five per cent level, the minimum detectable effect on a two-arm difference in proportions is 2.80 standard errors of that difference, 2.80 being 1.96 plus 0.84. On the guardrail, with p = 0.0190 and 45,750 per arm, that standard error is the square root of 2 × 0.0190 × 0.9810 / 45,750, or 0.0903 points, so the MDE is 0.25. On the win metric, with p = 0.1240 over the same 45,750, it is 0.2179 and the MDE is 0.61, inside the expected 1.5-point lift. At 0.25 against a 0.50 tolerance, the safety margin on the guardrail is two.

She declined a safety margin of two, requiring a guardrail MDE of 0.20, which needs 0.037278 × (2.80/0.0020)² = 73,065 per arm. The ramp supplies 45,750; six further days at 8 per cent add 0.48 day-equivalents, giving 1.23 and 75,030 per arm, at which the MDE recomputes to 0.20. The test runs twenty days because of a figure nobody on the growth team had read.

4. When the frame holds, and when it inverts

The practice reduces to four checkable conditions.

The frame is actively misleading in three situations. First, when the status quo is the harm: if a product withholds something users need, review latency is a cost borne by those the review protects. Second, when equipoise is absent. Balaka's three prohibited-tier refusals withheld crisis routing from a holdback, where no uncertainty exists about which arm serves the user, so randomisation only distributes a known harm. Third, where the population is too small for a guardrail to have power, governance cannot be measurement: Rajchoudhury's instruments see nothing short of fourteen accounts churning.

5. Hard edge cases and the organisational seams

Multi-product firms create the classic seam: a test owned by one surface, a harm landing on another. Balaka's notification tests belong to growth but produce distress flags measured by the clinical team, and for two quarters each used a different 72-hour window, so one test had two readings. The repair is to give a guardrail's definition to whoever bears the harm.

Two-sided markets break the unit of consent: a supply-side incentive changes what the demand side sees, so the party who agreed is not the party exposed. Regulated contexts invert the default, from may we test this to may we ship anything untested. Hardware adds irreversibility: a firmware ramp cannot be recalled from a device gone offline.

AI-native products are Brihat's case, and are new in two ways. The treatment is a distribution rather than a rule, so harm sits in a tail no average reveals: v4 is acceptable on 78.0 per cent of drafts against 71.5, and worse on the 0.75-point increment citing policy wrongly. The exposed population is third-party. At full exposure 9,400 seats at 34 drafts a day is 319,600 drafts, and 0.75 per cent of that is 2,397 extra wrong citations daily. Agents send 62 per cent of all drafts unedited; applying that rate to erroneous drafts puts 1,486 before a complainant daily, which assumes agents catch a wrong citation no better than anything else, so the true figure is lower. Those two figures use the offline 0.75-point gap; the canary's measured 0.61 gives 1,950 and 1,209. Mature firms run the canary on accounts that asked for the model and defer the notice question.

6. Eight things experts see that competent practitioners miss

The tier belongs to the subject, not the surface. The tell is a tiering table whose rows name features rather than populations and mechanisms. The obvious reading is that risk lives in the thing changed; it lives in who is exposed and how slowly damage shows. Balaka's streak test touches a notification: Tier 0 by surface, Tier 2 by subject.

A ramp buys information only where a stage is powered. Stage 1 exposes 1,830 per arm, where the guardrail standard error is 0.451 points and the MDE 1.26 — two and a half times the 0.50 tolerance. Stages 1 and 2 together, 11,590 per arm, reach 0.50 exactly, and their 72-hour windows close on day 10, two days after stage 3 begins. The tell is a ramp whose gates are dates rather than sample sizes.

Power the guardrail, not the win. The tell is a sample-size memo quoting one MDE. Balaka's two differ by a factor of two and a half, 0.25 points against 0.61, and only the guardrail's binds. Experts read it first and derive the duration from it.

A percentage is not a harm statement until it is multiplied out. “We only exposed one per cent” has no units. One per cent of Balaka's inflow for three days is 1,830 people; one per cent of Brihat's drafts is 3,196 a day. The tell is a share quoted with no count.

Equipoise is a precondition, not a nicety. If you already know which arm is better for the user, you are not testing, you are rationing. The tell is a hypothesis written as a prediction with no stated uncertainty on the guardrail.

Consent is a gradient and terms of service are its weakest rung. Between a clause nobody read and a signed per-test authorisation sit product notice, segment opt-in and account-level agreement. The tell is an ethics section citing a clause number; Rajchoudhury's pilot accounts consented at account level, strong for the agent and silent for the complainant.

Asking for consent is not free, and the cost is not only sample bias. The documented “A/B effect” is that people object to an experiment comparing two arms they each find unobjectionable, so asking can suppress a welcome change. The tell is a plan treating the ask as costless.

Disclosure has three audiences and most programmes serve only the last: the exposed user, the regulator, the reader of an eventual paper. The tell is a policy that exists only for publications; Balaka tells exposed users nothing and its regulator everything.

7. Across product types and company stages

The tiering logic does not change across product type, and saying it does is the commonest overclaim here. What changes is who the exposed person is and whether they can be asked. In consumer products that person is the user and samples are large enough for guardrails to have power, so governance is thresholds and stopping rules. In B2B and enterprise the exposed person is an employee of the customer who cannot decline, the sample is accounts rather than people, and governance moves to contract: Brihat's pilot is 4.6 per cent of accounts and 10.0 per cent of seats, and the agreement speaks in accounts, so the smaller figure governs. AI products add a tail rather than a mean, and the best programmes govern the held-out set as carefully as the ramp.

Stage changes the machinery, not the question. A seed-stage firm cannot power a guardrail, so its governance is a written list of what it will not test, and a veto. A growth-stage firm acquires the ability to measure harm later than the ability to cause it; that gap is where the failure below happened. A late-stage firm has the measurement and loses the memory.

8. Three worked examples

One: powering the guardrail. The redesigned test exposes 75,030 per arm over twenty days and resolves a 0.20-point rise in a 1.90 per cent distress-flag rate. Under the fourteen-day design a 0.20-point rise is 2.21 of that design's 0.0903-point standard errors, or 1.96 plus 0.25, so it would have been caught about sixty per cent of the time rather than eighty.

Two: the canary. Brihat ran v4 from 2 to 10 February across 11 accounts holding 940 seats, 10.0 per cent of the 9,400, split 470 on v4 and 470 held back — so 470 of 9,400 seats, or 5.0 per cent, carried the new model. At 34 drafts a seat a day over nine days each arm produced 143,820 drafts. The v4 arm returned 2,762 wrong citations, a rate of 1.92 per cent, against the control's 1,884, or 1.31 per cent. The 0.61-point gap has a standard error of 0.047 points treating drafts as independent, so thirteen standard errors; seats were the randomised unit, so the honest figure is smaller. It realises 81 per cent of the 0.75-point gap predicted offline, where 1.25 against 2.00 per cent on 2,400 tickets gave a standard error of 0.365 and 2.06 of them, a p of about 0.04. Because both models scored the same tickets, a paired test would be tighter still.

Three: the failure. On 5 May 2025 Balaka tested moving the subscription prompt from day 7 to day 2. It touched pricing display: Tier 1, approved in two days. Its guardrail was the 72-hour uninstall rate: 4.1 per cent treatment against 4.0 per cent control over 128,000 new users an arm, a difference of 1.29 standard errors, correctly not called a finding. It shipped to all new users on 2 June. Over the next eleven weeks the share completing a first guided session fell from 41.0 to 33.5 per cent: 7.5 points, 18.3 per cent relative, and on weekly cohorts of about 85,000 a standard error of the difference of 0.24 points, so about thirty of them.

Balaka rolled back on 11 September, completion then standing at 33.9 per cent. By 5 December it had recovered to 39.2, still 1.8 points short, a residual attributed to a cohort that never formed a habit. The repair was the mandatory latency-class field, and a rule that Tier 1 may not be used where the declared mechanism is slower than the guardrail window.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Tiering by surface. Sign: no submission has ever been promoted at triage. Diagnostic: when was a Tier 0 last escalated? Cost late: the rollback of the May 2025 test.

Guardrails shorter than the mechanism. Sign: every guardrail has the same window. Diagnostic: what is the slowest way this could hurt someone? Cost late: harm ships at full exposure while the dashboard stays green.

The council that has never refused. Sign: a complete log and a hundred per cent approval rate. Diagnostic: show me the last refusal. Cost late: the first refusal arrives only after a regulator asks.

Consent laundering. Sign: the legal memo and the ethics memo are one document. Diagnostic: which rung are we on, and who is exposed but not on it? Cost late: a position that collapses on the first third party.

Exposure without denominators. Sign: risk discussed only in percentages. Diagnostic: how many named people, over how many days? Cost late: a one-per-cent exposure putting 3,196 drafts a day before strangers.

Disclosure deferred to publication. Sign: the only written rule is for papers. Diagnostic: what would we tell an exposed user who asked next week? Cost late: the answer gets drafted under deadline.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Must a review board include outsiders? For: the exposed population has an interest no employee can represent, and externals are the only structural check on a body that shares a bonus plan. Against: outsiders cannot tell a Tier 2 from a Tier 0, and their latency pushes borderline tests into self-certification, delaying the fixes that protect users. It fails if escalation and refusal rates hold steady after outsiders join; nobody has published that.

Is per-test consent coherent at all? For asking: nothing else distinguishes a subject from a resource, and the A/B effect describes preferences, not a licence to override them. Against: that same finding shows people reject a comparison while accepting both arms, so a request is not neutral: it suppresses welcome changes and skews the sample toward the already-engaged. It resolves only with a consent mechanism whose take-up leaves the estimate usable.

Is the ethical object the design or the treatment? The consumer-protection reading is that a manipulative message is wrong at any exposure, so C1 does all the work. The counterfactual reading is that this proves too much, condemning the test while licensing the launch that exposes everyone. The first fails if harm is linear in exposure, making Exhibit 2's arithmetic an ethical instrument rather than a cost model. Whether it is linear is unknown, and both camps cite the same missing evidence.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this reads the guardrail before the hypothesis and asks for the latency class before the expected lift. They state the denominator and window with any rate, They can name the last test their organisation refused, and treat a hundred per cent approval rate as a defect report. Most tellingly, they are the person who says review latency is itself a harm borne by users, and then measures it.

12. Two decisions, and three questions

Ruidas approved the redesigned test on 9 February: twenty days, the ramp as filed, the 2,600 crisis-routing users excluded, and a stopping rule at a 0.50-point rise in distress flags. Her reasoning: the alternative was not safety but the same notification on one manager's judgement. Rajchoudhury declined the comparison he had proposed. He will ship v4 only to accounts whose agents see a citation-verification prompt. Drafts it flags are expected to go out at 18 per cent, against the 62 at which drafts now go out unedited; if every wrong citation were flagged, that would take the daily figure at full exposure, on the offline gap, from 1,486 reaching a complainant to at most 431. He notified the other 229 accounts before the pilot numbers were final.

  1. Balaka's council changed, withdrew or refused 13 of its 17 Tier 2 submissions. What further figure would tell you whether that is a gate working or a threshold set at the wrong tier?
  2. The wrong-citation gap is 2.06 standard errors offline and thirteen online. What would each have to show for notice to be unnecessary?
  3. C1 and C4 are met for the streak-loss notification and C3 is open. On what evidence would you close C3, and who at Balaka could produce it?

13. Going deeper

  • Experimentation culture, what governance constrains; without it a council reviews nothing.
  • Why dark patterns emerge without malice, the mechanism C1 catches and why it needs a second reader.
  • Writing an experiment hypothesis, where the latency class and guardrail tolerance bind.
  • A/B testing fundamentals, the machinery assumed throughout; unlocks section 5's consent-unit problems.
  • Significance, power, sample size, peeking, the arithmetic behind the 0.20-point MDE and why stopping rules need sequential methods.
  • When you can't A/B test, Brihat's 240-account problem, and what replaces a guardrail without power.
  • Qual + quant feedback loop, the instrument that sees a slow mechanism early.
  • Feature flags and flighting, the control plane a ramp and a rollback both need.
exp40v2-exp.long.term.holdouts:
Long-term holdouts

A randomised group kept untreated for months, so a release programme can be asked the question its own experiments cannot: what did all our wins add up to?

Section oneTwo decisions, seven weeks apart

On Tuesday 14 April 2026 Nabamita Yatinandi took one slide into Ghungroo's quarterly product review. Ghungroo, an audio subscription app with 28.4 million monthly logged-in actives, had shipped 31 tested winners in the 182 days from 1 October 2025 to 31 March 2026. Their reported lifts added to 15.8 per cent on weekly listening hours per active user. Behind it sat a randomised group of 426,000 users, 1.5 per cent of the base, held out of the programme. In March the treated arm averaged 4.56 listening hours a week. The holdout averaged 4.41.

Seven weeks earlier, on Monday 23 February 2026, Nayanmoni Yugborgohain faced the mirror image. Ghatana Systems sells warehouse-execution software to 1,480 paying accounts carrying ₹214 crore of annual recurring revenue, ₹14.46 lakh an account on average. Over the 275 days from 1 April to 31 December 2025 it shipped 19 changes that compounded, on paper, to 7.0 per cent on lines picked per user-shift. Nandalal Yuvamajumdar, who runs customer success, had just told her that withholding them from 74 named accounts was a contract decision, not a measurement one. She had no holdout, and the best one she could build would be too coarse to measure the claim's size.

The two decisions are the same at different scales. Both hold a stack of individually significant wins and no credible estimate of what it is worth together; both suspect, correctly, that it is worth less than its parts; both must decide what they will pay to find out. The argument of this page is arithmetic: a holdout is cheap where n is large and nearly useless where n is small, and the reason is variance, not money.

Section twoThe idea, and the four positions on it

A long-term holdout is a randomised group kept off some or all of a product's shipped changes for months, so a release programme's cumulative effect can be read against a counterfactual allowed to drift. Three properties do the work: assignment is random, withholding persists across many releases, and the comparison uses the originally randomised set, not whoever survives. Remove any one and it is something else: a non-random group is a matched study, one change withheld an ordinary A/B test, survivors-only a selection effect in a lab coat.

The design predates software. Catalogue houses kept a universal control group — a random sample permanently suppressed from every campaign — because the incremental revenue campaigns claimed, summed, exceeded the business they could see. The question it was invented for is not "does this change work" but "what did they all add up to". Online it was formalised in the 2010s alongside a discovery: short tests are biased in one direction, as users learn and novelty decays. Hohnhold, O'Brien and Tang's 2015 account of long-term ad effects at Google and the surrogate-index estimator of Athey, Chetty, Imbens and Wager are the canonical responses.

Four positions divide practitioners, irreconcilably. Auditors sign "the sum of experiment-reported lifts is biased" and refuse "the holdout tells you which change to undo". Decay theorists sign "measure the short-to-long ratio once, turn it into a correction factor, then stop" and refuse "keep a standing arm indefinitely". Surrogate modellers sign "a validated index of short-run proxies beats a holdout on cost per decision" and refuse "an index detects a harm channel it was never trained on". Abstainers sign "withholding value is a real tax and the estimate is not identified under interference" and refuse "cumulative effect need not be measured".

Section threeMechanics in depth, worked through

First, experts admit what novices never do: "untreated" is a managed fiction. Ghungroo's holdout received three mandatory changes — payment rails, a security patch, a consent notice — under written exemption, each logged with an approver; all 31 tested winners were withheld. Second, the key matters more than the fraction: Ghungroo randomises on hashed account identity, not device, so phone-plus-tablet is one unit. Third, the estimate is intention-to-treat on the set as randomised on 1 October 2025, churned users at zero.

Percentage lifts compound rather than add, and compounding runs against the optimist. Ghungroo's eight largest winners compound to 12.07 per cent; with the remaining 23 at a pooled 4.3 per cent the claim is 16.89, not 15.8. The holdout measured 3.40 per cent. The realisation ratio is 3.4 points of the 16.9 points claimed, or 20.1 per cent.

Days live for the named eight sum to 914, so (914 + 23 × 91) ÷ 31 = 97.0. The three exempt mandatory changes are not tested winners and appear in no row.

That ratio is worth arguing about, and is not evidence of dishonesty. Three separable mechanisms contribute: winner's curse, since a change ships only when its estimate clears a bar; decay, as novelty fades; interaction, since two changes competing for one screen cannot both deliver. Exposure is not among them: the 45-day minimum in Exhibit 1 means all 31 winners were live through March, so the March gap is an end-state gap. Exposure would bite only on a full-period average — the Figure 1 gaps mean 0.092 hours, or 2.1 per cent.

Finally, the arithmetic that governs everything. For two arms with total N and holdout fraction p, the variance of the difference goes as 1/(p(1−p)N), inflated against a balanced split by 1/(4p(1−p)) — at p = 0.015, 16.9 times, leaving an effective sample of 4p(1−p)N, or 5.9 per cent of the base. With a standard deviation of 3.1 hours on the March per-user mean, the gap's standard error is 3.1 × √(1/426,000 + 1/27,974,000) = 0.00479 hours, so the 0.15-hour gap is 31 standard errors. The detectable effect at 95 per cent confidence and 80 per cent power is 2.80 × 0.00479 = 0.0134 hours, 0.30 per cent of 4.41.

Section fourWhen it applies, and when it misleads

First: the detectable effect must be small relative to the claim audited. Ghungroo passes with room to spare, 0.30 per cent against a 16.9 per cent claim. Yugborgohain does not: her 74-account holdout resolves to 4.66 per cent against a 7.0 per cent claim, so a true effect within 4.66 points of 7.0 — roughly 2 to 12 per cent — would give a result she could not distinguish from her own.

Second: withholding must be mechanically enforceable at the unit of randomisation. Ghungroo passes, because a server-side flag on an account key blocks 31 changes with no human in the loop. Ghatana fails differently: its changes are sold, invoiced and announced, and a customer-success manager who tells a withheld account the truth has done her job, not broken a rule.

Third: months of accumulation must be the right window for the outcome. Both pass: listening hours and picked lines both carry habit formation a 14-day test cannot see.

Where the idea actively misleads is narrower than critics claim but real. It misleads when the arm degrades for reasons no customer would have met — unpatched integrations, a frozen design language — so the gap carries a rot term attributable to neglect. It misleads when effects travel between units. And most reliably of all when a null is read as "the programme did nothing".

Section fiveHard edge cases, and what mature companies actually do

In multi-product firms the holdout fractures: an account held out of one app but treated in another is a unit in two states, and a firm-wide holdout multiplies foregone value while underpowering each product. In two-sided businesses individual randomisation is simply wrong, since a withheld seller's buyers are treated; valid designs cluster by city, category or time, collapsing effective sample size through the arithmetic that defeats Ghatana. In regulated products withholding may be unlawful rather than awkward — a consent flow cannot be held back — which is why Ghungroo's exempt register exists and its length is a quality metric.

Hardware plus software puts the holdout on the wrong side of a bill of materials: firmware can be withheld, a sensor cannot, so the arm speaks to software on identical hardware and not to the product. AI-native products are sharper still, because the model learns from treated behaviour: a held-out cohort does not merely miss a feature, it sits downstream of a retrieval index and reward model shaped by everyone else, so "the system as it was" ceases to exist by month two. Mature teams hold out the interface and concede the model.

At the seams, practice diverges from description. Firms say they run a standing holdout; what they run is a time-boxed arm with a pre-registered end date, a named owner who can veto exemptions, and a published detectable effect, re-randomised between cycles because an arm randomised three years ago has an indefensible attrition profile.

Section sixEight things that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

Each has a tell by which an expert recognises it in the wild, and in each the obvious reading is wrong.

One — compounding, not addition

The tell is a deck that adds lift percentages; adding looks conservative; it is not. Compounding Ghungroo's ledger gives 16.89 per cent against the additive 15.8, so a ratio computed off the slide flatters by construction.

Two — powered for the mean, not the margin

The tell is that no subgroup detectable effect has been printed. Ghungroo's podcast-only segment is 6.1 per cent of the base, so 25,986 of the 426,000 holdout users. With a segment standard deviation of 2.6 hours the standard error is 0.0163 hours (treated segment 1,706,414) and the detectable effect 1.51 per cent on a 3.02-hour baseline — five times coarser than the global 0.30 per cent, exactly where harm surfaces first.

Three — the exemption register

The tell is an expert who asks for the register before the result. Three exemptions in 34 changes looks like noise. But an exemption with no named approver is indistinguishable from a leak, and an unreviewed register turns the holdout into a lower bound of unknown size.

Four — removal is not the inverse of never-having

The tell is a snapback quoted as though symmetric with a forward holdout. Removal triggers loss aversion and retraining costs that never existed for someone who never had it, so the two estimate different quantities. Ghatana's single-arm snapback ran 1.7 standard errors from its forward claim, which sizes the asymmetry not at all.

Five — the cost that binds

The tell is a practitioner who prices engineer-weeks rather than lost revenue. Ghungroo's holdout cost ₹17.89 lakh over six months — blended revenue per active ran ₹23.30 a month in the holdout against ₹24.00 treated — or 4.4 basis points of the ₹408.78 crore the two arms booked between them. What nearly killed the 2024 attempt was 14 engineer-weeks a month on a withheld path.

Six — a null is a statement about your instrument

The tell is a summary reporting no cumulative effect without an interval. That reads as caution; it is the opposite. A null at Ghungroo's precision excludes effects above 0.30 per cent. The same null at Ghatana's excludes only effects above about 3.3 per cent — enough to refute 7.0, not to size it.

Seven — the denominator is the set as randomised

The tell is an expert asking when the denominator was frozen. Holdout users churn faster, receiving a worse product; computing the gap on survivors compares the treated population with the holdout's hardiest residue, and the bias can flip the sign.

Eight — interference decides the unit, and the unit decides the budget

The tell is "clustered or individual?" asked before "how big?". Ghatana's accounts cluster 68 users at an intraclass correlation of 0.21, a design effect of 1 + 67 × 0.21 = 15.07, so its 5,032 held-out users are worth 334 independent observations against the treated arm's 6,344. On a 182-line baseline with a standard deviation of 54 lines that is a detectable effect of 4.66 per cent. Cluster structure, not sample size, sets what a holdout can see.

Section sevenHow this differs by product type and company stage

Only one thing varies much across product types, and the rest follows: how many independent units you can randomise.

From that axis the type differences follow. Consumer products at scale can run a standing holdout at trivial cost and should. B2B and enterprise cannot, and the substitutes — staggered rollout, new-cohort randomisation, extended single-experiment controls — answer narrower questions honestly rather than the broad one dishonestly. Platforms and marketplaces must cluster, costing an order of magnitude of precision and buying validity. Hardware can randomise firmware but not silicon. AI products face a counterfactual that decays as the model absorbs treated behaviour, arguing for short, frequently re-randomised arms.

Stage changes the answer less than expected, and saying so beats inventing a difference. A seed-stage company has no business running a holdout: effects are large, the sample small, the binding constraint direction rather than magnitude. The design earns its cost where the firm starts quoting cumulative gains to people who can act on them — a board, sometimes a regulator. There it becomes an audit function, which is why it so often ends up owned by finance.

Section eightThree worked examples, including one that failed

Exhibit 3 — Three holdout attempts. The periods differ, so the measured gaps are not comparable.
AttemptDesignClaimMeasuredVerdict
Ghungroo 20240.2% of 24.1m, device key, 12 months, 26 winners+9.1% additive+2.4%Abandoned: 18.6% leakage, 3 winners unwithholdable
Ghungroo 2025–261.5% of 28.4m, account key, 182 days, 31 winners+16.89% compounded+3.40%Realisation ratio 20.1%, accepted
Ghatana snapback74 accounts, 28 days, single arm, no control+7.0% compounded (1.9, 1.2, 0.9, 0.8, 0.6; 1.4 pooled)−9.8%1.7 SE from the claim; suggestive only

The 2024 attempt is the instructive failure. On paper it was powered: 48,200 held-out users against 24,051,800 treated gave a standard error of 0.0141 hours and a detectable effect of 0.94 per cent on a 4.22-hour baseline, well inside a 9.1 per cent claim. It failed for three reasons no power calculation sees. Randomisation was keyed on device, so 8,965 of the 48,200 holdout users, 18.6 per cent, appeared on a treated key; read as pure attenuation, a true 3.0 per cent gap reads as 2.44, close to what they saw. Three of the 26 winners could not be withheld. And the claim was additive, so the denominator was wrong too.

The recovery matters more than the post-mortem. Nitai Yashchakrabarti, who runs Ghungroo's experimentation platform, did four things, none statistical. He moved randomisation to the account key and instrumented leakage weekly, which is why the 0.4 per cent figure is known. He made the exempt register a document with approvers. He raised the fraction from 0.2 to 1.5 per cent, buying the segment analysis. And he gave the arm a pre-registered end date, converting a permanent engineering tax into a six-month project. Note the price: by the April 2026 review the 2024 logs were 469 days old against a 400-day retention, so the old estimate cannot be recomputed.

Ghatana's snapback is the third case and the most misread. From 12 January to 8 February 2026 it removed nine months of changes from the same 74 accounts Yuvamajumdar later refused to randomise, and their lines per user-shift fell 9.8 per cent against their own December baseline. There was no control arm, so the gap has no standard error of its own. The naive conclusion is that the programme was under-claimed. But benchmarked against the randomised design's 1.66 points, 9.8 sits 1.7 standard errors from the claimed 7.0, and that interval includes it. Yugborgohain read it only as a reason to doubt that 7.0 was conservative.

Section nineFailure modes, and the questions that catch them

Six failures account for most dead holdouts. None shows up in the final estimate: each produces a reportable-looking number, so the diagnostic must be asked on a schedule.

Exhibit 4 — Failure modes, early warning signs and diagnostics.
FailureEarly warningDiagnostic questionCost of catching it late
Leakage across keysLeakage rises above 1% in month twoWhat share of holdout units touched a treated surface last week?Estimate attenuated; rerun the window
Silent exemptionsRegister grows with no named approverName every change that reached the holdout, and its approverGap becomes an unknown lower bound
Powered for the mean onlyNo subgroup interval ever printedWhat is the detectable effect where harm appears first?A harm channel hides in noise for two quarters
Arm becomes the roadmap's judgeTeams ask it to arbitrate single featuresWhich decision changes if this number moves?A six-month lag on every ship decision
Code-path rotEngineer-weeks on the withheld path rise monthlyWhat does another month of this arm cost?Arm killed mid-flight, yielding nothing
SurvivorshipHoldout active base shrinks faster than treatedIs the denominator the randomised set or the survivors?The gap can flip sign

Two are organisational, not technical. An arm asked to arbitrate individual features will always lose, since its latency is months and a ship decision days: the right answer to "what does the holdout say about my feature" is nothing. Code-path rot is the only failure here that worsens the better the programme goes.

Section tenWhere experts genuinely disagree

Standing versus time-boxed. The strongest case for a permanent arm is that without one every quarter's claimed lift is unfalsifiable, and the price is basis points — 4.4 at Ghungroo. It rests on realisation ratios clustering below one wherever anyone has measured. It is wrong if the decay multiplier is stable: then one measurement yields a correction factor and the standing arm is waste.

Holdout versus surrogate index. The strongest case against holdouts is that a validated index of short-run proxies gives a long-run read in two weeks, and that holdouts are too coarse at segment level — 1.51 per cent against 0.30 — to catch what they are sold as catching. It rests on surrogate estimators recovering known long-run effects out of sample. It is wrong if the programme changes the proxy-to-outcome mapping, which is what a team optimising the proxy does.

Whether the arm measures the product or its neglect. The stale-arm objection holds that after six months the holdout is not the old product but an unmaintained one, so the gap carries a rot term. It rests on bug rates and engineer-weeks in the withheld path, both measurable. It is wrong where the register is disciplined and rot instrumented — a claim about engineering practice, not statistics.

Whether account-level holdouts are permissible at all. The strongest version is contractual, not statistical: an account paying ₹14.46 lakh a year that discovers it was invoiced for withheld features has a claim, and no measurement argument answers it. It is wrong only where contracts permit randomised withholding from the first day, which almost none do.

Section elevenWhat mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied holdouts argues about the fraction. Someone who has internalised them argues about the key, the register and the end date, and states the detectable effect before the arm exists. They give the realisation ratio's denominator as a compounded figure unasked. They refuse to let the arm adjudicate a single feature, or outlive its date. Most tellingly, they can say which decision the number will change — and if none, they do not build it.

Section twelveThe decisions, and three questions

Yatinandi kept the holdout and narrowed it: 1.5 per cent re-authorised for six more months with a hard end date, plus a dedicated eight-week test on podcast-only users sized to resolve 0.6 per cent. With a 2.6-hour segment standard deviation and a 3.02-hour baseline that needs 180,100 of the 1,732,400 podcast-only users, 10.4 per cent of the segment. Her reasoning: the global arm had done its job and could not do the next one. Yugborgohain declined the randomised account holdout and randomises new accounts at onboarding instead — 156 per arm from the 312 that sign in a typical nine months, so the read is nine months out, at a detectable effect of 4.43 per cent: about five per cent tighter than the design she rejected, still too coarse to size 7.0, and the only design the contract permits. She committed never to publish a cumulative installed-base figure. Yashchakrabarti thinks Yatinandi is wrong to time-box anything.

  1. Ghungroo's holdout cost 4.4 basis points and returned a realisation ratio of 20.1 per cent. What would that ratio have to be for Ghungroo to be right to shut the arm down?
  2. Yugborgohain's new-account design is tighter than the one she rejected but estimates a different quantity. Which of Ghatana's decisions depend on the quantity she gave up measuring?
  3. The 2024 and 2025–26 holdouts cover different programmes and the 2024 logs are past retention. What would Ghungroo have had to build in 2024 to make them comparable now?

Section thirteenGoing deeper

A/B testing fundamentals
A holdout is an A/B test held open; every identification assumption carries over.
Proxies for long-term value
The holdout validates a proxy, and alone can invalidate one.
Writing an experiment hypothesis
Without a pre-registered decision rule a holdout becomes a standing argument.
Significance, power, sample size, peeking
Unlocks the detectable-effect arithmetic that decides whether a holdout is worth it.
When you can't A/B test
Supplies the substitutes B2B needs: staggered rollout, synthetic control, switchback.
Experimentation culture
Explains why a standing arm changes how teams claim.
Qual + quant feedback loop
Harm below a segment's detectable effect surfaces in interviews first.
Feature flags and flighting
The enforcement layer: without server-side flags on the randomisation unit, nothing holds.
exp20v2-exp.long.term.holdouts:
Long-term holdouts: what did all our wins add up to?

1. The slide Madhabi Vasu asked for

On Monday 12 January 2026, Moushumi Viswas, head of growth analytics at Eloka, a grocery delivery app serving Kolkata and Guwahati, opened the slide her chief financial officer, Madhabi Vasu, had requested in November. It listed the eleven experiments Eloka shipped during 2025. Each had won its A/B test (a randomised comparison of two versions of the product), and each readout had reported a gain in orders per shopper over fourteen days. The gains summed to 22.0 percentage points; compounded, they implied 24.3 per cent.

Vasu's question was plain. The 2026 plan assumed the team would repeat 2025, and she wanted to know what 2025 had delivered. Revenue per shopper had risen, but prices, festivals and a new Guwahati warehouse had moved too, and none of those could be separated from the growth team's work by looking at the revenue line. Viswas had one instrument that could answer. In January 2025 she had set aside 36,000 of 1.2 million shoppers, 3 per cent, and withheld every launch from them. If that group now trailed the rest by about a fifth, the team was a growth engine. If it trailed by 5 per cent, the plan rested on a number four times too large, and a bonus scheme paid on test lifts had rewarded gains that never survived. She had three days to find out which.

2. The idea

A long-term holdout is a random slice of users, usually one to five per cent, deliberately kept on an older experience while everyone else receives each new launch, and compared with the rest for months. It is an A/B test that is never closed. The ordinary test asks whether this change beats that one over two weeks; the holdout asks what the whole programme of changes has done to people who never received it.

The practice answers a specific weakness. A short test measures a single change in isolation, over the days when novelty is strongest, and it cannot see harm that arrives slowly, such as a quieter drift in complaints or repeat purchases. Teams at large web companies, including Microsoft, Google and Booking.com, described standing holdouts in published accounts of experimentation from roughly 2010 onward, because short-test wins rarely summed to the same total. The term borrows from forecasting, where a holdout sample is data kept aside to check a model.

Viswas could say it in one sentence: our launches are only real if the people who never received them are measurably behind.

3. How it works

The first step is to randomise once. Eloka hashed each shopper identifier with a fixed secret value, and the lowest 3 per cent of hash values became the holdout. Because the assignment is a function of the identifier, the same shopper lands in the same group every day, on every device.

The second step, which teams leave implicit, is to write down what "withheld" means. Eloka decided that holdout shoppers would receive no feature, ranking change, promotion mechanic or copy change, but would receive security patches and legal notices. Someone then had to maintain the old app alongside the new one, which is the real engineering cost and the reason most holdouts quietly die. Two decisions are easy to miss: the size (Eloka chose 3 per cent so that a gain of about 1.2 per cent could be seen, as section 4 shows) and the unit, here the shopper, because a household that orders from two phones would otherwise straddle both groups.

Third, holdout shoppers are excluded from all new experiments, otherwise the group drifts away from the January 2025 experience. Fourth, the metrics are fixed in advance: a long-horizon outcome (orders in a ninety-day window) plus guardrails (complaints, cancellations). Fifth, everyone assigned is counted, whether or not they opened the app. Sixth, a reading calendar and an end date are agreed, so nobody peeks on a whim. Finally, at the review, the group difference is converted into money and compared with what the team claimed, which is the step that makes a holdout a management instrument and not only a statistical one.

4. A worked example

Over 1 October to 29 December, holdout shoppers placed 9.80 orders on average; exposed shoppers placed 10.34. The difference is 0.54 orders, a lift of 0.54 / 9.80 = 5.5 per cent. With a standard deviation of 8.0 orders per shopper, the standard error of the difference is 8.0 x sqrt(1/36,000 + 1/1,164,000) = 0.043. The 95 per cent interval is 0.54 plus or minus 1.96 x 0.043, or 0.456 to 0.624 orders, which is 4.7 to 6.4 per cent. The summed claims, 22.0 points, were four times that; the measured gain was a quarter of the sum.

Money follows. Eloka earns about ₹38 contribution per order, so 0.54 orders is ₹20.52 per shopper per quarter. But complaints per order were 3.5 per hundred in the holdout and 4.1 in the exposed group: 0.343 and 0.424 complaints per shopper (9.80 x 0.035 and 10.34 x 0.041), a difference of 0.081. At ₹60 a complaint that is ₹4.86, leaving ₹15.66 net. Across 1,164,000 exposed shoppers the programme earns about ₹1.82 crore a quarter; the 36,000 holdout shoppers forgo ₹5.64 lakh, 3.1 per cent of the gain.

Now change one input: shrink the holdout to 1 per cent.

Quantity3% holdout1% holdout

Standard error (orders)0.0430.073

The cheaper holdout still answers Vasu's question, since 4.0 per cent is far from 22. It would struggle with finer questions, which matters in the next section. Note also that the money rows scale linearly with the holdout: each shopper withheld costs ₹15.66 a quarter, so the choice of size is a choice about how much certainty a company will pay for.

5. Nuances

It measures the programme, not any launch

A holdout reports the cumulative effect of everything withheld. It cannot say that the wallet cashback earned 3.4 points and the substitution preferences 0.9, because those effects are mixed in one group difference. Anyone who needs a per-feature figure must run a dedicated experiment, and should expect it to disagree with the original readout.

Why the claims overstate

Lifts do not add. Tests overlap on the same shoppers, a reorder button and a cart reminder both capture the same repeat order, and two-week tests catch novelty. Both claims are generous; the sum merely errs less, because compounding builds on gains that were never additive.

Count everyone assigned

Analyse by assignment, not by who saw a feature. Dropping inactive holdout shoppers selects the survivors of the old app and flatters it, which shrinks the measured gap. The same logic applies to the exposed group: someone who never opened a new screen is still counted as treated, because the launch may have changed what the home page sent them.

Fade is information

If lifts decay, the holdout shows the decay that fourteen-day tests cannot. It also validates proxies. Eloka's fourteen-day order count promised 22.0 points and the ninety-day outcome delivered 5.5, so the proxy overstated the long-term effect roughly fourfold, a ratio that blends overlap and fade; it is a rough correction for future tests only if the launch mix stays similar.

What it cannot tell you

It does not reveal what a different roadmap would have produced, nor effects on people outside the product, such as couriers. It is a comparison against the old app, not against the best alternative. Nor can it prove that a null result means no harm: a gap inside the noise is silence, not reassurance.

What it is confused with

A before-and-after comparison is not a holdout, since seasons move both groups. A single-test control group lasts weeks. A holdout is randomised, concurrent and long. A reverse experiment, which removes one shipped feature from a sample, is a different and useful tool for per-feature questions.

Questions before relying on it

Is the old experience still working, or has it rotted as servers and partners changed? Did holdout shoppers leak through logged-out use or new accounts? Is the harm acceptable, given they receive a deliberately worse product?

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace

Consumer products suit holdouts best, with large populations and quick purchase cycles; Eloka's 36,000 shoppers is ample. In B2B the unit is the account, and three per cent of 200 accounts is six, too few for any interval. Teams there use larger shares, matched pairs or a rotating holdout, and read the result as a judgement, not a significance test. Contract renewals, which arrive annually, are the outcome that matters, so the horizon lengthens to twelve or eighteen months.

In a marketplace, holdout buyers share sellers and couriers with everyone else, so their outcomes are partly shaped by exposed users' behaviour, and the gap can mis-state the true effect, in either direction. Geographic holdouts reduce that interference, at the price of noisier comparisons. Early-stage companies should rarely run one: traffic is thin and the old app is a burden. Large companies run them as standing infrastructure, usually with several teams sharing one holdout so that the cost is paid once, and a platform group owning its integrity. The difference is less about statistics than about who has the patience and headcount to keep an old product alive.

7. Common mistakes

Contamination. The symptom is a gap that shrinks without explanation. The belief behind it is that assignment is automatically permanent. The cheapest diagnostic is to log, monthly, how many holdout shoppers were served any new feature; the answer should be zero.

Assigning credit. The symptom is a slide ranking launches by their holdout contribution. The belief is that a total can be divided. The diagnostic is to ask which comparison produced each number; if the answer is "the same group difference", the ranking is invented. A well-run team publishes the programme figure and treats per-launch figures as provisional.

No decision rule. The symptom is a holdout nobody has read in eight months. The belief is that data collection is the point. Write, before launch, the gap that would change the plan, and the date on which the group is released. Otherwise a cost review cancels it unread.

8. What good looks like

Handled well, Viswas would have written the rule in January 2025: read on the second Monday of each quarter, report the interval beside the claimed lifts, and release the holdout after twelve months. Her slide would show claimed and measured gains together and the complaint guardrail, and would state the limits of attribution. Eloka's incentive scheme would pay on the holdout-confirmed gain. Vasu would see in one page how large the programme was, how sure the company could be, and what each point of confirmed growth cost to hold back. The portrait needs only a rule written before the result was known.

9. What Viswas decided

She told Vasu that 2025 delivered about 5.5 per cent more orders per shopper, worth ₹15.66 net per shopper a quarter, and that the 2026 plan should assume gains of a quarter of test sums. She proposed a fresh 2 per cent holdout and bonuses on confirmed gains. Vasu agreed, because the number was smaller but defensible, and because the plan now carried a check that would report again in April. Viswas also asked for the 2025 holdout to run three more months so that a second ninety-day window could confirm whether the 5.5 per cent was holding, growing or fading.

Learn next how proxies for long-term value are built, since the fourteen-day metric failed here; then A/B testing fundamentals, to see what a holdout inherits from the two-week test and what it cannot repair.

Two questions to sit with. If Eloka's holdout had shown 22 per cent, what would you have suspected first? And what would you do if the holdout's harm were small but your company's values forbade deliberately worsening anyone's product?
exp40v2-exp.sequential:
Can I look at the test every day without lying to myself?

Sequential testing and always-valid inference: what it buys, what it costs in power, where it is the wrong tool, and why two capable teams decided opposite things on the same mathematics.

1. Two decisions, three weeks apart

At 09:40 on Monday 14 September 2026, Debosmita Kayal opened the experiment console at Shiuli Retail Technologies. Shiuli runs 2.28 crore sessions a month and routes a 2 per cent slice into experiments, which supplies 7,500 sessions per arm per day. Test SH-412 had replaced a three-field address form with one autofilled block. On day eight, control was completing orders on 8.40 per cent of sessions and treatment on 8.73 per cent; the two-sided test put the gap at p = 0.0393 on the control-arm variance. Kayal, who runs growth, wanted to ship Tuesday.

Dyutiman Kamilya, who runs experimentation, refused, and the console agreed with him. Beside the p-value it printed an always-valid interval of −0.17 to +0.83 percentage points, which contains zero. His point was not that Kayal's number was wrong, but that the eighth look is not the first.

Three weeks later, on Monday 5 October, Devdeep Kotal sat through a design review at Shilabati Compliance Cloud, an enterprise workflow product with 1,240 paying accounts. Kotal wanted to test automated evidence-matching against the manual step, measured as hours of rework per account per week: baseline 6.40 hours, standard deviation 4.80, and a 0.60-hour effect worth shipping. His data scientist, Dibyajyoti Kuila, proposed a four-look group-sequential design so the firm could release in the December train. Kotal asked what Kamilya would answer differently: is there enough information for an early look to mean anything?

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

A fixed-horizon test promises one thing: collect n observations, compute one statistic, and the chance of a false rejection is 5 per cent. The promise is void the moment you evaluate that statistic repeatedly as data arrive, because you have many chances to cross one line. Armitage, McPherson and Rowe computed the inflation exactly in 1969.

Exhibit 1 — What peeking actually costs
Equally spaced looksRealised false-positive rateExact value
10.04900.050
20.08230.083
30.10660.107
50.14080.142
100.19250.193
200.24690.248

200,000 replications, seed 20261025; standardised partial sums of unit-variance increments; nominal two-sided 0.05 at each look; stop at the first crossing. Monte Carlo standard error ≤ 0.0010. Right column: Armitage, McPherson and Rowe (1969).

Always-valid inference is any procedure whose error guarantee holds uniformly over all sample sizes, so the stopping rule need not be declared in advance. It rests on a non-negative martingale Λn with expectation 1 under the null; Ville's inequality then gives P(supn Λn ≥ 1/α) ≤ α. Reject the first time it exceeds 1/α and you are safe however often you look, and whatever made you look.

Sequential analysis began in munitions inspection and matured in oncology. Abraham Wald built the sequential probability ratio test at Columbia's Statistical Research Group in 1943, to clear lots with fewer rounds fired. Clinical trials then forced the problem open, since an interim look showing harm is an obligation. Pocock (1977) and O'Brien and Fleming (1979) gave the two canonical boundary shapes; Lan and DeMets (1983) freed the timing of looks by recasting design as error spent against information accrued. Robbins had shown in 1970 how to build confidence sequences holding for all n. The A/B tradition arrived last, when Optimizely replaced its fixed-horizon engine with a mixture sequential test in 2015; time-uniform bounds and e-values have since generalised it.

Four positions coexist. The fixed-horizon school will sign that a pre-registered test at a declared n extracts the most decision per observation, and that peeking is a governance pathology; not that teams honour horizons. The group-sequential school will sign that the number and timing of looks is a design parameter to be costed, but not that you may add a look because yesterday's number looked promising, since its guarantee is conditional on the schedule. The always-valid school will sign that the stopping rule need not be specified, and that this costs a constant-factor widening of every interval; not that it is negligible. The Bayesian school will sign that a posterior is unaffected by the stopping rule, but not that a decision rule built on it inherits a frequentist guarantee.

3. Mechanics, worked through

Start with the clock. Sequential designs are indexed by information fraction t = Ik/Imax, not calendar time, information being the reciprocal of the estimate's variance. A group-sequential design fixes Imax, then allocates error across looks. The Lan–DeMets O'Brien–Fleming spending function α*(t) = 2{1 − Φ(z0.025/√t)} is miserly early and generous late. Exhibit 2 spends it over four looks.

The always-valid construction replaces the budget with a martingale. Mix the alternative over a normal prior of scale τ and the likelihood ratio is closed-form, with Vn = 2σ²/n the variance of the difference in arm means and θ̂n the observed difference:

Λn = √( Vn / (Vn+τ²) ) · exp{ θ̂n² τ² / ( 2 Vn(Vn+τ²) ) }
