The second line is the first inverted: the set of null values not rejected is an interval, and since the rejection rule is valid for all n, so is the interval. Take Shiuli's eighth look. The metric is binary, so σ² = 0.0840 × 0.9160 = 0.076944; at n = 60,000 per arm, Vn = 0.153888/60,000 = 2.5648 × 10−6 and the standard error is 0.16015 pp. With τ = 1.00 pp and α = 0.05 the exponent is (0.0033)²(10−4) / (2 × 2.5648×10−6 × 1.025648×10−4) = 2.070, so Λ = 0.15815 × e2.070 = 1.25 against a threshold of 20. The half-width is 0.5046 pp, giving −0.17 to +0.83 pp. At θ̂ = hn, Λ is exactly 20.0.

Three second-order effects separate practitioners. The choice of τ is a power decision disguised as a prior: set it to the effect you would act on, not the one you hope for. An estimate reported at a boundary is biased away from zero, since crossing selected it; the honest number comes from a post-launch holdout. And almost all realised savings come from futility boundaries, while almost all teams install only efficacy ones.

4. When it applies, and when it is actively misleading

Claim one: the horizon holds enough information that the sequential penalty still leaves usable power. At Shiuli it holds; at Shilabati it fails structurally. Kuila's fixed-sample requirement is 2(1.95996 + 1.28155)² × 4.80²/0.60² = 2 × 10.5074 × 64 = 1,345 accounts per arm, against 1,240 in total, randomised 620 and 620. More weeks do not help, because weeks within an account are correlated: with an intra-account correlation of 0.62 estimated from 26 pre-period weeks, m weeks on 620 accounts are worth 620m/(1 + 0.62(m − 1)) independent accounts — 929 at eight weeks, tending to 620/0.62 = 1,000. That is a ceiling, so the maximum power on the untrimmed metric at any horizon, by any unadjusted comparison, is Φ(0.60/√(2 × 23.04/1,000) − 1.95996) = Φ(0.835) = 79.8 per cent.

Claim two: stopping early has value. Shiuli ships continuously, so a day saved is a day of effect banked. Shilabati releases quarterly, so a design whose early stop cannot be acted on is pure cost. Claim three: the variance process is stable and estimable in advance. True for Shiuli's order rate; false, catastrophically, for its revenue per session, as section 8 shows. Claim four: the stopping rule will be honoured — not a statistical question, and the one that decides most cases.

The idea is actively misleading in three situations. Where the real inflation comes from many metrics, variants or post-hoc segments, an always-valid monitor controls the time axis and nothing else. Where sample size is the binding constraint, sequential methods only make a weak test weaker. And where the effect decays through novelty, the estimand changes with n, so a boundary crossed at one horizon is not evidence about another.

5. Hard edge cases and the organisational seams

In a multi-product estate the monitor is per metric, so a team watching 40 metrics continuously has controlled none jointly; mature firms designate one primary metric and treat the rest as monitoring. In two-sided marketplaces interference forces randomisation at city level, and twenty clusters cannot be rescued by any boundary. In regulated settings — payments overseen by the Reserve Bank of India, or trials under CDSCO and ICMR oversight — the pre-specified design with a named monitoring committee is the accepted filing object; an always-valid dashboard is not. In hardware-plus-software programmes information arrives in lots, so the information fraction is lumpy. In AI-native products observations are cheap, so anytime validity is nearly free; the hazard is reuse of one evaluation set, which sequential testing does not address.

The seam that bites is the console. Mature companies say they monitor continuously under an always-valid rule; more often they show a fixed-horizon p-value and a sequential verdict on the same card, so every launch argument is relitigated in whichever frame favours the arguer. The firms that fixed this removed the second number.

6. Nine things an expert sees that a competent practitioner does not

1. The clock is information, not time. A team scheduling looks weekly has scheduled them on traffic, which varies. The tell is a design document naming dates rather than sample sizes.

2. Under an always-valid boundary, looking more often costs no validity. The boundary does not depend on the schedule, so extra looks only add chances to cross it: in Exhibit 4 power rises from 0.8395 to 0.8613 and the median stopping point falls from 120,000 to 102,000 when looks go from 24 to 240. The realised null rate does rise, 0.0129 to 0.0272, but stays inside the 0.05 guarantee. The tell is a team batching looks weekly to be safe.

3. The guarantee is conditional on the variance model. Always-valid is not assumption-free but assumption-shifted: plug in a variance from an early window and the martingale property fails silently. The tell is a reported standard error tracking 1/√n exactly while the running sample deviation still climbs.

4. The stopped estimate is not the effect. Crossing a boundary selects for luck, so the magnitude at the stopping look overstates. The tell is a deck whose headline equals the number on the day the test stopped.

5. Unspent α is lost power. Ville's inequality is an inequality: Shiuli's monitor spends only 0.0272 of its 0.05 budget at 240 looks. An expert reads that gap as power left on the table; a novice reads it as safety.

6. It controls one axis. Time. Not metrics, variants, segments or randomisation faults. The tell is a team adopting always-valid inference after a bad launch without establishing that peeking caused it.

7. Pocock against O'Brien–Fleming is about where you want to be able to stop, not which is better. At five looks and 90 per cent power O'Brien–Fleming inflates maximum sample size by 2.6 per cent and will essentially never stop at the first look; Pocock inflates it by 20.6 per cent and will. Choose by claim two, not by elegance.

8. Futility is where the savings are. Most tests have no effect, so most of the expected sample-size reduction comes from stopping for nothing. The tell is a design with an efficacy boundary and no answer to what makes us ship nothing.

9. An always-valid significance badge never un-lights. The anytime-valid p-value is the running infimum, so it cannot increase. A badge flickering between significant and not is a fixed-horizon p-value wearing a sequential label.

7. How this differs by product type and company stage

The mathematics is identical everywhere; only the price of information differs. In consumer products observations are cheap, so the 55 to 70 per cent widening in Exhibit 3 is affordable and continuous monitoring is the right default. In B2B and enterprise the account count is fixed and the intra-account correlation, not the method, sets the ceiling; Shilabati's N/ρ is the general case. Platforms and marketplaces inherit the cluster problem and should work on the unit of randomisation. Hardware gets lumpy information and quarterly decisions, which favours few pre-planned looks. AI products can buy information, so they should buy it rather than economise on α.

By stage the honest statement is narrower than usually claimed. Seed-stage firms have no peeking problem but a power problem, which sequential methods worsen. Growth-stage firms with real traffic and weekly releases are where always-valid inference earns its keep. At scale the constraint moves from statistics to governance: who may see what, and when.

8. Three worked examples

One: Shiuli, SH-412. At the eighth look the fixed interval had already cleared 0.33 pp — Figure 2 puts that crossing at about 54,300 per arm — while the always-valid interval needs roughly 151,000, nearly three times the data for the same claim. Kamilya's argument was not that the effect was absent but that 91,000 more sessions per arm would settle it, with 24 days of horizon left.

Two: Shilabati. Kuila's four-look design was sound; the information was not there. Figure 3 shows why: 620 accounts per arm cannot be worth more than 1,000, and the O'Brien–Fleming design needs 1,345 × 1.022 = 1,375. Her recovery changed the measurement, not the method. Three: the one that failed. On Monday 9 March 2026 Shiuli tested a single-tap repeat-purchase button on revenue per session, baseline ₹96.60, with τ set at ₹8.00. At the end of day two, 15,000 sessions per arm, Λ was 27.3 against the threshold of 20, with an always-valid interval of ₹0.22 to ₹12.59 around a ₹6.40 lift. The team shipped on 11 March and briefed a full-rollout forecast of ₹6.40 × 2.28 crore sessions = ₹14.59 crore a month. Little arrived. The unchecked input was the variance: the standard deviation over those two days was ₹175.00, but over eighteen months of history it is ₹412.00 — 2.35-fold, understating the variance 5.54-fold, because high-value buyers arrive later in a week. Recomputing that look with ₹412.00 gives Vn = 22.63, Λ = 1.00 and an interval of −₹8.59 to +₹21.39. The variant was live 40 days; a 300,000-per-arm holdout then put the effect at +₹0.90, fixed 95 per cent interval ±₹2.08. The recovery was a variance floor from history, winsorisation at the 99th percentile on revenue metrics, and no monitoring before 25,000 sessions per arm.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Two numbers on one card. Early sign: a p-value beside a sequential verdict. Diagnostic: which did we agree to act on? Caught late, every decision becomes a negotiation over framing.

Plug-in variance from an early window. Early sign: a variance frozen at the first look. Diagnostic: plot the running standard deviation — is it flat? Caught late, this is the ₹14.59 crore forecast above.

Sequential monitoring covering an under-powered test. Early sign: no stated maximum information. Diagnostic: what is the maximum n, and the power there? Caught late, a year of inconclusive tests gets read as a year of null results.

τ set from hope. Early sign: the mixture scale exceeds every effect the team has shipped. Diagnostic: name the last three shipped effects. Caught late, a permanent widening of every interval that nobody attributes to it.

Stopping only for success. Early sign: no futility boundary. Diagnostic: what result makes us ship nothing? Caught late, the cost is every zero-effect test run to the horizon.

Quoting the stopped estimate. Early sign: the deck's number equals the number at the stopping look. Diagnostic: what does the post-launch holdout say? Caught late, forecasts overshoot and the programme loses finance's trust.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Group-sequential or always-valid? The group-sequential case rests on Figure 1: for a genuinely fixed horizon, O'Brien–Fleming at five looks costs 2.6 per cent in maximum sample size and lands its final boundary at 2.040, barely above 1.96, where the mixture boundary at the same horizon is 3.33 — intervals 63 per cent wider. The always-valid case is that horizons are not really fixed, so a guarantee conditional on a schedule nobody honours is worth nothing. Each side is wrong if the other's premise holds: group-sequential if stopping times are data-dependent, always-valid if they are not.

Does optional stopping matter at all? The Bayesian position is that the likelihood principle makes the stopping rule irrelevant to the posterior, so no correction is needed — correct as stated. The counter is that the decision rule — ship when the posterior probability of benefit exceeds 0.95 — has a frequentist error rate depending on the stopping rule and the prior, and under a diffuse prior that rate approaches the right-hand column of Exhibit 1. The Bayesian is wrong only if the prior is not really the organisation's belief.

Is peeking even the problem? The strongest sceptical position is that reversed launches are caused overwhelmingly by broken randomisation, metric redefinition, multiple variants and segment fishing, so an always-valid monitor optimises a second-order term while the first-order terms go unaudited. It would be wrong for any firm whose own audit put peeking as the proximate cause — and almost no firm has run that audit.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this talks in information rather than days, and names a maximum before the first look. They can say which inflation axis a method protects, and will not accept a sequential monitor as an answer to a multiple-metrics problem. They install futility boundaries and refuse to put a stopped estimate into a forecast. Above all they ask what the variance process is doing before what the boundary is, since that input voids everything else.

12. Decisions, and questions for discussion

Kamilya kept SH-412 running to its 32-day horizon with daily looks and added a futility boundary, reasoning that extra looks cost no validity under Shiuli's rule and that the median crossing point for the effect the team cared about was 120,000 per arm. Kotal abandoned the sequential design at Shilabati, authorising Kuila's winsorised metric and a single analysis at eight weeks.

  1. Shiuli's monitor spends 0.0272 of its 0.05 budget at 240 looks. What would you change to spend the remainder, and what would you give up?
  2. Shilabati's ceiling of 1,000 follows from an intra-account correlation of 0.62. What design change would lower it, and at what cost to what is being measured?
  3. Suppose the March test had used an 18-month variance floor and still crossed, at 25,000 sessions per arm. Which of the four schools in section 2 would call that launch correct?

13. Going deeper

  • Significance, power, sample size, peeking — the machinery this page corrects; without it Exhibit 1 is a curiosity.
  • Experiment pitfalls — places peeking among the other inflation axes.
  • Writing an experiment hypothesis — a stated minimum effect sets τ and the maximum information.
  • A/B testing fundamentals — randomisation, exposure and unit of analysis, which bind before any boundary.
  • When you can't A/B test — the Shilabati case in general form, and what to do when information is capped.
  • Experimentation culture — whether a declared stopping rule survives a launch deadline, which decides section 10.
  • Qual + quant feedback loop — where hypotheses worth a whole horizon come from.
  • Feature flags and flighting — what makes early stopping actionable, and claim two true or false at your firm.
exp20v2-exp.sequential:
Sequential Testing and Always-Valid Inference

Can you look at the test every day without lying to yourself?

1. A dashboard that refreshes every morning

On Monday 7 September 2026, Chiradeep Joddar, head of growth analytics at Raahgir, a Kolkata grocery and meal-delivery app with 1.8 million monthly users, approved a test plan he suspected would not survive the week. Chinmoyee Jamader, a product manager, had built a progress bar for the cart showing how far the shopper stood from free delivery. Half of 2,500 eligible users a day would see the bar; half would see the old cart. The outcome was conversion: the share of eligible users who ordered in their first session, currently 10.0 per cent.

His sample-size calculation called for 15,000 users per arm, twelve days, ending Friday 18 September. The vice-president of product wanted the bar live before the October festival peak, and the experiment dashboard refreshed a p-value each morning. Chiradeep knew the risk. A false win would commit fourteen engineers for six weeks to a feature that did nothing, pushing a payments-retry fix past the festival. A missed win would cost the festival itself. The question was whether anyone could look daily without fooling themselves.

2. The idea

Begin with the ordinary test. A p-value is the probability of seeing a gap at least as large as the observed one if the change truly does nothing. A team sets a significance level of 5 per cent, meaning it accepts a 5 per cent chance of declaring a winner when nothing is there (a false positive). That promise holds only if the sample size is fixed in advance and the result is read once. This is the fixed-horizon test.

Peeking breaks the promise. Each look is another chance for noise alone to cross the line, and a team that stops at the first crossing converts a 5 per cent error rate into something much larger. Peter Armitage and colleagues quantified this in 1969: four equally spaced looks, each at the usual 5 per cent threshold, produce a false-positive rate near 12.6 per cent, roughly one in eight.

Sequential testing is the family of designs that prices the looking in advance. Abraham Wald developed the sequential probability ratio test during the Second World War for inspecting munitions, publishing in 1945. Stuart Pocock (1977), Peter O’Brien and Thomas Fleming (1979), and Gordon Lan and David DeMets (1983) built the clinical-trial versions with planned looks. Always-valid inference, developed for web experiments around 2015 by Ramesh Johari and colleagues, goes further: its p-values and intervals stay valid at every moment, however the stopping decision is made. Chiradeep’s sentence for the meeting was: you may look as often as you like, provided the bar you apply was priced for the looking.

3. How it actually works

Every version follows the same steps. First, fix the significance level, the power, and the smallest effect worth detecting. Power is the probability of catching a real effect of that size; here, 80 per cent for a one-point lift. These give a starting maximum sample, as in a fixed-horizon test. Second, write down the looks: how many, and when. Third, choose a rule for the evidence required at each look. Fourth, at each look compute a z-statistic: the observed gap divided by its standard error, so that a value near 2 means the gap is about two standard errors from zero. Fifth, compare it with that look’s bar and stop only if it is crossed.

The steps practitioners leave implicit matter as much. The stopping rule must be written before launch, because a rule invented after seeing data is a peek in disguise. Users must be counted once, in the arm where they were first assigned. The arms must also hold the split promised, since a lopsided split signals broken assignment, and no boundary repairs that.

Two families differ in step three. Group sequential designs, such as Pocock’s, spend the 5 per cent error budget across a fixed number of looks. Pocock demands the same bar at every look; O’Brien–Fleming demands a very high bar early and nearly the ordinary one at the end. Always-valid methods instead track a running likelihood ratio, the factor by which the data favour “an effect exists” over “nothing is happening”. If nothing is happening, the ratio cannot drift upward for long, and a 1939 inequality by Jean Ville says it reaches 20 with probability at most 1 in 20.

4. A worked example, line by line

Chiradeep planned four looks at 3,750 users per arm each: the end of day 3, 6, 9 and 12. Planned size: 2 × 0.105 × 0.895 × (1.96 + 0.84)² ÷ 0.01² ≈ 14,735 per arm, rounded to 15,000, which also absorbs the roughly 2 per cent a four-look O’Brien–Fleming design adds. He chose O’Brien–Fleming for four looks, whose constant is 2.024: the bar at look k is 2.024 × √(4 ÷ k), giving 4.05, 2.86, 2.34 and 2.02.

z uses the pooled rate and an equal split.

Take look 2. Control converts at 750 ÷ 7,500 = 10.0 per cent and treatment at 825 ÷ 7,500 = 11.0 per cent. The pooled rate is 1,575 ÷ 15,000 = 0.105, so the standard error of the gap is √(0.105 × 0.895 × 2 ÷ 7,500) = 0.00501 and z = 0.010 ÷ 0.00501 = 2.00. A fixed-horizon reader would celebrate a p-value of about 0.046. The sequential reader sees that 2.00 is below the bar of 2.86 and keeps going.

Figure 1 shows why the bar matters. At looks 2 and 3 the black line sits just above the naive bar of 1.96, so the dashboard would have invited a launch, yet the final reading of 1.71 corresponds to a p-value near 0.09. Pocock’s constant bar of 2.36 is also unmet. Pocock spends more of the error budget early, so its final bar is 2.36 rather than 2.02.

Now the always-valid version, run beside it. Let the running likelihood ratio Λ average over effects spread around zero with a standard deviation τ of one point (0.01). With θ the observed gap and V its squared standard error, Λ = √(V ÷ (V + τ²)) × exp(τ²θ² ÷ (2V(V + τ²))). At look 2, V = 0.00501² = 2.506 × 10−5 and τ² = 1 × 10−4: the first factor is √0.2004 = 0.448, the exponent is 1.595, and Λ = 0.448 × 4.93 = 2.21. The test stops when Λ reaches 1 ÷ 0.05 = 20. The always-valid p-value is 1 ÷ the largest Λ so far, capped at 1.

Across the four looks the largest Λ is 2.21, so the always-valid p-value is 1 ÷ 2.21 = 0.45: far from 0.05, though the naive p-value at look 2 was 0.046. That gap is the price of valid peeking at any moment.

Change one input. Suppose look 2 had shown 870 treatment orders (11.6 per cent). Then z = 3.16, above the bar of 2.86, and Λ = 23.8, above 20: both methods stop legitimately. Narrow τ to 0.002 instead, and Λ falls to 1.82 on that 870-order data. The mixture width is a bet about effect size, and a bet placed too small is slow to pay.

5. Nuances a learner must absorb

Looking is not the sin; acting is.

Reading a dashboard changes nothing about the data. Harm arrives when a decision, such as stopping, shipping or extending, depends on an unpriced look.

Planned looks versus any looks.

Group sequential bars are tighter, but need a schedule fixed in advance. Always-valid methods permit unplanned looks and extensions at the cost of a larger average sample.

Early stops exaggerate.

A test that stops because noise helped the gap is, on average, reporting a gap larger than the truth. Expect the later measured lift to shrink, and report adjusted intervals, not raw ones.

Stopping early cannot repair the design.

Raahgir’s twelve days contained one weekend, a compromise Chiradeep recorded, because ordering behaviour differs by weekday and novelty fades.

Efficiency is on average, not guaranteed.

Sequential designs save sample when the effect is large and stop early. When the effect is zero they usually run to the maximum, and that maximum is a little larger than the fixed-horizon sample.

Confused with “Bayesian tests can be peeked at freely”.

A posterior probability is a statement about belief. If a team stops whenever it exceeds 95 per cent, the long-run false-positive rate of that decision rule can still exceed 5 per cent. The rule needs evaluating, not the label.

Time is not the only multiplicity.

Sequential methods control repeated looks at one metric. They do nothing for six metrics, three variants or twenty segments examined at once; each needs its own correction.

What it cannot tell you.

It cannot say whether conversion was the right metric, whether the lift is worth the engineering, or whether the groups were comparable. Ask before relying: what is the stopping rule, what is the maximum sample, and was the assignment ratio checked?

6. How it differs by product and by stage

Table 2. Where the idea bends
SettingWhat changes
ConsumerTraffic is abundant, so tests end in days; the danger is weekday and novelty effects, not sample size.
B2BFew accounts and slow cycles; a fixed sample may never arrive, so sequential rules help, though many tests end undecided.
MarketplaceBuyers and sellers share inventory, so arms interfere; sequential rules fix looking, not contamination.
Early-stage companyLittle traffic; only very large effects clear a high early bar, so many tests run to their maximum.
Large companyPlatforms ship always-valid defaults for thousands of tests, yet the multiplicity across tests remains.

7. Common mistakes

Resetting the clock. Symptom: tests run a few more days and end in wins at a suspicious rate. Misunderstanding: that extending is harmless. Diagnostic: compare each test’s planned and actual end dates in the log.

Reporting the raw lift at a stop. Symptom: launched features deliver half the promised gain. Misunderstanding: that a crossed bar certifies the size. Diagnostic: compare early-stopped tests’ promised lift with post-launch holdouts.

Treating the tool as a licence to skip planning. Symptom: experiments end at 800 users. Misunderstanding: that a valid p-value implies enough evidence. Diagnostic: ask for the maximum sample and the minimum effect before launch.

8. What good looks like

Handled well, Chiradeep’s test begins with a one-page note giving the metric, four looks, the O’Brien–Fleming bars, a minimum run covering a weekend, and the sentence “nothing ships on a look unless a bar is crossed.” On Saturday 12 September the vice-president asks about the 0.046; the answer is on the page, and nobody argues.

9. The decision, and what to learn next

On Friday 18 September Chiradeep reported z = 1.71 against a bar of 2.02. The lift was 0.6 points with an O’Brien–Fleming-adjusted interval of roughly −0.1 to +1.3 points (0.006 ± 2.024 × 0.00351). It excluded neither no effect nor a gain above the one-point target. He recommended against shipping on this evidence and against extending the test, which would have reset the clock. Instead he proposed a new test, after the festival, with a larger sample and an always-valid dashboard so that Chinmoyee could watch daily. Waiting forfeited the festival peak, but a false win would cost fourteen engineers six weeks.

Next, study how effect-size estimates are corrected after early stopping, and then variance reduction, which shortens tests more safely than any bar.

Two questions to sit with. If your team looks daily today, how many of its past winners would have survived a priced bar? And what decision in your organisation is currently triggered by a number no one has priced?
exp40v2-exp.platform:
Experimentation Platforms

What the software automates, and what no software can

1. Two decisions, eighteen days apart

On Monday 30 March 2026, Yuktika Gorai, vice-president of product at Morpankh, a Pune company whose vernacular audio-streaming app had 7.4 million weekly listeners, opened the readout for test HR-114, which had replaced the home screen with a “continue listening” rail over the four weeks to Sunday 29 March. Listeners who saw the rail streamed 2.4 minutes more per week, a gap the platform placed 8.66 standard errors from zero; the dashboard's revenue widget made that ₹1.02 crore a year. The next release train left on Monday 20 April, and nobody disputed the result.

Yuktika disputed what it was worth. Three weeks earlier the annual holdout had been read for the first time: a randomly chosen one per cent of listeners, 74,000 people, held out from every change shipped since Monday 7 April 2025. The 46 changes in that window had been measured, one at a time, as worth 12.0 extra minutes per listener per week between them. Against the holdout, the other 7,326,000 listeners were 4.0 minutes ahead. The platform had run 340 tests that year, flawlessly, and could not say why the arithmetic did not close.

In Bengaluru that same month, Yajur Gooptu, director of product at Mitrava Systems, had a report due on Friday 17 April. Mitrava sold enterprise workflow software to 412 paying accounts for ₹74 crore of annual recurring revenue, of which the largest 25 supplied ₹44.4 crore, or 60 per cent. The board had asked him to choose between building a platform — ₹1.4 crore of capital expenditure and ₹38 lakh a year to run, per a design document from his engineering lead, Yoginder Gantait — and licensing the vendor Morpankh used, at ₹62 lakh a year. Yeshasvi Golui, Mitrava's analyst, had sent a one-page memo arguing that both bought the same thing, and that the thing was unusable at Mitrava's scale.

2. The idea, and the four camps inside it

An experimentation platform holds the variants of a product as configuration, assigns users at random, records who was actually shown what, computes pre-agreed outcome measures per arm with their uncertainty, and refuses the result when its own integrity checks fail. The statistical content is old: Ronald Fisher formalised randomised field trials at Rothamsted in the 1920s, the Neyman–Pearson apparatus of power and error rates followed, and clinical trials and direct-mail split tests industrialised both long before the web. What the web added was not a method but a rate, so the binding constraint became consistency rather than ingenuity. Microsoft's internal platform, described by Ron Kohavi and colleagues in their 2020 book on trustworthy online controlled experiments, and Amazon's Weblab were built because tests were easy to start and easy to run badly. Commercial products followed from 2010, warehouse-native tools in the 2020s, language-model evaluation harnesses after that.

Four camps disagree about what the platform is for. For the trustworthiness camp the product is the refusal: it signs “a readout from a platform with no sample-ratio check is not evidence” and will not sign “more tests is better.” For the velocity camp it is cost per decision: it signs “tests per engineer per quarter is the number to manage” and will not sign “every test needs a reviewed pre-registration.” The causal-inference camp holds the default two-sample comparison to be the least interesting part, because interference, long-run effects and heterogeneity need designs no template covers; it signs “the platform's p-value is an input, not a verdict” and will not sign “a platform result generalises to the population.” The decision-theoretic camp wants the output to be an expected loss: it signs “a result at p = 0.2 with an asymmetric payoff should ship” and will not sign “95 per cent is a decision rule.” Nobody holds all four, and the choice shows up in what the platform may block.

3. Mechanics, including the steps left implicit

The pipeline has six automated stages and five human ones; the seam between them is where command of this topic lives (Figure 1).

Stage A holds both home screens as named configurations behind a feature flag. Stage B joins the listener's identifier to a salt unique to the experiment, hashes it, and takes the remainder modulo 1,000: 0–499 to control, 500–999 to treatment. The salt is the implicit step: because it differs per experiment, membership of one test says nothing about membership of another, which is what makes concurrent tests legitimate. Stage C logs an exposure when the listener reaches the changed surface. Morpankh held 750,000 listeners in the layer, a shade over ten per cent of the weekly base, and 480,000 of the 750,000 assigned were exposed, 64 per cent. Analysing all 750,000 would have diluted the 2.4-minute effect to 2.4 × 0.64 = 1.54 minutes — not a worse estimate of the same thing but an estimate of the effect of offering the rail, rather than of the rail on those who met it.

Stage D earns the licence fee. Its sample-ratio check compares arm sizes against the intended split: Morpankh's 480,000 exposures split 241,300 and 238,700 against 240,000 expected in each. The chi-square statistic is the sum over arms of (observed − expected)² / expected, here 1,300² / 240,000 twice: 7.04 + 7.04 = 14.08 on one degree of freedom, a probability below 0.001. A 0.54 per cent imbalance looks cosmetic and is not: assignment and logging disagree about who was in the test, and an estimate over a population you cannot enumerate has no usable standard error. Yuktika's platform had flagged HR-114 amber here; an engineer had marked it “known: SDK retry on cold start.”

Stage E computes the metric per arm, stage F the interval (Exhibit 1). The second-order mechanic worth knowing is variance reduction: if a listener's pre-period minutes correlate with in-test minutes at ρ = 0.60, regressing out the pre-period leaves a residual standard deviation of 96.0 × √(1 − 0.60²) = 76.8 minutes, and the same standard error of 0.277 minutes is reached with 153,600 listeners an arm instead of 240,000 — 36 per cent less sample. The effect did not change; only the interval around it.

The standard error of the difference is √(96.0²/241,300 + 96.0²/238,700) = 0.277 minutes, so 2.4 minutes is 8.66 standard errors from zero; the 95 per cent interval is 1.86 to 2.94 minutes, 1.45 to 2.30 per cent of the 128.0 control mean. Section 3 says why that split voids this estimate until the flag clears.

4. The conditions, as testable claims

Four conditions decide whether a platform can answer a question. Each is a claim about the world, not the software.

One: the randomisation unit can be isolated. Morpankh passes on the listener side and fails on the creator side: minutes moved to the rail come out of other listening, and a creator's plays depend on what other listeners saw. Mitrava fails at the seat level, because one administrator configures the workflow every seat in that account sees. Two: the minimum detectable effect at the available sample is smaller than the effect worth acting on. At 80 per cent power and a two-sided five per cent test, the MDE is about 2.8 × SD × √(2/n) per arm, the 2.8 being 1.96 + 0.84. Mitrava's account-level utilisation — monthly active seats over licensed seats — averages 0.46 with a standard deviation of 0.21 across accounts (Figure 2).

Mitrava's top 25 accounts carry change-control clauses forbidding un-notified interface variants, so the randomisable population is 387 accounts holding ₹29.6 crore of the ₹74 crore, 40 per cent. At 193 accounts an arm the MDE is 2.8 × 0.21 × √(2/193) = 5.99 points of utilisation, 13 per cent of the 46.0 base. Yajur's team had hoped to move utilisation by three points; at this variance no platform detects three points on 193 accounts. Three: the outcome is observable within the window you can hold the variant. Morpankh sees minutes in a week and cannot see a year of retention in four, which is the quantity the rail was meant to move. Four: the decision is reversible at roughly the cost of the test. Where it is not — a pricing change, a migration, a regulated disclosure — the cheap-iteration logic inverts: the option value of one more test is small against the cost of the first.

5. Edge cases, and what the seams do

In a multi-product company the platform's layer system makes different teams' tests orthogonal by construction. That removes confounding and hides interaction: if the rail helps only listeners who also got a redesigned search, orthogonal layers guarantee nobody sees it. Two-sided markets break unit isolation outright; the repair is to randomise clusters — cities, time slices, supply cohorts — which costs one to two orders of magnitude of effective sample, and a platform offering only user-level assignment will let a team run the invalid design. Regulated surfaces are the clearest limit: consent and purpose limitation under India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, SEBI and RBI disclosure rules and CDSCO change control for medical software constrain who may be randomised into what, and the platform enforces none of it. Hardware-plus-software products cannot flag firmware per user; they ship staged over-the-air cohorts: assignment by device batch, rollback in days, no clean within-period comparison. AI-native products add non-determinism: the same prompt returns different outputs, so a variant is a distribution rather than a screen, offline evaluation sets substitute for power, and cost and latency become guardrails. At the organisational seams the pathology is ownership: when the platform team owns both tooling and verdict, its objective becomes tests run; when finance owns the money conversion and product owns the metric, nobody owns the rate between them. Mature companies handle this with a named metric owner and a standing holdout. They say they pre-register every test; in fact they pre-register the primary metric and argue about the rest.

6. Eight things that separate an expert

Significance is not value. The platform's interval is on the metric; the exchange rate into money is an assumption nobody randomised. The tell is a readout with four p-values and no rupee figure, or one built on the weekly-active base. The obvious reading, that a tight interval means a solid business case, ignores the two steps after it.

Assignment is not exposure. The platform will analyse either, and vendor defaults differ. The tell is arm sizes exactly equal to the traffic allocation: real counts are smaller and differ between arms for a reason somebody should state. The obvious reading, that counting everyone is conservative, is wrong in a specific way: it shrinks the effect while leaving the interval respectable.

Sample-ratio mismatch is the one alarm worth waking up for. Most platform warnings are noise theatre; this one voids the estimate rather than shifting it. The tell is a chi-square beside the ratio with a comment explaining it away. The obvious reading treats a half-per-cent imbalance as rounding; an expert reads it as evidence that the analysed population is not the randomised one.

Variance reduction buys precision, never effect size. The tell is whether a pre-period covariate is stored at all; teams that cannot answer have not thought about power. A team that “got significance after switching on CUPED” has learned nothing about the size of the effect, only that its earlier interval was wider. The obvious reading confuses the estimate with its error bar.

The sum of wins is not the value of the year. Selecting on significance biases the shipped set upward, so adding shipped deltas double-counts noise and ignores interaction. The tell is an annual impact number built by summing test results. The obvious reading is that excluding losers makes it conservative; excluding losers is what creates the bias, and only a holdout measures the residue.

Layers are an organisational artefact. The tell is who may create one: where layers are self-serve, interaction effects are invisible by policy. Orthogonality does not make interactions absent, only unobserved, and the standard answer — that they average out across arms — is true for the estimate and false for the decision, which is whether to ship both.

The metric dictionary is the real product. The tell is two dashboards disagreeing about “active listener” while both cite the platform. The obvious reading calls this a data-quality bug. It is a governance hole, and worse than a bug, because the platform computes a confident interval off either definition — and the definition is where the argument is.

A platform raises throughput and lowers value per test at once. The tell is test count rising while the holdout gap stays flat. The obvious reading is that the programme has stalled. The truer reading is that cheap tests get spent on smaller questions, which is correct; the error is managing volume as value, which is how a team arrives at 340 tests and 4.0 minutes.

7. Where this differs by product and by stage

In consumer products traffic is abundant and effects are tiny, so the hard problems are the long run and the exchange rate into money. In B2B and enterprise the sample is the constraint: account-level randomisation with a crossover or switchback design, instrumented design-partner panels, interrupted time series — and the platform contributes flagging and safe rollout rather than inference. Platforms and marketplaces are the interference case and belong to cluster designs. In hardware the unit is a device cohort and rollback is slow, so the platform's gift is staged exposure, not statistics. In AI products its new job is versioning prompts, models and retrieval configurations as variants, with offline evaluation as the cheap screen.

By stage, less changes than people claim: the MDE formula does not care about a funding round. What changes is the input. Pre-product-market-fit, n is too small for anything but qualitative work and a platform is a distraction; in growth, traffic arrives and it pays for itself within a quarter; at scale the constraint moves to governing metrics. The real stage difference is the cost of being wrong — a reversible mistake at 50,000 users is a learning expense, and the same mistake at 7.4 million is a revenue event.

8. Three worked examples

(a) Morpankh's rail: the same effect, three valuations

Morpankh monetises at ₹11 per 1,000 streamed minutes. Annualised on the whole weekly base, 2.4 minutes × 7,400,000 listeners × 52 weeks is 923.5 million minutes, worth ₹101.6 lakh — the dashboard's ₹1.02 crore. But the effect was measured on exposed listeners, and only 64 per cent of those assigned reached the rail, so the defensible base is 7,400,000 × 0.64 = 4,736,000 and the figure is ₹65.0 lakh. Apply the holdout's ratio of realised to measured gains, one third — both sides of it already per listener, so it discounts persistence and not exposure twice — and it is ₹21.7 lakh (Figure 3). The test was impeccable; its value fell 79 per cent from the first base to the third.

(b) Mitrava's pilot, and the cost of a decision

Mitrava had already run one account-level test, on an onboarding checklist, across its 387 randomisable accounts split 193 and 194 for ten weeks. Utilisation came in 2.1 points higher in treatment. The standard error is 0.21 × √(1/193 + 1/194) = 2.13 points, so it sits 0.98 standard errors from zero, with a 95 per cent interval from −2.08 to +6.28 points. The team read it as encouraging. It could not have told the hoped-for three points from nothing. Exhibit 2 prices what each company gets.

(c) The failure: a year of wins that did not arrive

Morpankh's holdout is the approach failing while every individual test stayed valid. Four causes separate cleanly. Novelty: a rail is new once. Non-additivity: two changes competing for the same attention cannot both keep their gain. Displacement: minutes moved between surfaces were counted as created where they landed. Selection: shipping on significance over-states, so 46 wins averaging 0.26 restated minutes each delivered an average of 0.09. The recovery was not statistical: Morpankh made the holdout permanent and per-surface, required one named primary metric before launch, and computed every annualised rupee figure on the exposed base, discounted by the holdout ratio.

9. Failure modes and their early signs

  • Overridden integrity checks. Early sign: an amber flag with an engineer's explanatory comment. Diagnostic: what is the realised ratio, and its chi-square? Caught late, every decision in that layer is void.
  • Metric proliferation. Early sign: sixty metrics on a results page and three in the write-up. Diagnostic: which single metric was named in writing before launch? Caught late, nobody can tell a win from a search.
  • Peeking and early stops. Early sign: median realised duration below planned duration. Diagnostic: plot actual against planned duration. Caught late, the shipped set is inflated and the holdout gap is the bill.
  • Annualising on the wrong base. Early sign: a business case whose denominator is the weekly-active number. Diagnostic: what was the exposure rate? Caught late, a roadmap is prioritised on figures 56 per cent too high.
  • Ownership drift. Early sign: the platform team's objective is tests run. Diagnostic: who may veto a ship, and on what evidence? Caught late, it publishes results nobody is accountable for.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The velocity position at its strongest: the dominant error in product organisations is not a bad test but an untested opinion, and throughput is the only lever that reliably changes the ratio. Its evidence is that programmes cutting cost per test tenfold ship more measured wins per quarter. It would be wrong if marginal tests had near-zero expected value and Morpankh's one-third realisation were general. The trustworthiness position at its strongest: a wrong result is more expensive than no result, because it survives for years; its evidence is how regularly real logs show assignment imbalance. It would be wrong if bad results were self-correcting, which the 12.0-against-4.0 reconciliation suggests they are not. The decision-theoretic position holds that a 95 per cent threshold throws away cheap, positive-expected-value ships; it rests on payoff asymmetry, and would be wrong if priors were unknowable or gameable. Underneath sits an unsettled question: whether any platform can measure long-run value, or only a holdout can — and a holdout is 74,000 people deliberately kept on a worse product, a cost no camp has priced.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this asks whether the result is significant. Someone who has internalised it asks three questions first: what the denominator was and when it was measured, whether the arm contained only the thing being credited, and what the holdout says about the last twenty decisions of this shape. They treat the platform as a cost-reduction device for reversible decisions, irrelevant to the rest, and can name which of their metrics has two definitions. They also stop tests they proposed.

12. The decisions, and three questions

Yuktika reopened the amber ratio flag first, since a voided layer makes the question moot, then shipped the rail on 20 April and rewrote the business case to ₹65.0 lakh, with a stated holdout discount to ₹21.7 lakh. Her reasoning: with the split cleared, a 1.9 per cent effect measured at 8.66 standard errors is almost certainly positive, the change is cheap and reversible, and the thing worth fixing is not the test but the ₹101.6 lakh habit. Yajur recommended neither option. He proposed the vendor's flag-and-rollout tier at ₹19 lakh a year, ₹57 lakh over three years against ₹186 lakh of licence for the full platform, and spent ₹60 lakh on two instrumented design-partner panels and a switchback capability. Mitrava's constraint was 387 accounts, not software.

Three questions. First: Morpankh's holdout cost 74,000 listeners a year of improvements; at what programme size does that stop being worth paying, and what would you measure to find out? Second: Yajur gives up on randomised estimates for 60 per cent of Mitrava's revenue — what would you accept instead, and what would make you refuse it? Third: if the exchange rate from minutes to rupees is an assumption, who should own it, and what happens when they disagree with the team that proposed the test?

13. Going deeper

  • Feature flags and flighting — the substrate stage A sits on; without clean flags, assignment and exposure never separate.
  • Writing an experiment hypothesis — the discipline that fixes the single primary metric these failure modes return to.
  • A/B testing fundamentals — the estimator the platform automates; knowing it by hand catches the wrong population.
  • Significance, power, sample size, peeking — the MDE arithmetic that decided Mitrava's case before any vendor.
  • When you can't A/B test — switchbacks, synthetic control, interrupted time series: the menu Yajur bought instead of a platform.
  • Experimentation culture — who may stop a test, and who owns the metric dictionary.
  • Qual + quant feedback loop — the only route to why an effect decayed.
exp20v2-exp.platform:
Experimentation Platforms

What the software automates, and what it cannot

1. The renewal

On Monday 5 January 2026, Vidushi Ershad, head of product at Lumora Commerce, a Kolkata home-goods marketplace app, opened the renewal papers for an experimentation platform the company had trialled since October. The price was ₹60 lakh for twelve months, with a signature due by Friday 16 January. Lumora's finance lead had asked a fair question: what does the software do that two analysts and a spreadsheet did not? Those analysts handled about eleven tests a quarter, at roughly 18 hours of analysis each.

Vidushi had reason to distrust the spreadsheet. In August 2025 Lumora shipped a redesigned checkout after a test its team read as a six per cent lift in orders per user. Vamshi Eusuf, the lead analyst, later found that the two arms had been compared over different days, one including a weekend sale. The lift never reached the monthly revenue line.

The trial had also disappointed her. The dashboard had put a green tick beside a banner test that nobody could explain. She faced two ways to be wrong: pay for arithmetic Lumora could do itself, or keep trusting numbers that had already misled it. She needed to know where automation ended and judgement began.

2. The idea

An experimentation platform is software that runs randomised controlled experiments on a live product and reports their results under shared rules. In a randomised controlled experiment, often called an A/B test, users are split by chance into a control group, who see the current product, and a treatment group, who see a change. An outcome measure is then compared between the groups. Because chance alone decided who saw what, a difference larger than chance can produce is attributed to the change.

The method is older than the software. Ronald Fisher formalised randomised field trials at the Rothamsted agricultural station in the 1920s. Web companies industrialised the method in the 2000s, and Ron Kohavi and colleagues, whose 2020 book on trustworthy online experiments is a standard reference, describe how Microsoft built a platform so that many teams could test without each reinventing the statistics. Commercial products such as Optimizely followed from 2010. The problem they solved was not that tests were hard to start. It was that tests were easy to run badly.

The sentence Vidushi settled on for the finance meeting was this: the platform makes every test cheap and consistent to run, but it cannot make a test worth running or say what the result means.

3. How it actually works

Take the test Vamshi proposed during the trial: a one-tap button for returning customers paying through UPI, India's bank-to-bank instant payment network, against the existing three-screen flow. The platform automates five steps, and three human steps surround them (Figure 1).

Step A is a feature flag, a switch in code that shows a variant to chosen users; it lets the platform hold both checkout flows as named configurations rather than separate software builds. Step B is assignment. The platform joins the user's ID to a string unique to the experiment, hashes the result into a number from 0 to 999, and sends 0 to 499 to control and 500 to 999 to treatment. The same user always lands in the same bucket, and because every experiment uses a different string, membership in one test says nothing about membership in another.

Step C, exposure logging, is one practitioners leave implicit. The platform records an event when the user actually reaches the changed screen, and analysis counts only those users; counting everyone assigned dilutes the effect with people who never saw it. Step D, health checks, runs before anyone looks at outcomes. Step E is analysis: the metric per user, the difference between arms, its standard error and a confidence interval. Steps 1 to 3 remain Vidushi's team's.

Two more implicit duties belong to the platform. It reserves traffic in layers, groups of experiments allowed to share users only by explicit rule, so that two tests on the same screen do not contaminate each other. And it can fix the analysis window to whole weeks, because shoppers behave differently on a Saturday than on a Tuesday; a test covering one Saturday and two Tuesdays measures the calendar as much as the change.

4. A worked example

Lumora ran the test for two weeks. Each week 40,000 distinct returning UPI customers reached checkout, each counted once, so 80,000 entered the test and 40,000 went to each arm. The primary metric was orders per exposed user, which with one possible order is the conversion rate (Table 1).

Table 1. Checkout test, two weeks. Conversion = orders divided by users in the arm.

The standard error of a difference between two proportions is the square root of the sum of each arm's p(1-p)/n. Control gives 0.05 x 0.95 / 40,000 = 0.0000011875; treatment gives 0.054 x 0.946 / 40,000 = 0.0000012771. Their sum, 0.0000024646, has a square root of 0.00157, or 0.157 points. Dividing the 0.40-point gap by 0.157 gives a z-score of 2.55: the gap sits 2.55 standard errors from zero. The 95 per cent confidence interval, 0.40 plus or minus 1.96 x 0.157, runs from 0.09 to 0.71 points.

In money: 40,000 users a week is 2,080,000 a year. At an average order of ₹1,150, the 0.40-point lift is 8,320 extra orders, or ₹95.7 lakh of order value a year. The interval spans ₹22.1 lakh to ₹169.3 lakh. This is order value, not profit.

Now change one input: traffic. Suppose the team had looked after the first 20,000 users, about half a week in, and seen identical rates: 500 orders from 10,000 control users and 540 from 10,000 treatment users. The two variances become 0.0000047500 and 0.0000051084, summing to 0.0000098584, whose root is 0.00314, or 0.314 points. Quartering the data doubled the error (Table 2, Figure 2).

The interval for B contains zero, and also contains a gain of a full point. Same product, same rates; only the quantity of evidence changed. A platform that prints "+8% relative" in green does not show this difference unless someone insists on the interval.

5. Nuances a learner must absorb

The platform decides nothing

It computes an interval; it does not choose the primary metric, the minimum gain worth shipping, or the duration. A metric chosen after the results are visible is one of many that could have been chosen, which is why the decision rule must be written first.

The randomisation unit must match the analysis unit

If users are assigned but sessions are counted, a user with twelve visits contributes twelve linked rows and the interval comes out too narrow. Ask what unit the platform randomised and what unit the standard error treats as independent.

A mismatched split means stop

If 80,000 users were planned 50/50 and 40,900 arrived in one arm and 39,100 in the other, each is 900 from the expected 40,000. The chi-square statistic is 900 x 900 / 40,000 = 20.25 per arm, 40.5 in total, far beyond the 3.84 that marks the 5 per cent line. Something in assignment or logging is broken, and no outcome from that test can be trusted.

Looking early is not free

Table 2 hints at why. A team reading the checkout test on day three would have seen no result, and on day fourteen a clear one; neither look is wrong alone. The trouble begins when a team looks daily and ships on the first day the interval clears zero, because repeated looks at a fixed-horizon interval give chance many chances to cross the line. Platforms offer sequential methods that permit continuous monitoring, but they pay for it with wider intervals at any given moment.

More metrics, more false alarms

Track 20 independent metrics on a change that does nothing, test each at 5 per cent, and you expect 20 x 0.05 = 1 false flag. A dashboard that reports every metric is a machine for producing one green tick per experiment.

What it cannot tell you

The platform reports that the button raised conversion, not why. It cannot say whether a two-week gain survives novelty wearing off, whether it turns into profit, or whether the test was the best use of the fortnight of traffic. Those remain arguments, which data informs.

6. Consumer, B2B, marketplace; small and large

In consumer products traffic is abundant and the platform's value is volume and consistency. In B2B, a company with 200 customer accounts cannot randomise across thousands of users who share a contract; the unit becomes the account, power collapses, and teams rely on staged rollouts and qualitative evidence. In marketplaces, buyers and sellers draw on the same inventory, so treating some buyers differently changes what control buyers can buy. The groups interfere, and teams randomise by city or by time slot instead.

Size matters as much. To have an 80 per cent chance of detecting a true 0.40-point gain on a 5 per cent base, a test needs roughly 48,400 users per arm. A startup with 2,000 checkout users a week would need over 48 weeks, so flags and analytics serve it better than a platform. A large company needs the opposite: governance, a shared metric catalogue and rules for tests running at once.

7. Common mistakes

Treating a green dashboard as a decision. The symptom is wins that never reach the revenue line, as with August's checkout. The misunderstanding is that platform output is the decision rather than evidence for it. The cheapest diagnostic: ask for the decision rule, written before launch, and the health-check status of that test.

Stopping when the result turns significant. The symptom is tests ending on odd days and effects that shrink when repeated. The misunderstanding is that the interval stays valid however often it is read. Compare planned duration with actual duration.

Celebrating secondary metrics. The symptom is announcements of wins on a metric nobody named in advance. Count how many metrics were registered, and which one was primary.

Never validating the platform. The symptom is trust with no evidence of calibration. Run an A/A test, in which both arms see the same product, about 20 times; roughly one should flag a difference, and many more means the machinery is miscounting.

8. What good looks like

A well-handled version of the August checkout test would have begun with a one-page rule: ship the redesign if the lower end of the 95 per cent interval for conversion is above zero and payment failures rise by less than 0.3 points. It would have run two whole weeks, so each weekday appeared twice. The platform would have confirmed an even split before anyone read results. The review would have opened with the interval, then the money range, then one named owner for what happens next.

9. The decision

Vidushi signed the renewal on Thursday 15 January, a day early, with conditions. Each test would carry a written decision rule and a named owner, and the health checks would be reviewed before any outcome. She did not justify the ₹60 lakh by any single lift. She justified it by consistency: forty-four tests a year at about 18 analyst hours each is 792 hours of spreadsheet work that now becomes a review, and the ticks would be backed by checks Lumora could not reliably run by hand.

To go further, learn power and minimum detectable effect, which tell you what a test can see before it starts, then guardrail metrics, which stop a win on one measure from hiding a loss on another.

Two questions to sit with. Which of the five automated steps would you hand over last, and what would you need to see first? When the dashboard and the monthly revenue line disagree after a launch, which do you believe, and what would you check?
exp40v2-exp.velocity:
Experiment velocity and learning rate

Metrics, Analytics & Experimentation › Experimentation & Causal Inference

1. Two decisions, seven months apart

On Tuesday 6 October 2026, Gaurangi Mazumdar, vice-president of product at Velora — a consumer personal-finance app with 14.2 million monthly actives — had to sign a number. Velora's tested surface, its first-session deposit flow, takes in 120,000 new users a week: 1,560,000 in a thirteen-week quarter. Her platform could run six tests a quarter against that pool, or fifty-two. The previous October her predecessor had pushed past that range to fifty-eight, and that quarter was a near-total loss on the measurement that mattered. Her analyst, Gitimoni Mahanty, had just estimated what Velora's ideas were actually worth; it made the cadence question answerable, and it made the obvious answer wrong.

On Monday 9 March 2026, Gnanesh Mitter faced the same question with none of the material. Vaniya Systems sells distributor-management software to 1,180 paying accounts carrying 38,000 weekly active seats — a mean of 32.2 seats per account, though the twenty largest hold 34 per cent of the seats, 646 on average, while the other 1,160 hold 21.6. His board wanted to know whether to fund three engineers for two quarters on an A/B platform. His principal engineer, Gandharv Mukharji, had already found the awkward arithmetic: randomising accounts, Vaniya can detect a 41.0 per cent change in seats per account and nothing smaller. The platform would work perfectly and measure almost nothing.

Both decisions turn on the relation between how fast a team tests and how fast it learns — two quantities routinely assumed to be one, which come apart.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

Define experiment velocity as the number of decision-grade comparisons a team completes per unit time — completed, not launched, which is the first place the measure leaks. Define learning rate as the rate at which beliefs about the opportunity space improve: not the lift shipped but the sharpening of the estimate of which changes are worth trying. A losing test adds nothing to the first and much to the second — if someone wrote down what it ruled out.

The history predates the web. Fisher's factorial designs (1935) made concurrency respectable; George Box's evolutionary operation (1957) is the closer ancestor, arguing that a plant should run as a permanent sequence of small deliberate perturbations during production, because cheap small moves yield more information than a few large ones. Stefan Thomke made the cost curve explicit: as the marginal cost of a trial falls, the optimal number rises and the optimal quality of each falls. The web took that cost near zero, Microsoft, Booking.com and Netflix industrialised it, and the literature collapsed it into a slogan.

Four schools differ, and the test is what each will and will not sign. The throughput school signs: a programme running ten tests a quarter should reach fifty before it optimises any single test's design, but not that throughput should rise ahead of readout trustworthiness — Kohavi's work on trustworthy measurement is the main brake on naive velocity. The decision-value school, from Howard's value-of-information framing, signs: a test is worth running only if some result it could produce changes a decision, and will conclude a team should run fewer. The learning-stock school signs: a programme's output is its posterior, not its shipped lift. The craft school — Shape Up, most enterprise practice — signs: below a traffic threshold, A/B experimentation is theatre and judgement is cheaper, but not that experiments never pay at low volume, because switchbacks do.

3. Mechanics: the frontier, worked

Velocity is not free, and the price is power. If a quarter's pool is P users and you run T mutually exclusive tests, each gets P/T users and the minimum detectable effect scales as √T: doubling throughput costs 41 per cent on the MDE, not 100 per cent.

Velora has launched 416 tests since January 2024; 352 read out (84.6 per cent of those launched) and 240 carry a written entry in the results base (68.2 per cent of those that read out, 57.7 per cent of those launched). From those 240 Gitimoni fitted a shrunken distribution of true relative effects on activation, in six archetypes: of the 240, 6 ideas are worth +12.0 per cent, 18 worth +7.0, 48 worth +3.5, 96 nothing, 48 worth −4.0 and 24 worth −9.0 — 2.5, 7.5, 20.0, 40.0, 20.0 and 10.0 per cent. The mean idea is worth −0.175 per cent: the pipeline destroys slightly more value than it creates.

Exhibit 1 combines the halves at the Q3 2026 activation baseline of 11.5 per cent, two equal arms, 80 per cent power, two-sided 5 per cent, so MDE = 2.8 × √(2 × 0.115 × 0.885 / n) per arm. Velocity comes from concurrency, not shorter tests: every cadence holds a test between two and 2.6 weeks and varies the slot count. The pool is gross of the holdout.

4. When the frontier applies, and when it misleads

The frontier rests on four testable claims. One: the traffic pool binds. For Velora in 2025 it looked true and was false — section 12 shows the binding constraint was reading capacity; for Vaniya it is plainly false. Two: tests do not interact. Mutually exclusive allocation buys it, at the cost of eight slots at thirty thousand users each rather than eight overlapping at full pool. Three: the effect distribution is stable. Gitimoni's 240 entries span eleven quarters and two redesigns. Four: shipped lifts add. Both columns assume it; few who have run a global holdout believe it.

The frontier actively misleads in low-traffic, high-concentration settings — Vaniya's case, where the smallest viable test is already too small. It misleads where the decision is irreversible, pricing information while ignoring option value; and where the outcome lag is long, because a cadence computed on traffic rather than feedback latency prescribes a velocity the measurement cannot support.

5. Hard edge cases and organisational seams

Exhibit 1's lever is sample size; the stronger lever is the unit of randomisation. With 590 accounts per arm and a seat standard deviation of 81, MDE = 2.8 × 81 × √(2/590) = 13.20 seats, 41.0 per cent of the 32.2-seat mean. Adjusting each account for its pre-period value (CUPED) at a correlation of 0.78 cuts the standard deviation by √(1 − 0.78²) = 0.626 — a 37.4 per cent reduction in MDE, to 8.26 seats or 25.7 per cent relative, worth 2.55 times the sample. Still useless. The third option randomises days.

Vaniya's sync service completed a mean of 18,420 jobs a day under incumbent routing and 19,160 under the challenger, alternating daily across 84 days, 42 to each arm, with a day-level standard deviation of 1,340. The standard error of the difference is 1,340 × √(2/42) = 292.4, so the observed 740-job gap is 2.53 standard errors (two-sided p ≈ 0.011) and the MDE is 2.8 × 292.4 = 819 jobs, 4.44 per cent of the control mean. Alternation handles day-of-week effects but not serial correlation, and the standard error assumes independent days.

In two-sided marketplaces, user-level randomisation leaks through the clearing mechanism, so the honest unit is a region or budget split, which collapses the sample. In regulated lending, randomising a credit decision is unavailable, so velocity comes from pre-registered champion–challenger models with an auditable log. Firmware cannot re-randomise a cohort that has taken an update, so the release train sets the learning rate. AI-native products substitute offline evaluation suites, where re-running is free and staleness binds instead: Velora's 900-item retrieval suite showed a +6.1-point gain for one change and +1.8 points on a held-out 300-item set — a 0.30 ratio, the winner's curse as benchmark overfitting.

The organisational seam is worse than any statistic. In a multi-product company two teams test one surface, and exclusive allocation makes slots scarce. Mature companies say they arbitrate on expected value; what they do is give each team a fixed quota, so the quota, not the frontier, sets the cadence.

6. Eight nuances that separate the expert

Velocity measured at launch is not velocity. Velora launched 416 and read out 352. The tell is a dashboard counting starts; the obvious reading, that 64 tests were dropped for good reasons, is usually wrong, because abandonment correlates with inconvenient early readings.

Concurrency is not throughput. Eight overlapping tests on one surface are one eight-factor design nobody analysed as one. The tell is a sample-size column summing past the pool. Interactions are rare in magnitude and common in direction, so they bias the sum of lifts upward.

The square root cuts both ways. Because MDE scales as √T, throughput is nearly free where the effect distribution is sparse and ruinous where it is dense; the tell is a cadence argument with no estimate of it. Thirteen to twenty-six tests cost Velora nothing; twenty-six to fifty-two cost 5.85 points.

Win rate is endogenous. A team can lift its win rate to 60 per cent by testing only near-certainties. The tell is win rate rising while the mean absolute effect size falls; the obvious reading, that the pipeline improved, is the one the metric is built to produce.

Summed claimed lifts are not a quantity. They sum selected, noisy, differently-based estimates. The aggregate that survives audit is a holdout, costing 5 per cent of the pool and 2.6 per cent on every MDE, since 1/√0.95 = 1.026.

A loss is learning only if it was falsifiable in advance. The tell is a brief with a hypothesis and no decision rule — no statement of what result causes what action. Such tests cannot lose, only be reinterpreted; the finding sits in the brief.

Idea supply usually binds before test slots do. The tell is queue length falling while slot utilisation rises, which reads as efficiency and is starvation: a programme with an empty queue tests whatever is nearest, whose quality is the unconditional mean — −0.175 per cent.

Multiplicity grows with velocity. Twenty-six tests read across eight segments is 208 comparisons: if all were null, 208 × 0.05 = 10.4 spurious segment findings a quarter; at Velora's 40.0 per cent null share, 4.16. The obvious reading is that segment findings are bonus yield; the tell is a results base whose segment claims outnumber its headlines.

7. Across product types and stages

Consumer products at scale are the case Exhibit 1 describes, and most published methodology comes from them. Business and enterprise products differ in kind: the unit is the account, the sample is in the hundreds, and the ceiling is switchback-eligible server-side changes plus a design-partner panel. Platforms and marketplaces are constrained by interference rather than sample size, so velocity depends on how finely they cut non-interfering clusters. Hardware is bounded by a release cycle no platform shortens.

Where the difference is asserted and is not real: AI products. The inner loop moves to offline evaluation and the velocity figures become spectacular, but the constraint merely moves — to label supply and suite freshness — and the winner's curse arrives unchanged. By stage the honest statement is narrow. Seed-stage companies lack both the sample and small enough decisions. Growth stage is where the frontier bites hardest, because traffic has arrived and process has not. At large scale the constraint shifts to reading capacity.

Claimed lifts are each measured on the winning test's own primary metric, not on activation. Realised lift = (shipped-cohort rate − holdout rate) ÷ holdout rate: 0.50 ÷ 11.40 = 4.39 per cent, 0.53 ÷ 11.50 = 4.61 per cent. Ratio = realised ÷ claimed. Every relative MDE here uses the Q3 2026 baseline of 11.5 per cent; at Q4 2025's 11.40 per cent they would be about 0.5 per cent higher.

Q4 2025 ran 58 tests on 1,482,000 users, 25,550 each, an MDE of 9.72 per cent and so a standard error of 3.47 points, at which only the +12.0 per cent archetype is resolvable. The team read results daily — about twenty looks a test — which at a nominal two-sided 5 per cent threshold takes the effective one-sided false-positive rate to roughly 13 per cent and drops the declaration floor to 1.126 × 3.47 = 3.91 per cent observed. The model then predicts a 23.1 per cent declaration rate — 10.1 winners of 44 against 9 observed, 0.41 of a standard error of 2.79 — of which 44 × 0.40 × 0.13 = 2.3 were nulls.

The gap is not mainly the winner's curse. The nine were judged on their own primary metric among the users who reached the step changed; the 3.47-point standard error above is activation-scale, illustrating selection rather than reading those nine. Claimed lifts sum to 40.5 per cent on those primary metrics, and the mean reach share across the nine was 0.34, translating 40.5 to 13.77 points on activation. Shrinkage of τ²/(τ² + σ²) = 20.99/(20.99 + 12.05) = 0.635, with τ = 4.58 the archetype distribution's standard deviation, takes 13.77 to 8.75. The holdout measured 4.39: wrong base 26.7 of the 36.1-point discrepancy, shrinkage 5.0, and 4.4 points Velora cannot decompose.

The recovery is instructive for what it did not achieve. Q2 2026 cut to 26 tests, replaced daily peeking with a fixed horizon, and made a results-base entry a shipping condition. Documentation rose from 19 of 44 read-out tests to 24 of 24, 4.64 standard errors on a pooled 63.2 per cent, and briefs citing a prior entry from 3 of 58 to 11 of 26 — 5.2 to 42.3 per cent — 4.22 standard errors apart on a pooled 16.7 per cent. Those two moves are large against their own noise; the lift figures are not. Realised lift moved from 4.39 to 4.61 per cent, 0.22 points against standard errors near 1.03 each — 0.15 standard deviations — and the ratio from 0.11 to 0.17, 1.31. Gunamoy Mohanta, who runs the platform, read the win rate rising from 9 of 44 to 6 of 24 — 20.5 to 25.0 per cent — as evidence the pipeline had improved; on a pooled 22.1 per cent that is 0.43 errors.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Velocity theatre. Throughput rises, readout quality falls. Early sign: the share of launches that read out drops. Diagnostic: what fraction of last quarter's launches produced a decision? Caught late, a year of planning rests on claimed lifts.

The undocumented loss. Early sign: entries per read-out test below one. Diagnostic: name the last three tests that lost and what we now believe because of them. Caught late, two teams test one question.

Peeking. Early sign: durations clustering below the planned horizon. Diagnostic: how many looks did we take, and what is our effective alpha? Velora's daily looks took 2.5 per cent one-sided to roughly 13 and added about 1.8 null winners in a quarter.

Reading-capacity starvation. Early sign: a readout queue rather than a launch queue. Diagnostic: how many analyst-hours does a readout cost, and how many have we got? Velora found this last, when its readout standard rose from 4 hours to 11, and it decided the question.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Bar rule versus power rule. The bar school holds that banking a win the test had 19 per cent power to detect — the +3.5 per cent archetype at fifty-two tests — is indistinguishable from shipping on taste while generating an audit trail; its evidence is holdouts like Velora's, where Q4 2025's declared wins realised 11 per cent of claimed value. The power school holds that the bar rule discards real expected value to buy comfort, and Exhibit 1's dashed column is its evidence: 38.10 against 21.45. For the bar school to be wrong, shipped lifts would have to add approximately, so small positive expectations accumulate. For the power school to be wrong, a quarter's variance would have to matter as much as its mean.

Is win rate a property of the pipeline or of the test design? Velora's exhibit cannot separate them: the observed rate moved from 20.5 to 25.0 per cent while the MDE fell from 9.72 to 6.51 per cent and the effective one-sided alpha from 13 to 2.5 per cent, all at once. Either reading claims a decomposition of a 0.43-standard-error gap.

Are losses learning or waste? The learning-stock case is quantitative: the standard error on Velora's estimate of the +7.0 per cent archetype's 7.5 per cent share is √(0.075 × 0.925/240) = 1.70 points; a year at 26 tests a quarter adds 104 observations and takes it to 1.42, a 16.5 per cent reduction, and a year at 52 reaches 1.24, a 26.8 per cent reduction — a real return to velocity the bar-rule column cannot see, realised only if every test is documented. Velora documented 68.2 per cent.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this asks for more tests. Someone who has internalised it asks first what the effect distribution looks like, because without it no cadence can be defended; second, which constraint binds, because it is usually not traffic; and third, what a readout costs. The behavioural signature is a willingness to reduce throughput. The second is treating the results base as the programme's product, not its paperwork — the response to a loss is to ask what it rules out and check somebody wrote it down. The third is declining to aggregate claimed lifts.

12. The decisions

Discussion questions

  1. Exhibit 1's bar-rule maximum sits at twenty-six tests a quarter. What would have to be true of Velora's effect distribution for a cadence above twenty-six to be better, and which of section 4's four claims does your answer depend on?
  2. Gnanesh buys a harness that measures days rather than a platform that measures accounts. Which questions has he made unanswerable, and what would he have to observe to call the trade wrong?
  3. Velora's documentation rose to 24 of 24 while realised lift did not measurably move. Under what theory of learning rate is that quarter a success, and what evidence would distinguish it from self-congratulation?

Gaurangi signed twenty tests for Q4 2026, not twenty-six, for the reason Exhibit 1 omits. Readout cost has been rising: Q4 2025's forty-four averaged 4 analyst-hours, Q2 2026's twenty-four 9.5 — 228 hours against the 228.8 protected — and a readout to the holdout-era standard, with a pre-registered decision rule and a written entry, costs 11. Gitimoni has 1.1 full-time equivalents, 572 hours a quarter, 40 per cent of it protected: 228.8 hours, or 20.8 readouts at 11. Twenty tests at 74,100 users each give an MDE of 5.71 per cent, still inside the empty band between +3.5 and +7.0 per cent, so the holdout costs nothing in detectable share and the bar-rule yield is 16.50 against the frontier's 21.45. She leaves 4.95 points, 23.1 per cent of the maximum, for want of analyst hours — and funded what moves it: templated readouts and automated pulls, which at 7 hours a readout would support 32.7.

Gnanesh's answer was one page. Vaniya will not build an A/B platform. It will run switchbacks on server-side changes, hold a panel of eight design-partner accounts with written kill criteria, and keep an entry per readout. His argument: Vaniya's learning rate had never been limited by its test count, and a platform would raise the count while leaving the rate where it was.
