Experiment Velocity and Learning Rate

A case-style explainer for product managers

A target of sixty

On Monday 5 October 2026, Ekanksha Lalung, head of growth at Tamralipta Fresh, a Kolkata grocery-delivery app, opened a quarterly review with a number she had not chosen. Eshanya Lohar, the chief executive, wanted sixty experiments concluded in the October-to-December quarter, up from forty in the quarter just closed. The board would see the figure.

Lalung had the July-to-September ledger open. The team had launched 48 tests, concluded 40 and written up 14. In August it had also re-run a free-delivery-threshold test that lost in November 2025 and was never recorded; the repeat consumed three weeks of the checkout screen, where tests ran one at a time.

If she accepted sixty, the cheapest tests would multiply and the ledger would improve while the company learned no faster. If she refused, she risked looking like the person resisting the discipline the chief executive wanted. The question was which number deserved to be measured.

Lohar's reasoning was not foolish. She had watched competitors announce testing programmes and had read that the strongest product companies treat tempo as an asset. What she lacked was a way to tell tempo that compounds from tempo that merely accumulates.

The idea

Experiment velocity is the number of experiments brought to a recorded decision in a period. It counts conclusions, not launches. Learning rate is the number of decision-grade results the organisation gains in the same period, where a result is decision-grade only if it was written down well enough for someone else to find and use. Between them sits a third quantity, yield: the share of concluded tests that become such results.

A distinction follows at once. A test that is run, lost and forgotten counts toward velocity and contributes nothing to learning rate, and a test documented from a sample too small to mean anything contributes little more. The two measures therefore audit each other, which is the reason to keep both.

The idea answers an old failure. Product teams measured on features shipped were never asked what they had learned, and shipped confidently on intuition. Web companies in the 2000s, among them Amazon, Google and Microsoft, built platforms for controlled experiments; Ronny Kohavi, who led such work at Amazon and Microsoft, became its best-known chronicler. In the early 2010s growth teams, with Sean Ellis a leading voice, made testing tempo a managed number. Tempo alone, however, can be satisfied by trivial tests.

The sentence Lalung could repeat without sounding glib: velocity tells us how many questions we asked; learning rate tells us how many we can now answer.

How it works

The mechanism is a loop of six steps, shown below. First, the team writes a hypothesis and a decision rule before launch: what result ships the change, what kills it, what triggers a repeat. Second, it sizes the test. The minimum detectable effect (MDE), the smallest change worth acting on, is chosen from business value, then converted into a sample using the baseline rate. Practitioners often leave this step implicit and let traffic choose the MDE by default.

Third, the test runs for a fixed, whole number of weeks, since shoppers behave differently on weekdays and weekends. Fourth, the team applies the rule, flat results included. Fifth, someone records hypothesis, result with its interval, a guess at the mechanism, the decision and searchable tags. Sixth, and most often skipped, the next hypothesis begins with a search of that record.

Each step has a failure that is cheap to prevent and expensive to discover. Without a decision rule written beforehand, a flat result is reinterpreted afterwards as a near-win, and the team ships what it already wanted to ship. Without sizing, the run length is whatever the most impatient stakeholder will tolerate. Without a record, the loss is lost twice.

A worked example

Take the checkout screen. Its baseline order rate is 4.0 per cent and 120,000 eligible shoppers arrive each week. A usable rule of thumb, for 80 per cent power and a 5 per cent false-positive rate, is that each arm needs about 16 × p(1−p) ÷ d² shoppers, where p is the baseline rate and d the absolute change to be detected. For d = 0.4 percentage points, that is 16 × 0.0384 ÷ 0.000016 = 38,400 per arm.

This is the first pass. In the second, one input changes: the team insists on detecting 0.2 points. The sample rises fourfold, because it varies with the inverse square of the effect, to 307,200 shoppers, 2.56 weeks, rounded to three. Only four tests fit. Halving the target effect cost a third of the screen's velocity, because each halving quadruples the shoppers required.

At sixty tests and the same 35 per cent yield, learning rate is 60 × 0.35 = 21 results. Hold velocity at forty and lift yield to 65 per cent, and it is 40 × 0.65 = 26. The slower programme out-learns the faster one, because a cheap lever was the write-up, not the launch.

Nuances that separate users from understanders

Concluded is not launched

A test stopped early, abandoned or left running without a decision adds to launches but not to velocity. Tamralipta's eight such tests, the difference between 48 and 40, consumed build effort and traffic and returned no decision.

A loss is information already paid for

Published accounts from large web firms put the share of ideas that improve the target metric somewhere between about one in ten and one in three. Most tests therefore lose or come out flat. A programme that records only wins discards most of what it paid for, and a loss that explains why shoppers behaved as they did is often worth more than a win nobody understands.

Traffic and run rules set the ceiling

Once traffic needs more than the minimum run, velocity falls as the sample rises; below that, the run rule binds. A team can raise velocity by accepting larger effects, adding parallel surfaces, finding more traffic or shortening the minimum run.

Smaller means smaller scope

“Run more, smaller tests” means narrower changes, cheaper to build, not smaller samples. Cutting the sample below what the MDE requires produces flat results that look like evidence of no effect. A flat result from an underpowered test says only that the test was too blunt to see.

Overlap and interference

Two tests on the same shoppers can interact, and in a marketplace a change for buyers can shift what sellers see. Parallel tests raise velocity only if their effects do not contaminate each other, so the platform must say which tests may share users.

Velocity is not value

The measure cannot say whether the tests address problems worth solving. Sixty experiments on button colour would score higher than ten on pricing. When a count becomes a target, people supply the count. Velocity is a necessary check on tempo, never a measure of whether the programme is working on the right things.

Questions before relying on it

What is the denominator: launched or concluded? Who reads the record, and when? How many tests this quarter repeated an earlier one? A newcomer who cannot get these answers has a number, not a measure.

Consumer, B2B, marketplace; small and large

The loop is constant; the binding constraint moves. In a consumer app such as Tamralipta's, traffic is plentiful and the constraint is the number of surfaces. In B2B, few accounts mean controlled tests rarely reach adequate samples, so learning comes from staged rollouts and structured sales-call evidence. In a marketplace, interference dominates: a change that helps buyers may shift demand away from sellers who were not in the test, so the unit of randomisation becomes a region or a time slice, and runs lengthen.

Size matters as much. A start-up with 5,000 weekly shoppers needs 76,800 for the 0.4-point test, more than fifteen weeks, so it should test only large changes. A large company has the opposite problem: tests are cheap, and the failure is forgetting. Hundreds of teams can run the same sensible idea in ignorance of one another, and only a shared, searchable record prevents it.

Common mistakes

Four errors recur. Each can be seen from outside the team before the team admits it, and each has a diagnostic that takes less than a day.

The four share a root: each mistakes a proxy for the thing it was meant to track. Launches stand in for decisions, wins for knowledge, speed for sensitivity and a document for a memory.

What good looks like

A well-run programme reports two figures side by side: tests concluded and results written up. Every launch carries a decision rule. Every loss gets a mechanism guess, however tentative. Nobody proposes a test without a search of the record first. When a test loses, the review asks what shoppers were trying to do that the change obstructed, and the answer is filed where the next team will find it. The board sees a chart of results gained, not tests started.

The decision

Lalung did not simply refuse sixty; she reframed it. She proposed that Tamralipta hold concluded tests at forty, raise the written-up share from 35 to 65 per cent, and report both. That yields 26 results against the 14 of Q3 and the 21 that sixty tests would give at the old yield. The cost was 12 extra write-ups at about two hours each, 24 hours of analyst time, and a rule that no test launches without a search of the record. She would tell Lohar that sixty launches would be easy to deliver and hard to defend, whereas 26 findings could be shown to anyone who asked what the company now knew.

Her reasoning was that the board's number should track what the company knows. To learn next, she should take the growth experimentation process, which turns this loop into a weekly operating rhythm, and the statistics of power and sequential testing.

Two questions to sit with. Which of your last quarter's losses could a colleague find today, and what did one repeat cost? And at what count would a velocity target begin to change the ideas your team is willing to propose?
